It has been revealed that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

It has been revealed that A lot of noise was made about the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, but there's a handful of other premium machines running Nvidia's new RTX Spark chips. Lenovo's Pro 9n follows Microsoft's lead, making a fancy laptop with its own touches, like an OLED panel and a stylus that works on the touchpad.

This is also our first time looking at the 18-core version of the RTX Spark, which has fewer CUDA cores than the last one we tested, so we'll see just what kind of changes in performance you get if you don't opt for a higher-end configuration.

The Lenovo Pro 9n is clearly a tool. It's a dark gray box with a Lenovo logo and a slight extrusion to fit Lenovo's signature anti-notch for the camera. The lid is flat, with a rounded keyboard deck, like many of Lenovo's premium Yoga laptops. It's a playful look that's less noticeable when the system is matte black rather than colorful.

The keyboard deck, including a massive touchpad, is logo-free other than an Nvidia RTX Spark sticker, which keeps all of your attention on the backlit keyboard and 15.3-inch OLED screen.

There are plenty of ports, and I appreciate that both sides of the laptop have both USB Type-C and Type-A. The left side also has HDMI and a 3.5 mm headphone jack, while the right side includes an SD card slot and an e-shutter for the webcam.

At 13.66 x 9.53 x 0.66 inches, this isn't a small system, but it's still one you can reasonably fit in your backpack. It's wider and deeper than the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra (12.95 x 9.40 x 0.75 inches) but it's also thinner. Apple's new 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is a tad sleeker at 0.63 inches thick.

Recent findings suggest that the Pro 9n measured in at 3.64 pounds pounds, less than 4.41-pound Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra. The 16-inch MacBook Pro is a bit heavier than the Pro 9n at 4.1 pounds.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

5,120 CUDA cores, Blackwell-based.

15.3-inch, 2560 x 1600, OLED, touch, 165 Hz.

MediaTek Wi-Fi 7 MT7925, Bluetooth 5.4.

HDMI 2.1, 2s USB Type-A (10Gbps), 2x USB4 Type-C (40 Gbps), 3.5 mm headphone jack, SD card reader (UHS-II).

13.66 x 9.53 x 0.66 inches / 347 mm x 242 mm x 16.7 mm.

It has been revealed that the Lenovo Pro 9n features the lesser variant of the RTX Spark N1X, and this is our first look at a system with that config. This version has an 18-core CPU, down from the 20-core version we saw with the Surface Laptop Ultra. It also has 32GB of RAM and 1TB of storage.

On Geekbench 6, the Pro 9n came in slightly behind the Surface Laptop in both single-core and multi-core performance (given how heavy the Surface Laptop is, some of this could come down to cooling). The MacBook Pro with M5 Max won out, while the Asus ZenBook A16 with Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme beat both RTX Sparks.

In a recent development, the Pro 9n copied 25GB of files at a rate of 1,205.37 MBps. That's not terrible, but in the ultra-premium price band, you can get faster speeds. Every other laptop beat the Pro 9n here.

On Handbrake, the Pro 9n transcoded a 4K video to 1080p in 2 minutes and 1 second, or 7 seconds behind the Surface Pro with the 20-core CPU. The Pro 9n beat the Snapdragon-powered Zenbook here.

We use Cinebench 2026 to stress test laptops, running a multi-core benchmark ten times in a row. The Pro 9n stayed largely consistent — in fact, it even got better later on, as the cooling kicked into high gear. The system started with a score of 6,219.85, and topped out on run 6 at 6,417.45. Most of the runs were in the high 6,300s. The RTX Spark's Cortex-A725 cores ran at an average of 2.81 GHz, while the Cortex-X925 cores averaged 3.57 GHz.

It's worth noting that HWinfo, which we used for monitoring, was missing a single A725 core. This also happened on the Surface Laptop Ultra, though now we can tell which cores are which.

The Lenovo Pro 9n we reviewed came with the entry-level version of Nvidia's RTX Spark, which has an 18-core CPU and 5,120 CUDA cores. It can be upgraded to a 20-core / 6,144 CUDA core chip in some configurations, which is the same chip we saw in the Surface Laptop Ultra.

To test the difference in AI performance, we ran AgentPerf-Local using Qwen 3.8-27B-UD_IQ3_XXS in order to fit in the limited available GPU memory (both are 32GB systems, with the Surface allowing 24GB of allocated graphics memory and the Pro 9n accepting just 16GB). The benchmark simulates running conversations by playing back conversations, with a majority of the work involving processing prompts rather than generating tokens.

The difference between the two RTX Spark systems wasn't particularly significant here. The Surface Laptop Ultra completed the benchmark in 1,148.3 seconds, while the Pro 9n took 1,196.6 seconds. That's a 4.12% difference in favor of the higher-end Spark.

Recent findings suggest that beyond the difference in CPU cores, the version of RTX Spark in the Pro 9n we tested has 5,120 CUDA cores, down from 6,144 in the more powerful version in the Surface Laptop Ultra. (The beefier chip is also available in other configurations of the Pro 9n).

In a recent development, on 3DMark Steel Nomad, the Pro 9n earned a score of 2,796, falling behind the Laptop Ultra (4,355) and the MacBook Pro (3,865). It's still a more powerful system than the Zenbook with Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme (1,262).

Recent findings suggest that in gaming, the RTX Spark isn't really meant for much above 1080p (perhaps 1440p, depending on the game). So in the case of our benchmarks, the difference in CUDA cores didn't have a stark difference, with nearly identical scores on Shadow of the Tomb Raider and Cyberpunk 2077. Far Cry 6, which is more CPU-focused, ran better on the 20-core RTX Spark.

When I played 007: First Light, with the game at 1920 x 1200 and settings on medium, and DLSS set to ultra performance, the game ran just over 30 frames per second. With DLSS on "dynamic," the game ran smoother, between 40 and 72 frames per second as Bond moved through a swanky hotel, though there was some jankiness to it. The game also took a long time to load, possibly due to Windows' Prism emulation.

The 15.3-inch OLED touchscreen on the Pro 9n is quite nice. The 165 Hz panel is vivid and bright enough for most uses.

The trailer for Artificial showed off the colors and blacks, as the trailer descends from lush greens outside of Sam Altman's home to a dark tunnel, until he arrives in a bunker with blue lights that all but jumped off the screen.

Lenovo's OLED panel was the most vivid of our test group on our colorimeter, covering 198% of the sRGB color space by volume, significantly higher than the rest of the field, though it often appeared oversaturated. In fact, it arrivees out of the box on its default wallpaper with severe pops of green and white. The MacBook Pro's PROLED XDR display has lower numbers on the colorimeter, but looks far more natural than what Lenovo is offering here.

At 440.6 nits of brightness, the Pro 9n's display is good, but the MacBook Pro has it beat at 529.5 nits, while the Surface Laptop Pro reached an astounding 944 nits in our testing.

Sources indicate that lenovo's keyboard feels great. There's 1.5 mm of key travel, and you can feel it. It's deep, but punchy. The keycaps can be a bit slippery, though I typed at 106 words per minute on the monkeytype typing test, albeit with 2% less accuracy than usual.

It has been revealed that the haptic touchpad is huge, smooth, and responsive. Oddly enough, despite being haptic, there is a noticeable depression when you click down, especially at the bottom edge. It's an odd feeling when you notice it, especially when you can still configure how hard you have to press in Windows to register a click.

Lenovo includes a stylus in the box for use with the touch screen, which is good for signing documents. The pen, however, does not work on the touchscreen, which is an odd choice. The Yoga Pen Gen 2 (typically sold for $63 with a case that isn't included here) can attach magnetically to the Pro 9n's lid and charges over USB Type-C, so you can use the same charger as the laptop. It supports up to 8,192 points of pressure sensitivity with AES3.0, or up to 4,096 points on other protocols.

Lenovo's combination of two tweeters and two woofers does a decent job. They get nice and loud, easily filling a mid-sized office room with Justice's "Flower In A Hurricane.".

Recent findings suggest that the song's guitars and synths sounded excellent, as did SZA and Kevin Parker's voices. The drum beat was a bit low, but going into the Dolby Settings app, switching to the "Warm" music setting with boosted lows helped there.

There are 9 screws holding the bottom of the Lenovo Pro 9n on. The four closest to the hinge are longer than the remaining five, so be sure to keep them organized. You'll need a pry tool to remove the latches and release the base.

In a recent development, inside, there's not a ton to repair or replace down the line for the average person. The 92.5 WHr battery is held in place with a few screws. You can also easily access the included M.2 2242 SSD, and there's a second bay for another drive of the same length. I would always prefer a more standard 2280 drive, but if this is what lets Lenovo fit two drives on the board (or at least give you the option to add a second drive), I'll take it.

The Wi-Fi card is soldered to the board and partially obscured by the heatsink's thick heat pipes.

The Pro 9n ran for 10 hours and 30 minutes on average on our battery test, which browses the web, streams video from a server, and runs OpenGL tests with the screen set to 150 nits of brightness.

That's not too far off from other high-end Windows on Arm laptops, beating the Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme-based Zenbook A16 by 4 minutes, and it was 13 minutes behind the Surface Laptop Ultra with a more powerful version of N1X.

The MacBook Pro smoked them all though, running for 15 hours and 57 minutes on our test.

During our Cinebench stress test, we took skin temperature measurements to get an idea of how hot the Pro 9n gets during use.

Sources indicate that the center of the keyboard measured 98.5 degrees Fahrenheit, while the touchpad was 10 degrees cooler. The hottest point on the bottom of the laptop reached 101.5 F.

HWinfo hasn't been updated to be clear on which sensors are measuring what internally. We could make educated guesses, but we'll have more specifics when the software is updated.

According to recent reports, the 9.2-megapixel webcam on the Pro 9n should be more than enough for video calling in 4K, assuming your software supports it. While making calls, I found that the camera captured fine details, like graying hairs on the side of my temples (it's been a long month).

Recent findings suggest that the colors were a bit cool, however. I could do with more vibrancy and warmth to make it more realistic.

There’s just too much pre-loaded software on the Pro 9n. The most important app is Vantage, a catch-all app with your serial number, user guides, warranty status, a number of device settings, and access to support services. But it also houses a ton of ads.

The company also has direct links in the Start menu and taskbar to the Lenovo subscription portal to buy software. An additional user guide is also in the start menu. There's also Smart Connect, to pair and transfer files between your laptop, tablet, and phone, along with a dashboard to view them all. The company also has its stylus settings app and a link in the Start Menu to its Artificial Intelligence policy, which looks more like an internal document than something meant for consumers.

Lenovo also includes some bloatware, like trials of McAfee antivirus and a promotional trial of Dropbox.

Recent findings suggest that like other RTX Spark systems, the Pro 9n is running Windows on Arm. It's better than it's ever been, but there are still times when it feels laggy. More games and apps than before are compatible, but it's still not perfect.

Lenovo sells the Pro 9n with a 1-year warranty, which can be extended with additional coverage for more money.

We tested the Lenovo Pro 9n in a $3,249.99 configuration with an 18-core RTX Spark CPU and integrated GPU using 5,120 CUDA cores, 32GB of RAM, a 1TB PCIe Gen 4 SSD, and Windows 11 Pro.

The cheapest version, at $2,999.99, uses the same processor and RAM as our review unit, comes with Windows 11 Home, and has 512GB of RAM.

Bumping up to the higher-end 20-core, 6,144 CUDA-core GPU costs an extra $450 but also gets you 64GB of RAM and 1TB of storage as a base. Moving to 128GB of RAM is $1,400, while moving to a 2TB PCIe Gen 5 SSD is another $450.

The Lenovo Pro 9n is a minimalist, RTX Spark-based laptop with strong port selection and a lovely OLED screen. The keyboard has deep travel, and I don't mind a design that simply gets out of the way of your work.

According to recent reports, still, it's expensive, even with the base version of RTX Spark. Battery life is just past 10 hours, which I would like to see improve across the RTX Spark platform, and there aren't any AI features in Windows that make this chip special for anyone who isn't running local models.

If you are married to getting an RTX Spark machine, the Lenovo Pro 9n beats the Surface Laptop Ultra in three areas: It's lighter, has an OLED screen, and extra SSD slots (even if it is M.2 2242) for an upgrade down the line. Still, the Surface is a nicer, more premium design and has the fun, magnetic Surface Connect port.

Those who aren't running local models should probably be looking for a cheaper laptop. Those prioritizing battery life should consider a Mac. And those who like Windows on Arm can still consider Snapdragon X2, as Nvidia's entrance into this choppy sea should lift all ships.

高品質で多様なトレーニングデータなしに、日本文化を真に理解するAIを構築することはこれまでほぼ不可能でした。これを変えるため、NVIDIAは、日本の人口統計、地理的分布、文化的特性に沿ったペルソナを含む初のオープン合成データセット、Nemotron-Personas-Japan を公開しました。CC BY 4.0 ライセンスのもと提供される本データセットは、機微な個人データに依存することなく日本社会を反映した AI システム構築のための、プライバシー保護と規制対応を両立した基盤を提供します。.

NVIDIA のエンタープライズ向け合成データ生成システム、NeMo Data Designer を用いて作成されたNemotron-Personas-Japan は、すでに広く利用されている US Personas データセットの成功を機に日本版として開発されました。本リリースは、各国・地域におけるソブリン AI 開発を支援する合成ペルソナデータセットとデータ構築方法のグローバルコレクションの第一弾です。.

本データセットは、Nemotron モデルをはじめとするオープンソースの 大規模言語モデル(LLM) とシームレスに連携するよう設計されており、企業向けチャットボットから各種ドメインの AI エージェントに至るまで、日本語 AI アプリケーション向けのファインチューンを容易に行えるようになっています。.

NVIDIAの合成データ生成用マイクロサービスである NeMo Data Designer を用いて構築されています。この複合AIシステムは、複雑な Jinja テンプレート、Pydantic による検証、構造化出力、自動リトライ、および複数の生成バックエンドのサポートを可能にします。これらは、このような大規模な合成データセットの生成に必要なツール群です。さらに、以下のモデルも活用しています。.

Nemotron-Personas-Japan は、日本の公的な人口統計および労働統計に整合するよう設計されると同時に、AI トレーニングにおいて重要な以下の点を考慮して生成されました：.

このデータセットには、個人を特定できる情報（PII）は一切含まれていません。年齢、名前、職業などは公的な統計データの分布に基づいていますが、存命・故人問わず、実在の人物と結びつくことはありません。全てのペルソナは完全に人工的に生成されているため、実際の文化的パターンを保ちながらも、個人のプライバシーを損なうことなくトレーニングに利用できます。.

Nemotron-Personas-Japanは、日本のソブリン AI システムを開発する日本のモデル開発者向けに設計されています。現在、LLM開発者が使用する訓練データのほとんどは英語であり、日本やインドなど各地域の開発者は、母国語で高品質なデータを入手するのに苦労しています。.

本データセットを含め、NVIDIA の Nemotron-Personas の一連の取り組みは、こうした課題を直接解決するものです。地域固有のニュアンスを捉えつつ、開発者が地域固有の言語で多様かつ複雑なデータを生成できるようサポートします。データセットは国勢調査データ、日本人の命名規則、文化的特徴など地域のコンテキストに基づき、すべて母語で生成しています。.

そのため、日本で自分たちのモデルの採用を拡大し、日本の文化的コンテキストを理解したい すべての AI モデルの開発者の方々のお役に立てれば幸いです。.

本データセットに含まれる合成ペルソナを以下のようなことに活用できます：.

AI 開発には、実世界の人々を反映した多様で高品質な訓練データへのアクセスが長らく課題でした。企業向け AI の開発はプライベートデータが主流となっており、研究者、スタートアップ、そして特に利用可能なデータが少ない地域のAI開発者にとって障壁となっていました。.

Nemotron-Personas-Japan を CC BY 4.0 のもとで公開することで、企業レベルの高品質な合成データへのアクセスを可能とし、従来のコスト、プライバシーの懸念、地理的な制約といった障壁なしに、文化的背景を正確に反映した AI システムを誰でも構築できるようになりました。.

以下のコマンドで本データセットをダウンロードできます。日本文化と言語を真に理解する AIの開発にお役立てください。.

#126476. America’s next quantum breakthrough: The factory floor

America’s next quantum breakthrough: The factory floor

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, building a quantum computing firm has taught me something that wasn’t always obvious to me as a scientist.
  • It has been revealed that building a quantum computing organization has taught me something that wasn’t always obvious to me as a scientist.
  • For years, the prevailing wisdom in technology was to focus on what you do best and outsource the rest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, building a quantum computing firm has taught me something that wasn’t always obvious to me as a scientist. Developing a latest technology is one challenge. Figuring out how to manufacture it reliably, at scale, is another. And the second can be every bit as difficult as the first. For years, the prevailing wisdom in technology was to focus on what you do best and outsource the rest. It made good business sense. Building manufacturing capacity is expensive, complicated, and often far removed from the work that inspired someone to start a technology company in the first place. But that approach comes with a tradeoff. When you depend on someone else to manufacture your technology, you also depend on their capabilities, priorities, and timelines. For an emerging industry like quantum information, those dependencies can become significant obstacles. And I believe they have implications well beyond any one company. A LESSON WE’VE ALREADY LEARNED The United States has seen what happens when technological innovation and manufacturing become separated. American companies designed many of the advanced semiconductors powering today’s AI revolution, but much of the manufacturing capacity needed to produce them was developed overseas. That arrangement supported decades of innovation and economic growth. It also created dependencies that have become increasingly difficult to ignore. Now, the U.S. is investing heavily in rebuilding domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity. It’s a difficult and expensive undertaking, and one that will take years to fully realize. Quantum technologies give us an opportunity to think about these challenges earlier in an industry’s development. The U.S. has extraordinary strengths in quantum science. Our universities, national laboratories, and private companies have helped advance the field for decades. But the path from a scientific breakthrough to a useful product requires more than research. Much more. It requires specialized materials, fabrication processes, engineering expertise, and the ability to produce increasingly complex technologies consistently and economically. Those capabilities need to develop alongside science. WHY WE CHOSE TO BUILD I’ve experienced this challenge firsthand at Quantum Computing Inc. Our work in quantum photonics depends on highly specialized manufacturing processes. As we developed our technology, we had to think carefully about how much of our future we wanted to depend on outside manufacturing partners. For a growing company, investing in your own manufacturing capabilities is a consequential decision. It requires capital, specialized expertise, and a willingness to take on responsibilities that extend well beyond research and product development. We ultimately decided to build and acquire manufacturing capacity because we believe greater control over the critical and proprietary processes is essential to our long-term strategy. For other processes, we will leverage existing manufacturing capabilities and collaborate with industry partners to build a robust, reliable, and sustainable supply chain. We also see an opportunity to contribute to the broader ecosystem by making our manufacturing capabilities available to others. The quantum opportunity is far bigger than any one company. Advancing the industry will require collaboration and shared capabilities that benefit all of us. It’s time to work together to build that foundation and accelerate the growth of the quantum industry. NO ONE MANUFACTURING MODEL That decision has shaped how I think about innovation. When researchers and engineers have closer access to manufacturing, they can learn from what happens during fabrication and use that knowledge to improve the next design. Manufacturing becomes part of the development process itself. The experience gained along the way can be just as valuable as the equipment. There is no single manufacturing model that makes sense for every quantum company. Different technologies have different requirements, and outside foundries and specialized partners remain notable. But access to reliable manufacturing capacity can have a profound influence on how promptly an idea becomes something useful. BUILD AN INDUSTRY, NOT JUST A TECHNOLOGY Washington D.C. is beginning to recognize this challenge. A June executive order addressing quantum technology calls for strengthening domestic manufacturing capabilities and expanding partnerships between government and private industry. I welcome that attention. But building a manufacturing base requires more than funding announcements and policy commitments. It takes facilities, equipment, specialized talent, and years of experience developing processes that work consistently. It also requires demand from companies that are ready to move technologies out of the laboratory and into practical use. Other countries recognize the importance of these capabilities, with many having committed substantial resources to quantum technology. The United States has important advantages in research, entrepreneurship, and private investment. We should be building on those strengths now. That doesn’t mean every component needs to be manufactured domestically. International partnerships and global supply chains will continue to play important roles. But we should be deliberate about which capabilities are essential to our technological independence, making sure we have the capacity to develop and sustain them. FINAL THOUGHTS I’ve spent much of my career working to advance quantum technology. Like many scientists, I was initially drawn to the possibilities of what we could discover and what those discoveries make possible. Today, I spend just as much time thinking about what it takes to turn those possibilities into something people can use. That means manufacturing, supply chains, engineering, and all the difficult work that follows a breakthrough. The U.S. has an extraordinary foundation in quantum science. While proof of humanness taps into the film’s theme—bringing a sense of irony by making human art look artificial—not every observer is embracing the marketing trend. The official movie poster for Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s upcoming film about OpenAI, looks like AI slop, only it was drawn by human hands.

Industry observers note that anyone who has come across AI-generated images knows they often carry telltale mistakes. So when film studio Neon released the poster this week, owners on social media were quick to catch oddities in the illustration, leading some to suspect it was made using AI.

At first glance, the poster looks normal.

On a closer look, Andrew Garfield, who plays Sam Altman in the movie, doesn’t appear quite like himself, lingering somewhere in the uncanny valley. The background features San Francisco’s landscape, except the Golden Gate Bridge is underwater. The tree behind Garfield looks distorted, with a Pinocchio-like face surfacing from the trunk. The branches are no less strange, morphing into snakes.

The closer you look, the weirder it gets.

Just a few hours after the poster was rolled out on social media, Neon followed up with a video showing a human drawing the scene by hand, crediting illustrator Mike Thompson and creative studio Gravillis.

“Art made by humans,” Neon captioned the behind-the-scenes video on X.

Art made by humans (Gravillis Inc. and Mike Thompson). https://t.co/0xGxxMKchF pic.twitter.com/XWwBfYU7ym.

Users on social media quickly changed their tune, praising the studio and the movie’s creative team for their approach to the poster design.

“The poster for [Artificial] being made by an actual human artist while made to look like it was AI generated wow that’s luca GODagnino,” one user stated on X.

Recent findings suggest that another user added, “This poster is a masterpiece. So many fun, completely bizarre, and purposeful ‘AI Slop’ touches. Zoom in and see if you can spot them all.”.

Many also took notice that Neon didn’t just come out and say the poster was made by humans but rather made the effort to film a behind-the-scenes video and upload it as proof.

“Thank you for filming their processes and including the views of the artists in a world where what we see can be compromised or untrue,” one user said on X.

Sources indicate that neon is not the first company to show how its work was made as a way to stand apart from AI slop. In recent months, brands across retail and tech have done the same.

In August, Apple released a behind-the-scenes video of its claymation ad for the newly introduced Mac Mini. Prada’s animated holiday campaign includes sketches from the artist.

But behind-the-scenes footage works only when the ads themselves are craft-forward, leaning on labor-intensive handwork as a form of effort signaling.

While proof of humanness taps into the film’s theme—bringing a sense of irony by making human art look artificial—not every observer is embracing the marketing trend.

One X user proclaimed, “Anybody posting any type of art now has to prove to morons that it was genuinely created by them and not AI. What a shit hole time period we live in.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A wall of 100 Noctua PC fans was built by maker Sasa Karanovic because "why not." There's a little more to it, though, as the Toronto-based electronics and 3D printing expert wanted to test the capabilities of his new open-source open-hardware OpenFAN XL fan controller. A video indicates the setup and control of a 10x10 Noctua fan grid controlled via the 10 headers on the controller. A 50x2 setup was also shown working off the controller. Karanovic indicates that 100 fans was "no sweat" for the new controller, but it would max out at around 200 spinners in its current iteration.

It has been revealed that the maker explains in the video that they had this demo idea a while back but recently acquired 100 fans through a combination of "a ton of luck and a good friend." As the newly introduced OpenFAN XL controller has 10 headers, the natural first step in controlling them all was to make a grid of 10 x 10 units. That's a lot of fans, but there's also 200 fan grills, 800 screws, and oodles of wiring, including tens of fan splitters.

Recent findings suggest that so, the 100 fans aren't individually controllable, they are controlled in banks of 10 due to the 10 header channels. Thus, the granularity of control on offer here can only apply to 10 fans at the fewest in an array of 100 fans. The maker insisted that with 100 fans "our fan controller is not even breaking a sweat." Incidentally, the controller supports up to four integrated temperature probes to check if it is, actually, sweating.

Recent findings suggest that karanovic also sought to show the flexibility of his system by using wiring/splitters so that the first two headers controlled 50 fans each. If he'd had enough fans he could have theoretically expanded the cooling wall to 500 fans controlled by his OpenFan software in this way. But there are some other limits to the controller which means it tops out at around 200 fans.

In a recent development, in summary, this beastly cooling "contraption probably makes no sense," admitted the OpenFAN XL controller designer. However, he could have demonstrated it with some TrashBench-style shenanigans (or in an actual collab) by funneling a 100 fan-powered gust of air at a GPU, PC, laptop or so on.

Recent findings suggest that if you can think of a use for the OpenFan XL, you can make one yourself or grab one from Karanovic Research for $2,355, at the moment discounted from $2,926 on pre-order, by following the link in the intro. The product retail page more seriously pitches the controller as a useful product for server or other high-power device builders.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • People are trying to vibe code games.
  • I'll talk about the problem, how I fixed it, and where to go from here.
  • In a recent development, first, what is vibe coding?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People are trying to vibe code games. And it kind of works, at first. However, as the project grows, things begin to fall apart. Why? And what can we do about it?

I'll talk about the problem, how I fixed it, and where to go from here.

In a recent development, first, what is vibe coding? It's originally coined by Andrej Karpathy in a viral tweet where it's defined as where you "fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials and forget the code even exists".

However, since then, it's used descriptively to mean a lot of different things, anywhere from just "using AI when coding" to "not thinking about the code at all". In this blog post, I'll define it as: using AI as a high-level programming language to build something. Like other programming languages, this benefits from understanding what's going on under the hood, but doesn't necessarily require it.

With this interpretation, you could make a game without understanding code, though knowing the fundamentals still helps.

In a recent development, earlier I mentioned that "as the project grows, things begin to fall apart". This is because there is evidence that as the context window fills up, model performance begins to degrade. This is especially true for game development, where the context can grow very large, very swiftly.

To address this glitch, there are many personal ad-hoc solutions, such as writing LLM-specific context directly in the project files, or more comprehensive solutions like Claude Code Development Kit for large-scale context management.

I couldn't find a lightweight, accessible solution, which doesn't rely on significant domain knowledge. So I made one: 🧅 Shallot, a simple, lightweight, unopinionated context management system for Claude Code. It relies on two basic commands:.

Sources indicate that anecdotally, this works well. However, it works best when the project stays lean and well-organized, so all relevant context can easily fit in the model's context window. While Claude Code is used here, the same principles generalize to other models.

Beyond context management tools, platform choice is critical. The platform should ideally naturally keep projects lean through high-level abstractions, while also being something AI models understand well. So, what existing platforms are best suited for vibe coding?

I initially tried 3 different approaches to vibe coding games: Roblox MCP, Unity MCP, and web. For each, I tried to build a simple incremental game inspired by Grass Cutting Incremental, using Claude Code for each.

The official MCP server from Roblox. This allows AI to interact with Roblox Studio by sending commands to run code.

Roblox provides an excellent layer of abstraction for keeping the codebase lean and manageable, which is perfect for vibe coding. However, the walled garden and lack of context makes it infeasible for vibe coding, unless it's in-house at Roblox.

According to recent reports, the unofficial MCP server for Unity. This allows AI to interact with the Unity Editor: reading the console, managing assets, and validating scripts.

According to recent reports, unity is a powerful engine with a lot of capabilities. However, the complexity and variability of the engine makes it difficult for AI to consistently produce good results without significant user domain knowledge.

The open web platform, using three.js for 3D rendering, rapier for physics, and bitecs for game logic.

This approach had the best AI performance by far, likely due to the vast amount of web development data available during training. However, the low-level nature of the libraries meant that I had to essentially build a game engine before I could build the game itself. This allows us to work at a much higher level of abstraction, like we did with Roblox.

Although it required building an engine first, this approach was the only one that produced a fun result without heavy domain knowledge.

After these experiments, I had a clear picture: the web stack had excellent AI performance but was too low-level, while Roblox had perfect abstraction but lacked openness and context management.

So, what about combining the best of both?

Introducing VibeGame, a high-level declarative game engine built on top of three.js, rapier, and bitecs, designed specifically for AI-assisted game development.

There were three key decisions that went into the design of VibeGame:.

See it in action in this JSFiddle or the Live Demo.

This will create a simple scene with a ground plane and a falling ball. The player, camera, and lighting are created automatically. All of this is modular and can be replaced. Arbitrary custom components and systems can be added as needed.

This comes bundled with an llms.txt file containing documentation about the engine, designed specifically for AI, to be included in its system prompt or initial context.

Here's the game I built to test building a simple incremental grass collection game using VibeGame and Claude Code. It worked very well, requiring minimal domain knowledge for implementing the core game mechanics.

However, there are still some major caveats:.

Sources indicate that so, with a definition of vibe coding that is the one-shot "make me a game" approach, it doesn't work. However, with the definition of treating vibe coding like a high-level programming language, it works very well, but requires users to understand the engine's capabilities and limitations.

To try it immediately, I built a demo where you can develop a game directly in the browser using VibeGame with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct: Live Demo on Hugging Face.

You can also test it locally with a frontier model like Claude Code:.

Then, paste all the contents of the included llms.txt to CLAUDE.md, providing full documentation about the engine for the AI to reference (or point your own context management system to it). This works with other models as well.

The engine is currently very barebones and only supports very basic mechanics (unless writing it from scratch). However, initial results are promising.

Industry observers note that it's also worth exploring how vibe coding games could harness more proven engines. For example, building a high-level sandbox game editor on top of Unity or Unreal Engine (similar to how Unreal Editor for Fortnite is built on Unreal Engine) could provide a more controlled environment for AI to work with, while leveraging the power of established engines.

We're also likely to see more in-house solutions from major players.

AI adoption could disproportionately harm Black and Latino workers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it has become increasingly clear that the AI revolution is not just poised to upend white-collar jobs, despite what public discourse might suggest.
  • It has become increasingly clear that the AI revolution is not just poised to upend white-collar jobs, despite what public discourse might suggest.
  • According to recent reports, the effects of this upheaval will be uneven, which means certain demographic groups are more likely to be impacted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it has become increasingly clear that the AI revolution is not just poised to upend white-collar jobs, despite what public discourse might suggest. While entry-level roles are, in fact, on the decline in tech and finance—and employers continue to use AI as a rationale for layoffs—there is ample evidence that rapid AI adoption could interrupt pathways for workers without college degrees. The effects of this upheaval will be uneven, which means certain demographic groups are more likely to be impacted. Some of the jobs that have been deemed “highly exposed” to AI, including clerical and administrative roles, are largely dominated by women, and a fresh report from the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility posits that Black and Latino workers could also face major consequences. The report finds that Black and Latino workers are overrepresented in the sectors where automation and AI adoption will supplant work altogether, rather than augment work. While the overall rate of AI adoption is relatively stable across different demographics, Black and Latino workers will be affected more acutely by job displacement. Across working hours that are impacted by AI adoption, 40% of hours performed by Black workers and 41% by Latino workers will be displaced (as compared to 37% among white workers). That may not seem like a huge gap. But as the report points out, many of the jobs that are most exposed to AI have historically been pathways to the middle class, making them crucial drivers of social mobility across communities that have faced systemic barriers to entry. Black workers, in particular, dominate six jobs that are likely to see the biggest decline in labor demand, according to McKinsey, including postal mail carriers and customer service representatives; Latino workers are also especially likely to hold some of those jobs, namely dishwashers and hand packers. Black and Latino workers—along with workers in rural regions—are also much more likely to be in jobs that involve physical labor, which are more vulnerable to being automated through robotics and other AI-enabled systems. On the whole, lower-wage workers will face the greatest impact, and are 7.6 times as likely to need to transition into a new job when compared to higher-wage workers; people without a college degree are 1.8 times more likely to need to do the same. Meanwhile, white workers are better positioned to both avoid this level of AI disruption and actually benefit from AI adoption in a number of ways. It’s not just that they’re more likely to hold jobs where AI will enhance their work, boosting productivity rather than replacing employees outright. When compared to their Black and Latino counterparts, white workers are also 30% to 50% more likely to work in the industries where private capital will be deployed, yielding more jobs and wealth creation, the McKinsey report states. That means white workers already have more of a foothold in jobs involving robotics or semiconductors or biotech, setting them up for success as hundreds of billions of dollars pour into those industries. (Look no further than the Anthropic IPO this week, which has created thousands of millionaires.)  In other words: Without broader policy changes or reskilling initiatives, many Black and Latino workers may be forced out of their jobs and locked out of opportunities to cash in on the AI boom.

Sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

It has been revealed that the code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

Sources indicate that there's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Set three environment variables:.

It has been revealed that before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

The 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint says so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

The trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:.

Two design choices are worth calling out.

It has been revealed that use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:.

Recent findings suggest that most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

According to recent reports, the defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:.

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:.

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

According to recent reports, setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":.

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Sources indicate that don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

It has been revealed that don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Sources indicate that store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF reveals what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:.

Industry observers note that since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

It has been revealed that in the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

Recent findings suggest that in the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Industry observers note that across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:.

Recent findings suggest that the send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping hits theaters today and tells Haymitch Abernathy’s origin story. Abernathy is an unlikely hero forced into leadership in the rebellion by circumstances out of his control. This doesn’t mean the C-suite can’t learn a thing or two from him. Here are a few quick stats on the franchise and some of Haymitch’s best management lessons. [Image: Lionsgate] The Hunger Games franchise by the numbers The Hunger Games by Suzanne Collins, the first book in the original trilogy, was published by Scholastic on September 14, 2008. It was followed by Catching Fire in 2009 and Mockingjay in 2010. Before the second book even came out, Lionsgate acquired the film rights for the first book. It was a smart move because the four Hunger Games films have collectively made more than $1.45 billion at the domestic box office. Collins took a break after the first trilogy. A stand-alone prequel novel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, came out in 2020, telling the backstory of Coriolanus Snow. The 2023 film version made more than $166 million at the domestic box office. Sunrise on the Reaping was published in 2025. According to Deadline, the new film is expected to make at least $80 million at the domestic box office on opening weekend alone. Haymitch Abernathy: Reluctant leader archetype Haymitch Abernathy, played by Woody Harrelson in the original films and Joseph Zada in Sunrise, is an unconventional leader. He would rather be drinking away his sorrows than changing the fate of Panem—but sometimes management is thrust upon us. Abernathy excels at strategic planning. In the original books and movies, he is able to guide Peeta and Katniss through the games two times while organizing a rebellion right under the Capitol’s nose. This comes through very careful planning and deception. In the real world, however, business leaders need to be able to communicate a clear vision and how to execute it. Abernathy is rough around the edges—and his tough exterior allows him to work with a diverse range of difficult colleagues to get results. You could call him a people-first strategist. For instance, he was able to get through to Katniss and help her play the public relations game by pretending to have feelings for Peeta. She did that so well that her love for him ended up becoming real. In addition, Abernathy got the vain people of the Capitol to empathize with Katniss and Peeta and send them lifesaving supplies like medicine and water. Plan, collaborate, and adapt Similarly, managers will have to work with many different personalities, departments, or vendors. True leaders can approach each individual or organization in a way that uplifts their strengths. Back in Panem, all this planning doesn’t mean the reluctant Abernathy can’t adapt. He thrives under pressure. He was the victor of the 50th Hunger Games, the Second Quarter Quell. He had to compete against 47 other tributes, double the usual amount. He won by using the force field around the arena against his opponent. In business, as in the Hunger Games, not everything is going to go according to the five-year-plan. Sometimes you have to improvise solutions as problems arise. As it hits theaters, Sunrise will reveal more of Abernathy’s story and administrative prowess. The business world should take note.

Accelerating Qwen3-8B Agent on Intel® Core™ Ultra with Depth-Pruned Draft Models

📅 29 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (831 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Qwen3-8B is one of the most exciting recent releases—a model with native agentic capabilities, making it a natural fit for the AIPC.
  • With OpenVINO.GenAI, we’ve been able to accelerate generation by ~1.3× using speculative decoding with a lightweight Qwen3-0.6B draft.
  • By using speculative decoding and applying a simple pruning process to the draft, we pushed the speedup even further to ~1.4×.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Qwen3-8B is one of the most exciting recent releases—a model with native agentic capabilities, making it a natural fit for the AIPC.

With OpenVINO.GenAI, we’ve been able to accelerate generation by ~1.3× using speculative decoding with a lightweight Qwen3-0.6B draft.

By using speculative decoding and applying a simple pruning process to the draft, we pushed the speedup even further to ~1.4×.

We wrapped this up by showing how these improvements can be used to run a fast, local AI Agent with 🤗 smolagents.

According to recent reports, qwen3-8B is part of the latest Qwen family, trained with explicit agentic behaviors. It supports tool invocation, multi-step reasoning, and long-context handling capabilities, that make it well-suited for complex agent workflows. When integrated with frameworks like Hugging Face 🤗smolagents, QwenAgent, or AutoGen, it enables a wide range of agentic applications built around tool use and reasoning. Unlike single-turn chatbots, agentic applications rely on reasoning models that produce “thinking aloud” traces, intermediate steps that expand token usage, making inference speed critical to responsiveness. The combination of optimized inference and built-in agentic intelligence makes Qwen3-8B a compelling foundation for next-gen AI agents.

We started by benchmarking the 4-bit optimized OpenVINO version of Qwen3-8B on an Intel Lunar Lake integrated GPU, establishing this as our baseline for further acceleration.

It has been revealed that speculative decoding is a method to speed up auto-regressive generation. It works by using a smaller, faster model as a draft to propose multiple tokens in a single forward pass, which are then validated by the larger target model in one forward pass. In our setup, Qwen3-8B served as the target model while Qwen3-0.6B was used as the draft. This approach delivered an average of 1.3× speedup over the baseline.

It has been revealed that before initializing the LLMPipeline, make sure both the target and draft models are converted to OpenVINO. You can either download pre-converted models from the provided links or follow these instructions to convert your own.

Industry observers note that the speculative decoding speedup depends on the average number of generated tokens per forward step of the target, γ \gamma γ, the speculation window size, and the ratio between the target and draft models' latency c c c. A smaller, faster (though less accurate) draft can often deliver greater acceleration. This inspired us to shrink the draft model while still preserving its quality, i.e. E(#generated_tokens) E(\# generated\_tokens) E(#generated_tokens).

Speedup=E(#generated_tokens)γc+1 Speedup = \frac{E(\# generated\_tokens)}{\gamma c + 1} Speedup=γc+1E(#generated_tokens)​.

Recent findings suggest that our recent work reveals that model depth (number of layers) is a major contributor to inference latency. We drew inspiration from recent work on layer-wise compression[1]. In our approach, we identify blocks of layers that contribute little, measured using angular distance, and remove them. After pruning, we apply fine-tuning to recover accuracy. Using this method, we pruned 6 out of 28 layers from the Qwen3-0.6B draft model. To recover the quality of the pruned draft model, we further finetuned it using synthetic data generated by Qwen3-8B. The data was produced by generating responses to 500k prompts from BAAI/Infinity-Instruct dataset.

According to recent reports, the resulting pruned draft model delivered ~1.4x speedup compared to the baseline, an improvement over the ~1.3× gain achieved with the original draft. This outcome aligns with theoretical expectations - reducing draft latency improves the over-all speedup, enabling faster and more efficient inference.

This demonstrates how pruning + speculative decoding can unlock faster and more efficient inference—making local AI agents even more practical.

Check out the notebook and the Qwen3-0.6B depth-pruned draft model to reproduce our results step by step.

Sources indicate that to showcase the real-world potential, we deployed our optimized setup with the 🤗smolagents library. With this integration, developers can plug in Qwen3-8B (paired with our pruned draft) to build agents that call APIs and external tools, write and execute code, handle long-context reasoning and run efficiently on Intel® Core™ Ultra. The benefits aren’t limited to Hugging Face, this model pairing can also be used seamlessly with frameworks like AutoGen or QwenAgent, further strengthening the agentic ecosystem.

In our demo, we assigned the accelerated Qwen3-based agent a task: 👉 Summarize the key features of the Qwen3 model series and present them in a slide deck.

Here’s how it worked: 1. The agent used a web search tool to gather up-to-date information. 2. It then switched to the Python interpreter to generate slides with the python-pptx library. #126464. Your best people are training your AI. Pay them for it

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1742 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Your best people are training your AI. Pay them for it

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills.
  • It has been revealed that early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills.
  • When we looked into which AIs brought the most value, there was an obvious pattern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills. Within months, we were running five agents for every employee, which felt like a transformation until we looked at the actual output and efficiency. In my own finance org, only 30% of employee-built agents and skills actually moved the needle. When we looked into which AIs brought the most value, there was an obvious pattern. The successful agents were created by employees who understood where a process in their work typically tends to break, and could turn that knowledge into clear rules and processes for artificial intelligence. We went from treating AI skill-building as an open invitation and instead focused on the people who were building AI agents that moved the needle. That fixed the quality problem, but handed us a harder problem to solve. When you take your best talent’s craft and turn it into an AI agent, what does that employee get in return for their expertise and labor? As more companies have the best employees train their AI, leaders must have a response to this question. Define the bar, then pay against it When we changed our AI skill-building process, eligibility depended on a manager’s recommendation and a strong performance review. But identifying the right people is half the work. Companies also need to establish what qualifies as a high-value skill, and what it is worth, before anyone starts building one. We created a framework that categorizes skills, assigns value, and determines the reward. It’s simple but makes it clear what employees should aim for and gives us a consistent way to reward them. At ClickUp, every skill falls into one of four categories, and each category has its own measure of success. One, revenue acceleration skills are measured by the pipeline or bookings they add, and two, cost elimination skills are measured by the spend they remove, like canceling a software we no longer use. Time compression skills, three, are measured by how much faster a core process runs, like closing the books or responding to a customer. And executive bounties, four, are specific problems our leadership team has identified, each with a reward attached. The category tells employees what type of skills to build with AI, but the proof of impact is what determines how much the AI skill is worth. Before creating a latest AI skill, employees must record where the measure stands today, like how many sales meetings aren’t rebooked each month or how long it takes to close the books. Then they can build, and once the AI skill has been running long enough to show a consistent pattern of value, finance compares the new numbers against the starting point. Finance then subtracts the cost of running the AI skill, including tools and maintenance, and what remains is the value the employee created. We then look at what we would have paid to get the same result a different way. Hiring even a few experienced sellers is a major expense, so when one person’s AI skills deliver that same capacity, a standard raise no longer reflects what their work is worth to the business. To determine the reward, we also consider how long the value will last. A skill that solves a single, contained problem earns a bonus. A skill or system the employee will keep running and improving earns a permanent raise, since the tech giant will keep benefiting from that work every year. Together, these steps give us a dollar amount for each AI skill created, which we can use to determine the compensation ranging from a one-time bonus to becoming part of our “unicorn” group. Unicorns are employees whose AI work changes what an entire team can do, and they receive a merit increase of more than 30% along with eligibility for compensation up to $1 million at the top of the band. For example, one growth operations manager identified 17 places where we were regularly losing potential sales and built 11 AI skills to address them. Those skills recovered hundreds of thousands of dollars in pipeline and increased the number of sales prospects by 25%. They also saved every sales rep about 90 minutes in their day, which is equivalent to seven sellers’ worth of capacity. Because the results were large, verified, and directly tied to revenue, this employee joined our “unicorn” group. Reward your talent for making their expertise reusable Your best people are already training your AI. They are handing over the part of themselves that made them hard to replace, and the company can keep using that knowledge long after they have moved on. Hoarding what only one person knows feels like job security, but it is ultimately a ceiling. The people thriving in this model build the skill, hand over their knowledge, and move to the next problem. Each handoff allows them to take on a bigger, more interesting challenge. This is the model companies should build toward as AI moves deeper into knowledge work—rewarding people for making their expertise reusable. That judgment is intellectual property, and paying for it is how you build AI that works while retaining top talent.

Latest Update: Introducing RTEB: A Latest Standard for Retrieval Evaluation

📅 01 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR – We’re excited to introduce the beta version of the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB), a fresh benchmark designed to reliably evaluate the retrieval accuracy of embedding models for real-world applications.
  • It has been revealed that the performance of many AI applications, from RAG and agents to recommendation systems, is fundamentally limited by the quality of search and retrieval.
  • The current standard for evaluation often relies on a model's "zero-shot" performance on public benchmarks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR – We’re excited to introduce the beta version of the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB), a fresh benchmark designed to reliably evaluate the retrieval accuracy of embedding models for real-world applications. Existing benchmarks struggle to measure true generalization, while RTEB addresses this with a hybrid strategy of open and private datasets. Its goal is simple: to create a fair, transparent, and application-focused standard for measuring how models perform on data they haven’t seen before.

It has been revealed that the performance of many AI applications, from RAG and agents to recommendation systems, is fundamentally limited by the quality of search and retrieval. As such, accurately measuring the retrieval quality of embedding models is a common pain point for developers. How do you really know how well a model will perform in the wild?

This is where things get tricky. The current standard for evaluation often relies on a model's "zero-shot" performance on public benchmarks. However, this is, at best, an approximation of a model's true generalization capabilities. When models are repeatedly evaluated against the same public datasets, a gap emerges between their reported scores and their actual performance on new, unseen data.

To address these challenges, we developed RTEB, a benchmark built to provide a reliable standard for evaluating retrieval models.

While the underlying evaluation methodology and metrics (such as NDCG@10) are well-known and robust, the integrity of existing benchmarks is often set back by the following issues:.

The Generalization Gap. The current benchmark ecosystem inadvertently encourages "teaching to the test." When training data sources overlap with evaluation datasets, a model's score can become inflated, undermining a benchmark's integrity. This practice, whether intentional or not, is evident in the training datasets of several models. This creates a feedback loop where models are rewarded for memorizing test data rather than developing robust, generalizable capabilities.

Sources indicate that because of the above, models with a lower zero-shot score[1] may perform very well on the benchmark, without generalizing to new problems. For this reason, models with slightly lower benchmark performance and a higher zero-shot score are often recommended instead.

Sources indicate that misalignment with Today’s AI Applications. Many benchmarks are poorly aligned with the enterprise use cases that developers are building today. They often rely on academic datasets or on retrieval tasks derived from QA datasets, which, while useful in their own right, were not designed to evaluate retrieval and can fail to capture the distributional biases and complexities encountered in real-world retrieval scenarios. Benchmarks which do not possess these challenges are often too narrow, focusing on a single domain like code retrieval, making them unsuitable for evaluating general-purpose models.

Recent findings suggest that today, we’re excited to introduce the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB). Its goal is to create a latest, reliable, high-quality benchmark that measures the true retrieval accuracy of embedding models.

To combat benchmark overfitting, RTEB implements a hybrid strategy using both open and private datasets:.

It has been revealed that this hybrid approach encourages the development of models with broad, robust generalization. A model with a significant performance drop between the open and the private datasets would suggest overfitting, providing a clear signal to the community. This is already apparent with some models, which show a notable drop in performance on RTEB's private datasets.

RTEB is designed with a particular emphasis on enterprise use cases. Instead of a complex hierarchy, it uses simple groups for clarity. A single dataset can belong to multiple groups (e.g., a German law dataset exists in both the "law" and "German" groups).

In a recent development, A complete list of the datasets can be found below. We strategy to continually patch both the open as well as closed portion with different categories of datasets and actively encourage participation from the community; please open an issue on the MTEB repository on GitHub if you would like to suggest other datasets.

Recent findings suggest that RTEB is launching today in beta. We believe building a robust benchmark is a community effort, and we plan to evolve RTEB based on feedback from developers and researchers alike. We encourage you to share your thoughts, suggest newly introduced datasets, find issues in existing datasets and help us build a more reliable standard for everyone. Please feel free to join the discussion or open an glitch in the MTEB repository on Github.

To highlight areas for improvement we want to be transparent about RTEB's current limitations and our prepares for the future.

Our goal is for RTEB to become a community-trusted standard for retrieval evaluation.

Industry observers note that the RTEB leaderboard is available today on Hugging Face as a part of the new Retrieval section on the MTEB leaderboard. We invite you to check it out, evaluate your models, and join us in building a better, more reliable benchmark for the entire AI community.

In a recent development, [1] Zero-shot score is the proportion of the evaluation set which the model provider have explicitly stated to have trained on. This typically only includes the training split.

Observed a fun fact: English-only models tend to get worse performance on closed datasets, while multilingual models are better at closed dataset.

Sources indicate that is it because the baseline, MTEB, is a benchmark merely in English, and RTEB is multilingual? It's natural that multilingual model get better performance on multilingual benchmark instead of English.

RTEB is by default multilingual, however it has an English subset (at the moment denoted as RTEB(eng, beta) or RTEB English on the leaderboard selection menu).

There is also an argument that multilingual models are more robust to phenomena such as code-switching and foreign terms.

Are you planning on releasing an academic paper on RTEB?

It has been revealed that the discussion about English-only versus multilingual subsets demonstrates why a single retrieval average can hide notable differences. Would it be feasible to report lexical baselines alongside embedding models per language, including identifier-heavy and paraphrase-heavy slices? We recently evaluated BM25 plus semantic reranking on a small English-only workload: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That result doesn't tell us how the approach would perform on RTEB's multilingual or private datasets.

RTEB leaderboard have bm25 and some other baseline models https://leaderboard.mteb.org/benchmark/RTEB(beta)?pin=mteb%252Fbaseline-bm25s.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the frontier model races continues. A week after the launch of Anthropic’s Claude 5.2 and Google’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen, OpenAI is releasing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol as a “new standard for professional work.”.

According to recent reports, stepping back in time a few days, Anthropic last week launched Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2. The company’s latest models are “designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges with “improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision.” Anthropic states that Fable 5.2 beats Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Carbon virtually across the board in benchmarks including coding, cybersecurity, knowledge work, and more.

But, now, OpenAI is stepping up to the challenge.

OpenAI demonstrates that GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are more or less playing ball with Anthropic’s latest models, but often delivering similar performance at a drastically lower cost.

Of the two latest models, OpenAI claims that Sol is “smarter, more efficient, and lets you complete more tasks on the same paid strategy” as a “go-to model for everyday work.”.

Astra, meanwhile, is tuned for the highest-quality work in professional use cases such as documents, slides, coding, and more:.

It has been revealed that GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new quality bar for AI in complex professional work. Its slides, spreadsheets, and documents read less like AI, and more closely follow the templates you provide and the conventions of your field. It writes cleaner code and builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming, and 3D design.

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu customers in ChatGPT Work and Codex, with Astra being significantly more affordable compared to GPT-6 Astra. Pricing for Astra per million tokens lands at $8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output. Sol matches its predecessor at $2 for input, $0.10 for cached input, and $10 for output, again per million tokens.
