4 ways I gave my employees more time off without sacrificing results

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2439 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A decade ago, I couldn’t have told you the last time I took significant time off from work.
  • A decade ago, I couldn’t have told you the last time I took significant time off from work.
  • In a recent development, I wore “busy” like a badge of honor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A decade ago, I couldn’t have told you the last time I took significant time off from work. I wore “busy” like a badge of honor. As the business owner, I set the tone for the people on my team. Pushing ourselves to do more and work harder was woven into the fabric of our culture. Today, things could not look more different. Every summer, I take a monthlong vacation to travel with my family. When I work late nights or several days in a row without breaks, I make it up to myself with extra time off. My team gets a four-day workweek and generous PTO, and on top of that, we close our business for six weeks throughout the year and take time off together. And we’ve managed to make this shift without losing sight of high expectations and accountability. What changed? I did. After years of neglecting my health in service of my work, I came across two books that upended my perspective: Dying for a Paycheck by Jeffrey Pfeffer, and It Doesn’t Have to be Crazy at Work by David Heinemeier Hansson and Jason Fried. They highlighted me what my firm’s culture could look like if I took responsibility for changing it. For years now, creating better work-life harmony for me and my team has been my priority. To me, “harmony” means that work and life work together instead of against each other. But of course, it hasn’t been easy. My biggest challenge has been figuring out how to balance caring for my people with creating a sustainable future for my company. I certainly haven’t found all the answers, but several years into this journey, my team and I are able to prioritize our lives outside of work and get stuff done—including writing and launching a upcoming book, just this year. While it’s true that my company and team are significantly smaller than they were in the early days, I believe it’s possible for teams of any size to make shifts that support better work-life harmony. I want to share the biggest things we’ve implemented with the hope that they will spark some ideas of your own. 1. Break weeks Years ago, I took off two separate weeks during a busy time at work. I didn’t have a vacation planned; I just needed a break. When I returned after a week of doing whatever I felt like at home, I felt rejuvenated and inspired. I wanted that same feeling for my team, so I proposed a company-wide “Break Week.” I told the team we would close the business and use the time to recharge. We loved it. Being off at the same time allowed us to disconnect in a way we never had. No one felt like they were falling behind, and we returned with renewed energy. Now, we enjoy six Break Weeks throughout the year: one week at the end of the first three quarters and three at the end of the year. I see them as a way to guarantee that each person on my team—including me—is taking off at least that much time every year. I’ve realized that offering a benefit doesn’t guarantee that people will use it, so implementing a policy like Break Weeks shows my team that I’m serious about time off. You might wonder what our clients think about our closing our business so often, and at first, I worried about that too. I also worried about missing out on revenue. Not only have our clients embraced Break Weeks, but some have even implemented their own version of them. And when we have to turn away revenue, we work to make it up in other quarters. If we can’t, we see it as a reasonable trade-off. 2. Four-day workweeks  Break Weeks were a huge step toward making sure that my team prioritizes their lives outside of work, but for me, it was just the start. When I first proposed the four-day workweek, I knew I’d find it tough to commit to. But as the leader, I needed to model it. I told my team that if I ever had to work all five days, I’d make up for it another time, and I did. Today, I empower each person on my team to choose the day that works best for them to take off each week, and they can change it as needed. To make this work, team communication is critical. We maintain a time-off calendar and share frequent updates on deliverables and deadlines. Once again, I learned that it’s a leader’s job to create a structure that holds everyone accountable to using benefits; otherwise, it just doesn’t happen. 3. Human time off For years, I proudly touted our “unlimited” paid time-off policy. But, of course, there’s only so much time you can take off and expect to remain on payroll. To create better-defined guidelines, I decided to make a distinction between two types of time off: “human” time and vacation time. Human time covers doctor or personal appointments, sick time, mental health days, etc. My team knows that they can take time off for these things without my approval. If human time affects someone’s ability to get their work done, I expect them to communicate that with the team and create a plan. Vacation time, on the other hand, means that you are completely unplugged and unavailable. I ask that my team runs their vacation plans by me before they finalize them so that I can ensure that we’re still meeting the needs of the business. Since I implemented this distinction, I’ve noticed that not only is there more clarity and communication about time off, but the team is taking more of it and working together more proactively. 4. Sabbaticals  This year, I implemented sabbaticals as a way to honor the amount of time my team has chosen to give me and the company. Depending on the person’s tenure, these sabbaticals range from four to six weeks and are fully paid. Each person earns a sabbatical every five years. Because those on my team have been with me for 9, 14, and 15 years, respectively, we are in the process of figuring out the sabbatical schedule so that the needs of the business are still covered. I’m excited to see what we learn and the impact of this new benefit. None of this works without accountability and open communication. We evaluate ourselves and each other’s performance with 360-degree reviews every quarter. We strive to give feedback within 24 hours of an issue’s arising, and we don’t shy away from difficult conversations. If someone isn’t delivering on their results and their time off is affecting their performance, it’s my job to speak up. Since implementing these changes, I’ve noticed my team and I are approaching our work with more energy and enthusiasm. In busy seasons, we’re willing to sprint because we feel taken care of. While some benefits look different for me as the business owner, I’m still taking off more time than ever before. These benefits might sound expensive or over-the-top, but I believe nothing has greater ROI than building a culture where work-life harmony thrives.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Razer Basilisk V3 is right now available for a low price of $32.99 on Amazon, down from its regular list price of $69.99. Razer is known to offer some of the best gaming mice on the market, and if you are looking for a latest upgrade, this deal is worth your money. Offering an ergonomic design, the mouse comes with a variety of customizations and can cater to a variety of gaming genres.

The Razer Basilisk V3 is a wired gaming mouse featuring a right-handed design, a textured matte-black finish, and a thumb rest. It features 13 programmable inputs, including the scroll wheel controls, which can be configured for different commands, macros, and shortcuts. The mouse uses Razer's Focus+ optical sensor with a native sensitivity of 20,000 DPI, which can be increased to 26,000 DPI using Razer’s Synapse software. It also has a dedicated sniper button that can temporarily lower sensitivity for more precise aiming.

The Basilisk V3 features  11 programmable buttons via Razer's Synapse software and a multi-function trigger button for keybinding actions such as a push-to-talk button.

One of its main features is the HyperScroll Tilt Wheel, which supports both notched scrolling and a free-spinning mode. It also includes Smart-Reel Mode, which automatically switches to free-spinning when the wheel is scrolled promptly and returns to tactile scrolling at slower speeds. Other features include 11 customizable RGB lighting zones, three polling rate options of 125 Hz, 500 Hz, and 1,000 Hz, and second-generation optical switches. The mouse also features a 6-foot braided USB cable and weighs approximately 94 grams.

Considering its discounted price of $32.99, the Razer Basilisk V3 offers a solid set of features at less than half its original price. Its ergonomic design, customizable buttons, adjustable sensitivity, and versatile scroll wheel make it suitable for both gaming and everyday desktop use.

Breaking: WhatsApp starts rolling out built-in cloud backup on Android, and it’s free

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Meta’s WhatsApp is making a huge change to chat backups, with a new built-in cloud backup option on Android that doesn’t rely on Google, and is free.
  • Spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp for Android is adding its own cloud backup option.
  • According to recent reports, “WhatsApp cloud storage” is showing up in the WhatsApp for Android v2.26.46.4 beta enhancement, rolling out now, and includes 2GB of free storage for cloud backups.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta’s WhatsApp is making a huge change to chat backups, with a new built-in cloud backup option on Android that doesn’t rely on Google, and is free.

Spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp for Android is adding its own cloud backup option. Prior to this, the app relied on Google Drive backup for transferring chats between devices or keeping a backup in case of accidental deletion.

According to recent reports, “WhatsApp cloud storage” is showing up in the WhatsApp for Android v2.26.46.4 beta enhancement, rolling out now, and includes 2GB of free storage for cloud backups. Everything is still end-to-end encrypted. Beyond the first 2GB, WhatsApp Plus ($2.99/month) adds 100GB, and Meta One ($7.99/month+) offers up to 4TB of cloud storage. WhatsApp will keep your backup for at least 4 months after the subscription ends, even if you are over the 2GB gap.

You can still choose to use Google Drive backups instead of the built-in option, but those using devices without a Google account or who are running low on Google storage may appreciate the option to switch.

It’s unclear exactly when this will be available to all WhatsApp users.

📖 0% read

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:.

Recent findings suggest that the backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

Recent findings suggest that the problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

It has been revealed that typeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:.

At first glance, this looks reasonable.

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

It has been revealed that the return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly vital when working with:.

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

Industry observers note that zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:.

There are two crucial parts here.

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:.

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

Recent findings suggest that for a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:.

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/people.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

This is where OpenAPI becomes useful.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:.

Request and response structures.

Data types and validation constraints.

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:.

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

Swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a latest optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A simplified workflow looks like this:.

A typical configuration might look like this:.

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

However, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:.

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:.

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:.

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

Sources indicate that these tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:.

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:.

Generated-client consistency checks.

Consumer-provider contract verification.

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a manufacturer might have separate teams responsible for:.

Customer-facing frontend applications.

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

This becomes particularly important when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:.

Assign an owner to every important API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

Industry observers note that API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:.

Use Zod to validate incoming data.

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

You do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document notable endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that every year our hardware is a little more powerful, our models a little smarter for each parameter.
  • Enter the Neural Engine, Apple's custom AI accelerator that has shipped with every Apple device since 2017.
  • In a recent development, whilst this all sounds very appealing, unfortunately the Neural Engine is only accessible through Core ML, Apple's closed source ML framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that every year our hardware is a little more powerful, our models a little smarter for each parameter. In 2025, it is more feasible than ever to run truly competitive models on-device. dots.ocr, a 3B parameter OCR model from RedNote, surpasses Gemini 2.5 Pro in OmniDocBench, making OCR a truly no compromises on-device use case. Running models on-device is certainly appealing to developers: no smuggling API keys, zero cost, and no network required. However, if we want these models to run on-device, we need to be mindful of the limited compute and power budgets.

Enter the Neural Engine, Apple's custom AI accelerator that has shipped with every Apple device since 2017. This accelerator is designed for high performance whilst sipping battery power. Some of our testing has found the Neural Engine to be 12x more power efficient than CPU, and 4x more power efficient than GPU.

In a recent development, whilst this all sounds very appealing, unfortunately the Neural Engine is only accessible through Core ML, Apple's closed source ML framework. Furthermore, even just converting a model from PyTorch to Core ML can present some challenges, and without a preconverted model or some knowledge of the sharp edges it can be arduous for developers. Luckily, Apple also offers MLX, a more modern and flexible ML framework that targets the GPU (not the Neural Engine), and can be used in conjunction with Core ML.

In this three part series, we will provide a reasoning trace of how we converted dots.ocr to run on-device, using a combination of CoreML and MLX. This process should be applicable to many other models, and we hope that this will help highlight the ideas and tools needed for developers looking to run their own models on-device.

According to recent reports, dots.OCR consists of two key components: A 1.2B parameter vision encoder trained from scratch, based on the NaViT architecture, and a Qwen2.5-1.5B backbone. We will be using CoreML to run the vision encoder, and MLX to run the LM backbone.

In order to convert a model, it's best to understand the structure and function before getting started. Looking at the original vision modelling file here, we can see that the vision encoder is similar to the QwenVL family. Like many vision encoders, the vision encoder for dots works on a patch basis, in this case 14x14 patches. The dots vision encoder is capable of processing videos and batches of images. This gives us an opportunity to simplify by only processing a single image at a time. This approach is frequent in on-device apps, where we convert a model that provides the essential functions and iterate if we want to process multiple images.

Sources indicate that when kicking off the conversion process, it's best to start with a minimal viable model. This means removing any bells and whistles that are not strictly necessary for the model to function. In our case, dots has many different attention implementations available for both the vision encoder and the LM backbone. CoreML has lots of infrastructure oriented around the scaled_dot_product_attention operator, which they introduced in iOS 18. We can simplify the model by removing all of the other attention implementations and just focusing on simple sdpa (not the memory efficient variant) for now, commit here.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The owner of a dwindling empire of Wendy’s restaurants on Friday disclosed its intends to close several more stores, bringing its total number of shuttered locations to almost 100.
  • It’s a grim milestone for the popular burger chain as it works to execute on a turnaround strategy aimed at boosting sales and bolstering its brand image.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The owner of a dwindling empire of Wendy’s restaurants on Friday disclosed its plans to close several more stores, bringing its total number of shuttered locations to almost 100. It’s a grim milestone for the popular burger chain as it works to execute on a turnaround blueprint aimed at boosting sales and bolstering its brand image. The franchisee behind the closures, Meritage Hospitality Group of Grand Rapids, Michigan, is among the largest operators within the Wendy’s system, at one time owning roughly 375 locations across 15 states. It closed dozens of those restaurants in the months before a Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing in September, and has since shuttered additional waves of stores at regular intervals as part of cash collateral agreements with its lenders. How many Wendy’s stores has Meritage closed? According to court documents, Meritage has closed well over 90 Wendy’s locations since late last year, with many of those stores shuttered before its September bankruptcy petition. As is typical in Chapter 11 cases, Meritage is seeking to reject the leases on many of the stores that it closed pre-bankruptcy—roughly 60, court filings show—a list that includes a handful of Taco John’s and Morning Belle locations, in addition to Wendy’s. Since the bankruptcy, Meritage has also closed at least 41 additional Wendy’s restaurants, including six closures that were disclosed on Friday. The newly shuttered restaurants were located in Florida, Georgia, Michigan, and Ohio: 12135 Lem Turner Road Jacksonville, FL 32218 1928 Hwy 155 McDonough, GA 30252 3675 Cascade Road Atlanta, GA 30331 9556 US 31 So Interlochen, MI 49643 8258 Broadmoor Avenue Caledonia, MI 49316 914 Conant St. Maumee, OH 43537 Prior to the above six restaurants, Meritage disclosed waves of store closures on at least five separate occasions: 5 locations on September 25 5 locations on October 2 10 locations on October 9 13 stores on October 16 2 stores on October 30 Fast Company has reached out to Meritage Hospitality Group and Wendy’s for comment. What will happen to Meritage’s remaining stores? Meritage has owned Wendy’s restaurants since the late 1990s, but its relationship with the fast food giant appeared to turn increasingly contentious in recent years as its business faced headwinds on numerous fronts, including the soaring cost of beef. The franchisee has blamed Wendy’s for a strategy of “deep discounting” that it says squeezed profits. The Wendy’s Company, for its part, had sought to terminate Meritage’s franchise agreements, claiming to be owed more than $146 million in past-due royalties and other fees. Despite all this animosity, the two sides are working together to salvage what’s left of the Meritage fleet. Wendy’s disclosed earlier this month that it wants to buy up to 163 restaurants from Meritage. That deal, which is still subject to better bids, is expected to close early next year. Additionally, Meritage is moving to sell restaurants to various other buyers in separate deals, including one to sell 42 locations in Arkansas, Mississippi, Missouri, and Tennessee to an entity called Divine Infinity Operations. It’s unclear if additional Wendy’s locations could close before or after these asset sales are complete. This story is developing….

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nintendo raised the price of the Switch 2 earlier this year in response to rising NAND and DRAM prices, but on Black Friday, you can wipe out that hike with a variety of bundles available on Amazon. The core deal is the Mario Kart World Switch 2 bundle, which includes the game, the console, and three months of Nintendo Switch Online. It normally sells for $550, but Amazon has it marked down by $50, bringing the bundle down to its original price of $499.

Amazon is extending that sale to a variety of bundles it has available. You can pick up the kit alongside a Switch 2 Pro Controller, the upcoming Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, or a microSD Express card with the same discount. Note that with the base Mario Kart World bundle, the game is included as a redeemable code, not a physical cartridge.

This bundle includes the Nintendo Switch 2 console, a code for Mario Kart World, and three months of a Nintendo Switch Online Individual membership.

As you can read about in our Nintendo Switch 2 review published last year, the console is a major upgrade over the original version. The heart of the handheld is a custom Nvidia SoC that includes eight Arm Cortex-A78C CPU cores alongside an Nvidia GPU with 1,536 CUDA cores, hailing from the firm's Ampere generation. Alongside the SoC, the handheld sports 12GB of LPDDR5X memory along with 256GB of storage.

Showing off the capabilities of these upgraded internals is a larger 7.9-inch, 1080p LCD display. It's larger and brighter than the original Switch display, but it also comes with far greater capabilities, including variable refresh rate, HDR10 support, and a 120 Hz panel.

Sources indicate that the handheld is much larger overall, and it sports a redesigned Joy-Con mechanism that's far more resilient than the original Switch design. The kickstand more closely aligns with the Switch OLED, running along most of the edge of the display; the original Switch props up the console on one side, where it can easily fall over.

Sources indicate that overall, the performance jump is what stands out most. Nintendo has released several Switch 2 updates for flagship titles like Metroid Prime 4 and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom with support for higher resolutions and frame rates. Titles like the recent Ocarina of Time Remake and Donkey Kong Bananza target 60 FPS, though occasionally fall short of that mark.

Tech Report: BigCodeArena: Judging code generations end to end with code executions

📅 07 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1384 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Evaluating the quality of AI-generated code is notoriously difficult.
  • In a recent development, inspired by LMArena for LLMs, we've built a platform that allows anyone to compare code generation models side-by-side, but with a crucial difference: you can actually run the code and see what it produces.
  • In a recent development, the field of code generation has long struggled with reliable evaluation methods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Evaluating the quality of AI-generated code is notoriously difficult. While humans can easily spot whether a piece of code "looks right," determining if it actually works correctly, handles edge cases properly, and produces the intended result requires running and testing it. This is why today, we're thrilled to announce BigCodeArena -- the first human-in-the-loop platform for evaluating code generation models through execution.

In a recent development, inspired by LMArena for LLMs, we've built a platform that allows anyone to compare code generation models side-by-side, but with a crucial difference: you can actually run the code and see what it produces. Just submit a coding task, watch two different models generate solutions, execute both programs, and vote on which model produced better results. The outcomes are organized into a leaderboard that displays the community's highest-rated models.

In a recent development, the field of code generation has long struggled with reliable evaluation methods. Traditional benchmarks like HumanEval test code against predefined test cases, but these represent only a tiny fraction of real-world programming tasks. Human evaluation platforms exist for general chatbots, but they fall short for code: reading raw source code and mentally simulating its execution is cognitively demanding and error-prone, especially for longer programs or complex UI applications.

In a recent development, you ask two AI models to build a responsive photo gallery website. Both generate code that looks syntactically correct. But which one is actually better? Without running the code, it's nearly impossible to tell. One might produce a beautiful, functional grid layout, while the other might have subtle bugs or poor styling that only become apparent when rendered in a browser.

According to recent reports, this observation led us to a key insight: execution feedback is essential for humans to judge code quality reliably. That's exactly what BigCodeArena provides.

BigCodeArena extends the Chatbot Arena framework with powerful features specifically designed for code evaluation:.

Industry observers note that every code snippet generated by models is automatically executed in isolated sandbox environments. Whether it's a Python script, a React web app, a PyGame game, or a C++ algorithm, you can see the actual output, not just the source code.

We currently support 10 languages (Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, HTML, C, C++, Java, Go, Rust, and Markdown) and 8 execution environments:.

Unlike static code comparison, you can actually interact with the generated applications:.

Industry observers note that real programming isn't one-and-done. BigCodeArena supports multi-turn interactions, allowing you to refine requirements, ask for features to be added, or request bug fixes -- just like working with a real coding assistant.

Since launching in February 2025, BigCodeArena has collected over 14,000 conversations from more than 500 unique consumers, with 4,700+ high-quality preference votes comparing 10 frontier LLMs.

Our consumers have explored remarkably diverse coding scenarios:.

Python dominates with over 4,000 conversations, followed by JavaScript/TypeScript (3,359), HTML (1,601), and C++ (642). Among frameworks, direct Python interpreters lead usage (6,000 sessions), with React (2,729), Core Web (1,574), Streamlit (1,254), and PyGame (1,087) also seeing heavy use.

In a recent development, most interactions are focused and efficient: 76% of conversations consist of just 2 turns (one request, one response), with a mean conversation length of 4.12 messages. However, the platform supports extended multi-turn debugging sessions when needed, with some conversations exceeding 10 turns as customers refine complex applications.

From our 14K conversations, we filtered for high-quality pairwise comparisons: conversations with at least two turns and actual code execution. This yielded 4,731 voting samples, with each evaluated model receiving at least 700 votes. We aggregate these votes into Elo ratings using the Bradley-Terry model, which estimates the probability that one model beats another based on head-to-head comparisons.

To ensure robust rankings, we use 100 bootstrap resamples to construct 95% confidence intervals, so we can identify statistically significant performance differences between models.

We evaluate models under three settings to control for different factors:.

Rankings remain remarkably consistent across all three settings, revealing clear performance tiers:.

Top Tier: o3-mini and o1-mini consistently lead with the highest Elo ratings and tight confidence intervals. These models maintain top performance regardless of environment or language constraints, showing strong robustness across coding scenarios. Claude-3.5-Sonnet follows closely, particularly excelling when language is controlled.

Sources indicate that mid Tier: GPT-4o, o1, and Gemini-2.0-Pro/Flash form a competitive middle tier. GPT-4o demonstrates some sensitivity to language matching, suggesting room for improvement in multilingual consistency.

Open Source Models: Qwen2.5 variants and Llama-3.3-70B lag behind frontier proprietary models, highlighting the performance gap that remains between leading closed and open models.

Figure: Overall win rate heatmaps (percentage of all pairwise comparisons won) of each model in the sessions across languages (left) and execution environments (right). For each category, we only keep models that appear in at least 3 conversation sessions.

Breaking down performance by programming language reveals interesting patterns:.

Analyzing win rates by execution environment reveals how models handle different runtime contexts:.

Robust Performers: o3-mini maintains consistently strong performance across React, Streamlit, Gradio, Core Web, and PyGame, demonstrating excellent environmental adaptability.

Stable but Selective: Claude-3.5-Sonnet and Gemini-2.0-Flash show generally stable performance but with reduced win rates in complex UI-heavy environments like Vue and Mermaid.

Recent findings suggest that framework-Specific Weaknesses: Qwen2.5 models, while competitive in some web frameworks (Core Web, React), struggle significantly with interactive and visualization-oriented environments like PyGame, Vue, and Mermaid. These environments often require precise handling of control flow, graphics rendering, and package dependencies.

According to recent reports, these results highlight an key insight: aggregate Elo scores don't tell the whole story. Some models remain brittle under specific runtime constraints, and execution environment matters significantly for real-world deployment.

To advance research beyond crowdsourced evaluation, we're releasing two complementary benchmarks:.

Industry observers note that building on our 4,700+ preference votes, BigCodeReward tests how well LLMs can judge code quality when acting as reward models. The key finding? Execution results dramatically improve judgment accuracy.

When models can see execution outputs (screenshots of web apps, game visuals, program logs), their alignment with human preferences increases substantially:.

This reinforces our core thesis: you can't reliably judge code without running it -- and this applies to both humans and AI judges.

In a recent development, inspired by Arena-Hard-Auto, AutoCodeArena provides a scalable way to evaluate new models without waiting for thousands of human votes. We carefully selected 600 representative prompts from our crowdsourced data, spanning all programming topics and frameworks.

Using automated LLM judges (Claude-3.7-Sonnet) to evaluate code execution results against a GPT-4.1 baseline, we can rapidly benchmark latest models. This approach enables weekly leaderboard updates as new models are released.

Our automated benchmark evaluated 20+ cutting-edge models, including recently released systems:.

Figure: Win rates of recent LLMs on AutoCodeArena against a GPT-4.1 baseline, judged by Claude-3.7-Sonnet. The 50% mark represents parity with GPT-4.1. Models above this line outperform the baseline, while those below underperform. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals. Note: Claude-3.7-Sonnet is excluded from rankings to avoid self-judgment bias, and GPT-4.1 appears only as the reference baseline.

The results show that while proprietary models maintain an edge, open-source models are rapidly closing the gap, with some approaching GPT-4.1-level performance.

It has been revealed that bigCodeArena is open to everyone -- no account required! Visit https://huggingface.co/spaces/bigcode/arena to:.

Whether you're building a React dashboard, creating a PyGame game, solving algorithmic challenges, or generating creative visualizations, BigCodeArena lets you see which models truly deliver.

Following the BigCode Project's commitment to transparency, we're releasing:.

We envision BigCodeArena as a long-term project that evolves with the community:.

Evaluating code isn't like evaluating text -- you need to run it, test it, and interact with it. BigCodeArena makes this possible at scale, combining human judgment with real execution feedback to create the most reliable evaluation platform for code generation models.

Join us in building the future of code generation evaluation. Write a prompt, compare the models, and vote for your favorite. Your feedback helps the entire community understand which models truly deliver on the promise of AI-assisted programming.

It has been revealed that we'd love to hear your feedback! Connect with us on GitHub, join discussions in the Hugging Face Space community tab, or reach out to the BigCode Project at contact@bigcode-project.org.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Home is constantly rolling out new updates and, today, the organization is detailing some of its latest updates including a faster Gemini for Home experience and an upcoming Nest Thermostat upgrade.

In a post today, Google details several Google Home updates that are widely rolling out to owners.

The first was announced last week – home keys in Google Wallet. This leverages compatible NFC and UWB (Aliro) locks on newer Pixel and select Samsung Galaxy smartphones, letting you unlock your door by simply tapping your phone.

Cameras are also getting an upgrade for Activity Zones:.

…we’ve tightened Activity Zone boundary precision on our newest wired cameras to significantly reduce false alerts from passing cars, animals, and motion just outside your zone borders. We also redesigned the camera settings page to put Activity Zones front and center, and added a confirmation prompt on iOS when exiting an edited zone so you never accidentally lose your custom boundaries.

The Google Home website also gets faster scrubbing and fresh keyboard shortcuts – Left or Right arrow keys skip back or forward in 5-second increments, rapidly to jump 30 seconds or more.

Gemini for Home continues to get faster, with Google saying that the latest updates have resulted in an overall speed improvement of 20% on “everyday requests.” Gemini for Home has also expanded to six new countries including India, Taiwan, Singapore, Colombia, South Korea, and Brazil starting “next month.”.

Finally, Google is also preparing some useful upgrades for Nest Thermostat.

The first is a dashboard for Nest Thermostat users in the US and Canada that demonstrates “estimated cumulative savings” spurred by their thermostat. You’ll be able to see these savings in “the Climate space, thermostat controller, and Favorites widget.” The second is the abiltiy to use third-party room temperature sensors with the 4th-Gen Nest Learning Thermostat. Google has its own sensor for this that sells for $40, but there are more affordable alternatives that often bring more functionality too, so this is a really nice addition. Compatible brands will include IKEA, Eve, and Aqara.

According to recent reports, starting in December, Nest thermostat owners in the U.S. and Canada can check the app to see estimated cumulative savings. And they can also balance hot and cold spots with compatible third-party room sensors with their 4th-gen Nest Learning Thermostat.

In a recent development, A third upgrade is to the Dynamic Farsight faces on the latest Nest Learning Thermostat. “New” faces are coming with “designs to match your aesthetics,” while a new Lunar face will track moon phases.

According to recent reports, dynamic Farsight already lets you see the time, temperature, weather, and air quality from across the room, and starting this December, we’re rolling out newly introduced Dynamic Farsight faces with designs that match your aesthetics. Keep an eye out for seasonal animations on the Temperature face, or switch to our new Lunar face to track the phases of the moon right on your wall.

In a recent development, AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:.

Softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real owners can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free proposal is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app owners, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

It has been revealed that lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Industry observers note that base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every blueprint, Free included.

Recent findings suggest that base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Industry observers note that bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

According to recent reports, bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

In a recent development, replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Recent findings suggest that core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

It has been revealed that glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

It has been revealed that glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

Bubble is a visual builder that targets the browser as well as native iOS and Android, with an AI agent that drafts pages and logic before you refine them by hand. One editor covers the design, the database, the logic and the privacy rules behind each page.

It has been revealed that bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web prepares run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

Recent findings suggest that v0's Free blueprint gives latest users $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

In a recent development, figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Figma's Starter plan is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

In a recent development, collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real manufacturer data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

In a recent development, three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

It has been revealed that agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human owners.

Building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

Recent findings suggest that the caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

Recent findings suggest that it’s been nearly three years since Best Buy decided to ditch selling physical copies of movies, stripping its inventory from both its brick-and-mortar stores and its online catalog. But with the growing rise of 4K Blu-ray collections as a vinyl-esque collector’s item, the electronics giant has slowly begun dipping its toes back into the physical media game.

As spotted by TheHDRoom on Twitter and on the 4K Blu-ray subreddit, Best Buy is now selling 14 different 4K Blu-rays on its website, marking another step in the brand’s slow return to selling physical media. These films include:.

Sources indicate that technically, Blu-ray returned to Best Buy’s online storefront in August of 2025, when it opened a third-party marketplace similar to Amazon or Walmart. These titles, however, are shipped and sold by Best Buy. Everything’s still online-only, unfortunately, save for The Odyssey, which launched in-store shelf displays alongside yesterday’s release date. It shouldn’t come as too much of a surprise that The Odyssey is getting some special treatment; in addition to its status as a box office juggernaut, Nolan’s previous movie, Oppenheimer, initially sold out of physical copies in its first week of release in 2023.

Outside of these 14 titles, additional Blu-rays continue to be sold through Best Buy’s third-party marketplace.

Upgrade, 11/20: Best Buy confirmed to The HD Room on Twitter that The Odyssey is just the first 4K Blu-ray to return to physical locations, as it plans to continue adding “some” Blu-rays back to its stores.

In a recent development, the Odyssey may/will be joined by other 4K UHD titles at Best Buy in the future: "The Odyssey inspired a homecoming of our own – some physical media is returning to Best Buy. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, windows 7 may have been retired years ago, but that hasn’t stopped enthusiasts from finding ways to bring modern hardware and features to Microsoft’s beloved operating system. A newly introduced community project is now giving Windows 7 the ability to support modern Nvidia, AMD, and Intel graphics cards, along with DirectX 12 and Vulkan 1.4 capabilities.

Developed by enthusiasts EAZY BLACK, kryptik, and VisualEhrmanntraut, the project backports WDDM 2.2 from Windows 10. Interestingly, Windows 7 originally rolled out with WDDM 1.1, while Microsoft introduced WDDM 2.0 with Windows 10 in 2015 and WDDM 2.2 with the Creators Enhancement in 2017. Microsoft also introduced a limited version of DirectX 12 for Windows 7 in 2019; however, that implementation was only meant for developers to port select games to the older operating system.

According to a post by @TheBobPony on X, Nvidia's RTX 40 and RTX 50 series, AMD's Radeon RX 7000 and RX 9000 series, and select Intel Arc graphics cards are supported. Screenshots confirm that the backport enables GPUs to be recognized by Windows 7 as well as third-party apps like GPU-Z. It is also claimed that features such as ray tracing and DLSS also work on compatible hardware. Older GPUs, including Nvidia's RTX 30 series and AMD's Radeon RX 6000 series, may also benefit from the project. That said, actual feature support depends on the graphics card, driver implementation, and application.

It has been revealed that for anyone who still prefers Windows 7 or relies on older software and hardware, this project is worth exploring, especially if you intend to extend the usefulness of the operating system. Customers can also combine it with the VxKex compatibility layer, allowing newer Windows apps to run on older operating systems. You can grab the project files and modified drivers by heading to the W7Revived website.

Sources indicate that there’s a reason why enthusiasts continue to keep Windows 7 alive. Released in 2009 as a successor to Windows Vista, it offered a familiar interface, solid performance, and a straightforward desktop experience. It became one of Microsoft’s most popular operating systems and remained a favorite among PC enthusiasts and everyday owners long after the arrival of Windows 10.

In fact, Windows 7 still has some life left in it. We recently tested the aging operating system against Windows 11 on a modern PC running on an AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, Radeon RX 6950 XT, and 64GB of DDR5 memory. The tests included eight DirectX 11 and two DirectX 9 titles, with Windows 7 delivering better performance in certain scenarios, particularly CPU-bound games, along with stronger 1% lows in some titles.

A compound AI approach to Indian personas grounded in real-world distributions.

India represents one of the world's largest AI opportunities — with over 700 million internet consumers, a multitude of languages, and a rapidly growing developer ecosystem. Yet, most open datasets reflect Western norms and English-only contexts, creating a data gap that limits AI adoption in India's multilingual, multi-script environment.

Today, we're releasing Nemotron-Personas-India, the first open synthetic dataset of Indic personas aligned to India's real-world demographic, geographic, and cultural distributions. Licensed under CC BY 4.0, this dataset offers a privacy-preserving, regulation-ready foundation for scaling AI systems that reflect Indian society—without relying on sensitive personal data.

According to recent reports, built with NeMo Data Designer, NVIDIA's enterprise-grade synthetic data generation microservice, Nemotron-Personas-India extends our global collection of Sovereign AI datasets. It builds on the success of our US and Japan persona datasets and includes newly introduced features designed specifically for India's culturally rich landscape.

This dataset integrates seamlessly with Nemotron models and other open-source LLMs, making it easy to fine-tune AI systems for Indian use cases—from multilingual chatbots to culturally-grounded specialized copilots.

This release complements our earlier suite of Hindi evaluation datasets — including ChatRAG-Hi, IFEval-Hi, MT-Bench-Hi, GSM8K-Hi, and BFCL-Hi — supporting a complete pipeline from synthetic data generation to rigorous model evaluation for Indian AI systems.

Recent findings suggest that produced using NeMo Data Designer, NVIDIA's microservice for synthetic data generation. This compound AI system enables generation with complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and supports multiple generation backends – the necessary tooling to scale a synthetic dataset of this size. We also leveraged the following models:.

This dataset was aligned to India’s official demographic distributions from the 2011 Census and expanded to include attributes essential for trustworthy AI training:.

It has been revealed that no real names. No re-identification risk.

According to recent reports, all personas are fully synthetic. While grounded in real-world distributions from the 2011 Census and Parsed Indian Electoral Rolls data, no data is tied to any living or deceased individual. This ensures developers can safely train AI systems without privacy risks or regulatory barriers.

Built for India, Ready for the World.

Nemotron‑Personas‑India is designed for developers building Sovereign AI systems for the Indian market, as well as global teams looking to adapt models to India’s unique linguistic, cultural, and social context.

Most open datasets today reflect English-speaking, Western norms—limiting AI performance in India’s multilingual, multi-script, and demographically complex environments.

With Nemotron‑Personas‑India, teams can:.

Sources indicate that india's 1.4 billion people speak hundreds of languages and live across vast cultural, economic, and geographic divides. India's National AI Portal estimates over 7,000 AI startups and research institutions are working to build locally relevant AI systems, and the Digital India initiative and government programs like IndiaAI are accelerating adoption.

According to recent reports, but progress is constrained by a fundamental gap: high-quality, culturally grounded training data that reflects India's demographic reality. Without representative datasets, AI systems struggle with code-switching between English and Hindi, fail to understand regional occupational categories, and miss cultural context essential for trust and adoption.

The dataset improves diversity of synthetically-generated data, mitigates biases, and prevents model collapse (degradation caused by uncurated training on another model's outputs) by reflecting India's real geographic and demographic distributions.

Nemotron-Personas-India supports Indian model builders in developing Sovereign AI systems that incorporate important region-specific demographics and cultural context.

Want to build AI systems that understand India's culture, languages, and people?

Whether you're an Indian model builder developing Sovereign AI or a global developer seeking better regional adoption, Nemotron-Personas-India provides the authentic, privacy-safe foundation your applications need.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

According to recent reports, weekly. Free. One click to leave.

It has been revealed that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

This guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

Sources indicate that • A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

• Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

According to recent reports, • Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

• Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

• Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

CudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it says it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

Sources indicate that limitations and gaps: the page shows different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your plan. It says to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

In a recent development, strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

Limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and says other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The organization’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and initiative prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

Copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it claims it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

Sources indicate that limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid initiative prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

According to recent reports, originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

In a recent development, strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, claims very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

Turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

Strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

Limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

Sources indicate that sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

Strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page says false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

According to recent reports, limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

Sources indicate that the table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

• False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

• Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

• Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

Industry observers note that • Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

• Moving targets. Latest models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

Industry observers note that • Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

OpenAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

It has been revealed that most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

• Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

In a recent development, • Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and upgrade as latest models appear.

It has been revealed that • Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

In a recent development, • Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Which Tool Fits Which Situation?

Because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

from dataclasses import dataclass.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control.

group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical".

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):.

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function.""".

flagged = detect(s.text) >= threshold.

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0}).

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through.

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged.

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan").

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan").

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}").

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2.

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),.

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),.

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),.

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),.

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

• Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

Recent findings suggest that • Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

Sources indicate that • Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

• Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

• Protect privacy. Do not paste confidential or personal text into a tool unless you have checked how it handles data.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

They can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

Recent findings suggest that yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

Sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

According to recent reports, A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

Recent findings suggest that AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

💡 Key Takeaways
