It has been revealed that 🧭TL;DR: Hugging Face AI Sheets is an open-source tool for supercharging datasets with AI models, no code required. Now with vision support: extract data from images (receipts, documents), generate visuals from text, and edit images—all in a spreadsheet. Powered by thousands of open models via Inference Providers.

Recent findings suggest that we are excited to release a massive update to Hugging Face AI Sheets, the open-source tool for building, transforming, and enriching data with open AI models. AI Sheets leverages Inference Providers, which means you can use thousands of open models powered by the best inference providers on the planet.

In a recent development, the first version of AI Sheets made structuring and enriching textual content a breeze. Now, we're adding vision to AI Sheets.

Recent findings suggest that images are everywhere—product photos, receipts, screenshots, diagrams, charts, logos. These documents contain structured information waiting to be extracted, analyzed, and transformed. Today, you can finally work with visual content directly in AI Sheets: view images, analyze them, extract information, generate newly introduced ones, and even edit them in real-time —all in the same workflow.

Industry observers note that images contain valuable information—product catalogs, support tickets, research archives, receipts, documents. Now you can upload images directly or use datasets with images, and use vision models to extract, analyze, and structure the information inside them.

It has been revealed that just like text columns, you can iterate on prompts, manually edit outputs, and use thumbs-up to teach the model what you want. Your feedback becomes few-shot examples for better results.

Example: From receipts to structured expenses.

Imagine you're back from a trip with a stack of receipts. Upload them to AI Sheets and create a column with a prompt like: Extract the merchant name, date, total amount, and expense category from this receipt.

AI Sheets processes each receipt and gives you a clean table with all the details extracted. You can edit any mistakes, validate good results with thumbs-up, and regenerate to improve the rest. Export the final dataset as CSV or Parquet for your expense tracking tool.

In a recent development, or maybe you're digitizing handwritten recipes from old family notebooks. Create columns to extract ingredients, cooking time, and cuisine type—turning your personal archive into a searchable, structured dataset.

Need visuals for your content? AI Sheets can generate and edit images directly in your spreadsheet using AI models, keeping your entire content creation workflow in one place.What you can do:.

It has been revealed that example: Creating a content calendar with visualsImagine you're planning a month of social media posts about healthy recipes. You have a spreadsheet with post titles and descriptions, but no images yet.

Create an image column with a prompt like: Generate an appetizing food photo for: {{title}}. Style: bright, overhead shot, natural lighting.

AI Sheets generates a unique image for each post. Not quite right? Create another column to edit them: Transform the image to have a rustic wooden background and add fresh herbs as garnish.

You can iterate on generation and editing prompts and try different approaches. Your entire content calendar—copy and visuals—lives in one spreadsheet, ready to schedule or export.

Now let’s see AI Sheets in action. We will use open models to unlock the knowledge within handwritten recipes like the ones you could find from your grandma.

Text columns include summarization, keyword extraction, translation, and custom actions.

Supercharge your OCR Pipelines with Open Models

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We have added Chandra and OlmOCR-2 to this blog, as well as OlmOCR Scores of the models 🫡.
  • It has been revealed that TL;DR: The rise of powerful vision-language models has transformed document AI.
  • By the end, you’ll know how to choose the right OCR model, start building with it, and gain deeper insights into document AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We have added Chandra and OlmOCR-2 to this blog, as well as OlmOCR Scores of the models 🫡.

It has been revealed that TL;DR: The rise of powerful vision-language models has transformed document AI. Each model comes with unique strengths, making it tricky to choose the right one. Open-weight models offer better cost efficiency and privacy. To help you get started with them, we’ve put together this guide.

By the end, you’ll know how to choose the right OCR model, start building with it, and gain deeper insights into document AI. Let’s go!

Industry observers note that optical Character Recognition (OCR) is one of the earliest and longest running challenges in computer vision. Many of AI’s first practical applications focused on turning printed text into digital form.

With the surge of vision-language models (VLMs), OCR has advanced significantly. Recently, many OCR models have been developed by fine-tuning existing VLMs. But today’s capabilities extend far beyond OCR: you can retrieve documents by query or answer questions about them directly. Thanks to stronger vision features, these models can also handle low-quality scans, interpret complex elements like tables, charts, and images, and fuse text with visuals to answer open-ended questions across documents.

Recent models transcribe texts into a machine-readable format.The input can include:.

OCR models convert them into machine-readable text that comes in many different formats like HTML, Markdown and more.

On top of text, some models can also recognize:.

Some models know where images are inside the document, extract their coordinates, and insert them appropriately between texts. Other models generate captions for images and insert them where they appear. This is especially useful if you are feeding the machine-readable output into an LLM. Example models are OlmOCR by AllenAI, or PaddleOCR-VL by PaddlePaddle.

Recent findings suggest that models use different machine-readable output formats, such as DocTags, HTML or Markdown (explained in the next section Output Formats). The way a model handles tables and charts often depends on the output format they are using. Some models treat charts like images: they are kept as is. Other models convert charts into markdown tables or JSON, e.g., a bar chart can be converted as follows.

Similarly for tables, cells are converted into a machine-readable format while retaining context from headings and columns.

Different OCR models have different output formats. Briefly, here are the common output formats used by modern models.DocTag: DocTag is an XML-like format for documents that expresses location, text format, component-level information, and more. Below is an illustration of a paper parsed into DocTags. This format is employed by the open Docling models.

The right model depends on how you initiative to use its outputs:.

Industry observers note that documents can have complex structures, like multi-column text blocks and floating figures. Older OCR models handled these documents by detecting words and then the layout of pages manually in post-processing to have the text rendered in reading order, which is brittle. Modern OCR models, on the other hand, incorporate layout metadata to help preserve reading order and accuracy. This metadata is called “anchor”, it can come in bounding boxes. This process is also called as “grounding/anchoring” because it helps with reducing hallucination.

OCR models can either take in images and an optional text prompt, this depends on the model architecture and the pre-training setup.Some OCR models support prompt-based task switching, e.g. granite-docling can parse an entire page with the prompt “Convert this page to Docling” while it can also take prompts like “Convert this formula to LaTeX” along with a page full of formulas.Other models, however, are trained only for parsing entire pages, and they are conditioned to do this through a system prompt.For instance, OlmOCR by AllenAI takes a long conditioning prompt. Like many others, OlmOCR is technically an OCR fine-tuned version of a VLM (Qwen2.5VL in this case), so you can prompt for other tasks, but its performance will not be on par with the OCR capabilities.

Industry observers note that we’ve seen an incredible wave of upcoming models this past year. Because so much work is happening in the open, these players build on and benefit from each other’s work. A great example is AllenAI’s release of OlmOCR, which not only released a model but also the dataset used to train it. With these, others can build upon them in new directions. The field is incredibly active, but it’s not always obvious which model to use.

To make things a bit easier, we’re putting together a non-exhaustive comparison of some of our current favorite models. All of the models below are layout-aware and can parse tables, charts, and math equations. The full list of languages each model supports are detailed in their model cards, so make sure to check them if you’re interested. All models below have open-source license except for Chandra having OpenRAIL license and Nanonets license being unclear. The average scores are taken from model cards of Chandra, OlmOCR, evaluated on OlmOCR Benchmark, which is English-only. Many of the models in this collection have been fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-VL or Qwen3-VL, so we also provide Qwen3-VL model below as well.

According to recent reports, while Qwen3-VL itself is a powerful and versatile vision-language model post-trained for document understanding and other tasks, it isn’t optimized for a single, universal OCR prompt. In contrast, the other models were fine-tuned using one or a few fixed prompts specifically designed for OCR tasks. So to use Qwen3-VL, we recommend experimenting with prompts.

Here’s a small demo for you to try some of the latest models and compare their outputs.

In a recent development, there’s no single best model, as every problem has different needs. Should tables be rendered in Markdown or HTML? Which elements should we extract? How should we quantify text accuracy and error rates? 👀While there are many evaluation datasets and tools, many don’t answer these questions. So we suggest using the following benchmarks:.

Sources indicate that when testing different OCR models, we've found that the performance across different document types, languages, etc., varies a lot. Your domain may not be well represented in existing benchmarks! To make effective use of this fresh generation of VLM-based OCR models we suggest aiming to collect a dataset of representative examples of your task domain and testing a few different models to compare their performance.

Sources indicate that most OCR models are small, having between 3B and 7B parameters; you can even find models with fewer than 1B parameters, like PaddleOCR-VL. However, the cost also depends on the availability of optimized implementations for specialized inference frameworks. For example, OlmOCR-2 comes with vLLM and SGLang implementations, and the cost per million pages is 178 dollars (assuming on H100 for $2.69/hour). DeepSeek-OCR can process 200k+ pages per day on a single A100 with 40GB VRAM. With napkin math, we see that the cost per million pages is more or less similar to OlmOCR (although it depends on your A100 provider). If your use case remains unaffected, you can also opt for quantized versions of the models. The cost of running open-source models heavily depends on the hourly cost of the instance and the optimizations the model includes, but it’s guaranteed to be cheaper than many closed-source models out there on a larger scale.

According to recent reports, while the past year has seen a surge in open OCR models, this hasn't been matched by as many open training and evaluation datasets. An exception is AllenAI's olmOCR-mix-0225, which has been used to train at least 72 models on the Hub – likely more, since not all models document their training data.

According to recent reports, sharing more datasets could unlock even greater advances in open OCR models. There are several promising approaches for creating these datasets:.

It's worth noting that many such datasets exist but remain unused. Making them more readily available as 'training-ready' datasets carries a considerable potential for the open-source community.

We have received many questions about getting started with OCR models, so here are a few ways you can use local inference tools and host remotely with Hugging Face.

Recent findings suggest that most cutting-edge models come with vLLM support and transformers implementation. You can get more info about how to serve each from the models’ own cards. For convenience, we show how to infer locally using vLLM here. The code below can differ from model to model, but for most models it looks like the following.

Recent findings suggest that and then you can query as follows using e.g. OpenAI client.

Transformers provides standard model definitions for easy inference and fine-tuning. Models available in transformers come with either official transformers implementation (model definitions within the library) or “remote code” implementations. Latter is defined by the model owners to enable easy loading of models into transformers interface, so you don’t have to go through the model implementation. According to recent reports, MLXMLX is an open-source machine learning framework for Apple Silicon. MLX-VLM is built on top of MLX to serve vision language models easily. Hugging Face Jobs for Batch Inference.

For many OCR applications, you want to do efficient batch inference, i.e., running a model across thousands of images as cheaply and efficiently as possible. A good approach is to use vLLM's offline inference mode. As discussed above, many recent VLM-based OCR models are supported by vLLM, which efficiently batches images and generates OCR outputs at scale.

Recent findings suggest that to make this even easier, we've created uv-scripts/ocr, a collection of ready-to-run OCR scripts that work with Hugging Face Jobs. These scripts let you run OCR on any dataset without needing your own GPU. Simply point the script at your input dataset, and it will:.

If you are interested in document AI, not just OCR, here are some of our recommendations.

Recent findings suggest that visual document retrieval is to retrieve the most relevant top-k documents when given a text query. If you have previously worked with retriever models, the difference is that you search directly on a stack of PDFs. Aside from using them standalone, you can also build multimodal RAG pipelines by combining them with a vision language model (find how to do so here). You can find all of them on Hugging Face Hub.

Industry observers note that there are two types of visual document retrievers, single-vector and multi-vector models. Single-vector models are more memory efficient and less performant; meanwhile, multi-vector models are more memory hungry and more performant. Most of these models often come with vLLM and transformers integrations, so you can index documents using them and then do a search easily using a vector DB.

If you have a task at hand that only requires answering questions based on documents, you can use some of the vision language models that had document tasks in their training tasks. We’ve observed owners trying to convert documents into text and passing the output to LLMs, but if your document has a complex layout, and your converted document outputs charts and so on in HTML, or images are captioned incorrectly, the LLM will miss out. Instead, feed your document and query to one of the advanced vision language models like Qwen3-VL not to miss out on any context.

Product teams keep asking engineers for the same feature: “Can customers fix the reaction in this clip without reshooting it?” It lands on the backlog as “add expression editing,” and it hides a lot of decisions.

This guide compares the realistic integration options in 2026, sketches a pipeline architecture, models costs, includes a small runnable job helper, and covers the consent and audit logging you need before changing a real person’s face. Vendor details change quickly, so check each vendor’s documentation before you build against it.

Information about features, pricing, APIs and policies in this article was checked on November 10, 2026 and may change. Check each vendor’s documentation before you build against it.

The tools split into two families.

Sources indicate that performance transfer is great for animation, but someone has to record a new take for every change. If your promise is “fix the reaction in the footage you already have,” direct editing fits better.

DRAMA is an AI facial changer from SyncMonster. In the web app, users upload a video or image (MP4, MOV, JPG, PNG), pick a face, choose an emotion, and set intensity on a slider from subtle to strong. The app offers four core emotions (Happy, Sad, Angry, Excited) plus presets such as Surprised, Serious, Evil and Intimidating, with the extra presets on paid plans. It supports emotion blending and editing one face in a group shot without touching the others. SyncMonster states that edits keep the original resolution, lighting and details such as glasses and beards, which is a vendor claim you should test on your own footage.

For developers, SyncMonster publishes public API documentation for DRAMA. Here is what those docs state, as checked on November 10, 2026:.

The emotion values exposed in the API are the four core emotions, and the extra app presets did not appear in the API docs. The docs describe polling only, with no webhooks mentioned, and they do not publish rate limits, an SDK, or a numeric maximum video duration (an error code exists for exceeding a duration limit).

In a recent development, runway exposes Act-Two through its developer API as the character_performance endpoint. You send a character (image or video) and a driving performance video, and Act-Two transfers facial expression, and optionally body and hand motion, onto the character. Output is 24fps.

Recent findings suggest that runway’s API pricing guide lists Act-Two at 5 credits per second of output, with credits priced at $0.01 each, so $0.05 per second. Earlier documentation mentioned a 15-credit minimum per generation, and the current pricing page does not list one, so check for minimums before you budget short clips. The documentation also exposes an expression intensity setting to control how strongly the performance is applied.

It has been revealed that the catch is the input requirement: every edit needs someone to act the upcoming reaction. That suits character animation, but it is a heavy ask for a user who wants a slightly warmer smile in an interview clip. It also drives one character per generation.

LivePortrait is an open-source portrait animation framework from Kuaishou’s KwaiVGI group. It animates a source image or video using a driving video or a saved motion template, supports video-to-video portrait editing, and offers retargeting controls for eyes and lips.

The README sets up a Python 3.10 conda environment and expects Git and FFmpeg, with an NVIDIA GPU recommended. It also notes that Apple Silicon runs roughly 20x slower than an RTX 4090, and that Humans mode needs PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=1 on a Mac. That matters if you were hoping to prototype on a MacBook and ship the same setup. A basic run adapted from the README looks like this:.

Also read the repository’s license file before you initiative any commercial use.

According to recent reports, the Hugging Face Spaces demo is handy for experiments, but production means owning GPU provisioning, queueing, model updates and quality review. You still steer with a driving input rather than a “happier by 30%” control.

Rule of thumb: if expression editing is a feature rather than your product, buy. If you need on-prem processing or model-level changes, build on LivePortrait and budget for ops.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that permissions alone can't catch this.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who claims they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight. The agent can read the file and send email, so it fulfills the user request. Semantic governance policies, available in Preview in Gemini platform, enable enterprises to govern their agents and provide guardrails to stop that call before it runs. They check each tool call an agent proposes against what the user asked for and against rules you write in plain language.

Industry observers note that permissions alone can't catch this. They say what an agent can do, not whether a particular call follows your rules. A model can also be talked out of the rules in its system instructions, by a user with a good reason, or by a document telling it to do something nobody asked for, a technique called indirect prompt injection. So the check has to sit outside the agent. Semantic governance policies are enforced through a policy enforcement point, such as Agent Gateway, alongside the agent governance controls we expanded in October, so policies stay separate from your agent's code.

Semantic governance policies check each tool call your agent's model proposes, before it runs, against two things:.

A call has to pass both checks to run.

Today, the policy enforcement point that Semantic governance policies support is Agent Gateway. You need to configure your agent so all your agent egress traffic goes through Agent Gateway, facilitating traffic between your agent and its model. When the model responds with a tool call, Agent Gateway sends the proposed call to the Semantic governance policy engine for evaluation before the response reaches your agent.

In the policy engine, an LLM judge evaluates the proposed call against the conversation so far, the agent's system instructions and tool descriptions, and your policies.

If the call passes, the response reaches your agent unchanged. If it doesn't, the engine replaces the response's content, tool calls included, with a configurable denial message, so the call never runs. Either way, the verdict and the judge's rationale go to Cloud Logging in your project. Responses that contain only text, such as an answer, a plan, or a question back to the user, aren't evaluated, because they take no action.

  • SentenceBERT or SBERT) is a popular open-source library for generating high-quality embeddings that capture semantic meaning.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that today, we are announcing that Sentence Transformers is transitioning from Iryna Gurevych’s Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at the TU Darmstadt to Hugging Face. Hugging Face's Tom Aarsen has already been maintaining the library since late 2023 and will continue to lead the project. At its newly introduced home, Sentence Transformers will benefit from Hugging Face's robust infrastructure, including continuous integration and testing, ensuring that it stays up-to-date with the latest advancements in Information Retrieval and Natural Language Processing.

Sentence Transformers (a.k.a. SentenceBERT or SBERT) is a popular open-source library for generating high-quality embeddings that capture semantic meaning. Since its inception by Nils Reimers in 2019, Sentence Transformers has been widely adopted by researchers and practitioners for various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including semantic search, semantic textual similarity, clustering, and paraphrase mining. After years of development and training by and for the community, over 16,000 Sentence Transformers models are publicly available on the Hugging Face Hub, serving more than a million monthly unique users.

According to recent reports, "Sentence Transformers has been a huge success story and a culmination of our long-standing research on computing semantic similarities for the whole lab. Nils Reimers has made a very timely discovery and has produced not only outstanding research outcomes, but also a highly usable tool. This continues to impact generations of students and practitioners in natural language processing and AI. I would also like to thank all the people and especially the contributors, without whom this project would not be what it is today. And finally, I would like to thank Tom and Hugging Face for taking the project into the future.".

"We're thrilled to officially welcome Sentence Transformers into the Hugging Face family! Over the past two years, it’s been amazing to see this project grow to massive global adoption, thanks to the incredible foundation from the UKP Lab and the amazing community around it. This is just the beginning: we’ll keep doubling down on supporting its growth and innovation, while staying true to the open, collaborative spirit that made it thrive in the first place.".

Recent findings suggest that sentence Transformers will remain a community-driven, open-source project, with the same open-source license (Apache 2.0) as before. Contributions from researchers, developers, and enthusiasts are welcome and encouraged. The project will continue to prioritize transparency, collaboration, and broad accessibility.

According to recent reports, the Sentence Transformers library was introduced in 2019 by Dr. Nils Reimers at the Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at Technische Universität Darmstadt, under the supervision of Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych. Motivated by the limitations of standard BERT embeddings for sentence-level semantic tasks, Sentence-BERT used a Siamese network architecture to produce semantically meaningful sentence embeddings that could be efficiently compared using cosine similarity. Thanks to its modular, open-source design and strong empirical performance on tasks such as semantic textual similarity, clustering, and information retrieval, the library quickly became a staple in the NLP research toolkit, spawning a range of follow-up work and real-world applications that rely on high-quality sentence representations.

In 2020, multilingual support was added to the library, extending sentence embeddings to more than 400 languages. In 2021, with contributions from Nandan Thakur and Dr. Johannes Daxenberger, the library expanded to support pair-wise sentence scoring using Cross Encoder and Sentence Transformer models. Sentence Transformers was also integrated with the Hugging Face Hub (v2.0). For over four years, the UKP Lab team maintained the library as a community-driven open-source project and provided continued research-driven innovation. During this period, the project's development was supported by grants to Prof. Gurevych by the German Research Foundation (DFG), German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF), and Hessen State Ministry for Higher Education, Research and the Arts (HMWK).

In late 2023, Tom Aarsen from Hugging Face took over maintainership of the library, introducing modernized training for Sentence Transformer models (v3.0), as well as improvements of Cross Encoder (v4.0) and Sparse Encoder (v5.0) models.

The Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at Technische Universität Darmstadt, led by Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych, is internationally recognized for its research in natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning. The lab has a long track record of pioneering work in representation learning, large language models, and information retrieval, with numerous publications at leading conferences and journals. Beyond Sentence Transformers, the UKP Lab has developed a number of widely used datasets, benchmarks, and open-source tools that support both academic research and real-world applications.

Hugging Face would like to thank the UKP Lab and all past and present contributors, especially Dr. Nils Reimers and Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych, for their dedication to the project and for entrusting us with its maintenance and now stewardship. We also extend our gratitude to the community of researchers, developers, and practitioners who have contributed to the library's success through model contributions, bug reports, feature requests, documentation improvements, and real-world applications. We are excited to continue building on the strong foundation laid by the UKP Lab and to work with the community to further advance the capabilities of Sentence Transformers.

Fixing Google’s Feedburner problem, and caching that half works

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Joshua

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a previous post, I talked about how Google’s Chrome Releases blog was serving stale results on its Atom feed, and had set up a redirect from its RSS feed (which was serving up-to-date results) to … the stale Atom feed.
  • And the RSS feed (which historically was serving fresh results) was redirecting to the Atom feed:.
  • Well, lo and behold, a few days ago I came to discover that the RSS feed could still be accessed, if you added a secret parameter, ?redirect=false:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a previous post, I talked about how Google’s Chrome Releases blog was serving stale results on its Atom feed, and had set up a redirect from its RSS feed (which was serving up-to-date results) to … the stale Atom feed. This meant results were up to a few days old. This was particularly annoying because my CCBot parsed the blog’s feed to notify me (Opera!) about Chromium vulnerabilities which were fixed. When I wrote that post, the Atom feed was days behind:.

And the RSS feed (which historically was serving fresh results) was redirecting to the Atom feed:.

Well, lo and behold, a few days ago I came to discover that the RSS feed could still be accessed, if you added a secret parameter, ?redirect=false:.

Since we can now pull in fresh results from the Chrome Releases blog, it means that CCBot can start working properly again. Its source is still on GitHub, and I’m sure Opera still uses it (lol).

In terms of the feed caching problem I also previously wrote about, where the Feedburner Atom feed refused any caching techniques which RSS feeds typically allow to be utilized, it turns out the redirect=false feed supports them. Sort of.

According to recent reports, feedburner itself hasn’t changed at all. It still doesn’t send an ETag, it still ignores If-Modified-Since, and it still tells everybody not to cache anything:.

Sources indicate that it’s also still serving outdated results. For example, on the 30th of October, a post published at 07:58 PT was still missing from the Feedburner feed nearly two hours later.

The redirect=false feed, on the other hand, does respond with 304 Not Modified. Sometimes. Because of course it’s inconsistent. The same request, with an If-Modified-Since in the future, made twelve times in a row:.

Looking at the date and age headers, we see the first request in each second gets a full 200, and every request after it in that same second gets a 304 with an age: 0 header.

Sources indicate that age is the header a cache adds when it answers with its own stored copy instead of asking the server behind it. The feed is served with cache-control: public, must-revalidate, proxy-revalidate, max-age=1, so whatever sits in front of Blogger’s blogger-renderd server (presumably some Google frontend) is allowed to keep a copy for one second. While that copy is fresh, the cache handles the If-Modified-Since itself, correctly, and replies with a 304. Once it has expired, the request goes through to blogger-renderd, which ignores If-Modified-Since completely and sends back the whole feed.

Adding a cache-busting parameter to the URL makes every request miss the cache, and then it’s a 200 every single time:.

So for anything that polls the feed every few minutes, the one-second copy will always have expired by the time the next request comes in, and If-Modified-Since never gets a 304.

Sources indicate that what’s also interesting is that If-None-Match does work on the redirect=false feed. The catch is that you get an ETag if and only if you ask for a compressed response (wtf). Without Accept-Encoding: gzip, there’s no ETag at all:.

Asking for only br or zstd doesn’t help, because the server doesn’t support them, so it sends the feed uncompressed, without an ETag.

Once you have the ETag, sending it back in If-None-Match gets a 304 every time, even with the cache-busting parameter (so these all come from blogger-renderd itself), and with or without --compressed:.

In a recent development, this saves quite a bit, which I had originally intended and wanted to do. The full feed is 1,725,860 bytes uncompressed and 57,817 bytes gzipped, and a 304 is practically nothing. Feedburner still sends 55,792 gzipped bytes (1,615,960 uncompressed) every time.

All of this is different to what I found in my original post. Back then, the blogger.com URL was still served by the old GData API (that’s what the sunset and link headers in that post were about), and it answered If-Modified-Since with a 304. Those headers are gone now, and the responses come from server: blogger-renderd (see the redirect=false response at the start of this post), which is the same server that handles the blog’s own feeds on chromereleases.googleblog.com.

That’s probably also the real reason for the redirect in my last post. The documentation I quoted in my original post noted that the old GData feed URLs would keep working, but that “the response is the same as blogspot.com feeds”. The Chrome Releases blog’s own feeds were already redirecting to Feedburner at the time (that’s Blogger’s “Post feed redirect URL” setting), so once the GData API was finally switched off, the blogger.com URL started redirecting too. So it probably wasn’t me emailing Feedburner’s support after all, too bad.

redirect=false is how you get around that setting, and it’s not quite as undocumented as I originally thought: a Feedburner help page about Google Webmaster Tools mentions http://mybloggerblog.blogspot.com/feeds/posts/default?redirect=false as a feed URL format that “should always work” for Blogger owners.

Oh, and the “RSS feed” I’ve been talking about in these posts is actually an Atom feed (content-type: application/atom+xml), and the real RSS version is accessed with ?alt=rss&redirect=false, which behaves exactly the same way on both blogger.com and chromereleases.googleblog.com.

Another interesting thing is that every one of the blog’s feed URLs redirects to http://feeds.feedburner.com/GoogleChromeReleases, with http, not https, even when the feed itself was requested over https:.

That means a feed reader that starts off on https://chromereleases.googleblog.com/feeds/posts/default gets downgraded to plain HTTP when it follows the redirect, and instead of sending it back to https, Feedburner just serves the whole feed over plain HTTP:.

In a recent development, so, if you’re polling a Blogger feed that’s redirected to Feedburner, use ?redirect=false, ask for gzip, keep the ETag, and send it back as If-None-Match. Python’s requests (as used by CCBot) already asks for gzip by default, so it’s only the last two you need to do yourself.

TL;DR - Starting today, every one of the 2.2M+ public model and datasets repositories on the Hugging Face Hub is being continuously scanned with VirusTotal.

With tools like TRL, TorchForge and verl, the open-source community has shown how to scale AI across complex compute infrastructure. But compute is only one side of the coin. The other side is the developer community; the people and tools that make agentic systems possible. That’s why Meta and Hugging Face are partnering to launch the OpenEnv Hub: a shared and open community hub for agentic environments.

It has been revealed that agentic environments define everything an agent needs to perform a task: the tools, APIs, credentials, execution context, and nothing else. They bring clarity, safety, and sandboxed control to agent behavior.

These environments can be used for both training and deployment, and serve as the foundation for scalable agentic development.

Modern AI agents can act autonomously across thousands of tasks. However, a large language model isn’t enough to get those tasks to actually run — it needs access to the right tools. Exposing millions of tools directly to a model isn’t reasonable (or safe). Instead, we need agentic environments: secure, semantically clear sandboxes that define exactly what’s required for a task, and nothing more. These environments handle the critical details:.

Sources indicate that to supercharge this next wave of agentic development, Meta-PyTorch and Hugging Face are partnering to launch a Hub for Environments: a shared space where developers can build, share, and explore OpenEnv-compatible environments for both training and deployment. The figure below reveals how OpenEnv fits in the upcoming post-training stack being developed by Meta, with integrations for other libraries like TRL, SkyRL, and Unsloth underway:.

In the current state of the repository, environment creators can create environments using step(), reset(), close() APIs (part of RFCs below). A few examples on how to create such environments can be seen here. Environment users can play with local Docker based environments for all environments already available in the repo. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago. The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid. There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits announced since that blog post (see 2026 survey), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI.

According to recent reports, the motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong. Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology. GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity. RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences. Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative.

According to recent reports, adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow. Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI. One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework. It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord. My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications. Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia.

In a recent development, the reasons for slow adoption may be melting away. Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging. But AI is changing the game. There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants. So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance?

According to recent reports, for these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming the language for AI rewrites of existing codebases. But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer. I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things.

My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the important quality criteria.

I think this is largely still true, but it depends greatly on which platform is being targeted. Windows still has no clear native choice (see Microsoft Hasn’t Had a Coherent GUI Strategy Since Petzold) and on Mac there is a bit of fragmentation between AppKit and SwiftUI. However, SwiftUI has performance complications (see Michael Tsai blog from 2025) and so it is clearly possible to do better on the performance front.

In a recent development, while desktop UI has remained stagnant, the situation on mobile is a bit different. Platforms continue to invest, and there are many fine details that are important for an app to look and feel native. One very notable example is Liquid Glass on iOS – if you use UIKit or SwiftUI, you can get that with little effort, but apps built with cross-platform toolkits won’t quite seem right. In addition, making gesture recognition, scroll dynamics, and IME 100% match the platform are not yet fully solved problems.

Industry observers note that thus, for mobile, an extremely viable path is to use the native toolkit for UI but do the common “business logic” in Rust. I’m not sure about the business logic, but for the UI, this is the decision that Shopify has made recently, abandoning React Native. I believe 1Password has this architecture. This is also the "Phoenix" initiative for Discord on mobile, while using GPUI on desktop.

That stated, there's been considerable progress in trying to build mobile UI entirely in Rust. Below is a short screencast of the editor demo in android-view. You can see that a lot of IME functionality works, including swiping, moving the cursor by rolling the space bar, and deleting in semantic chunks. Not shown in the video below, but composition regions (needed for CJK) also work, and there's basic accessibility through AccessKit.

Sources indicate that one of the significant unsolved problems as of the 2022 blog post was text layout. It is of course a hard problem to get right. I’m pleased to say that the ecosystem now has a good solution, in the form of Parley. It’s gotten there as a result of sustained investment from Google, Canva, and Dioxus (now Cognition), as well as contributions from the community. It seems to be used in the majority of new Rust UI toolkits. In addition, to help mitigate the risk of monoculture, Cosmic Text is a viable alternative.

It has been revealed that accessKit was just getting started in 2022, but is now solid infrastructure as well, and used by most UI toolkits. I should note, though, there is a difference between a good integration and a box ticking exercise. And there is more work to be done, for example to make rich text editing fully accessible. One other problem I'd like to see addressed is performance degradation when accessibility is enabled. This is a problem for egui in particular, as it has to build and diff a tree each animation frame, undercutting the benefits of its underlying immediate mode design.

Sources indicate that one topic I talked about extensively in the 2022 blog post is leveraging the system compositor. This problem is even more pressing today, especially with the increased importance of video. You really want a video playing in a hardware accelerated layer when possible, and on low end devices it’s the only hope for getting smooth frame rates.

Industry observers note that there has been some progress, notably the subduction library, but it certainly isn’t commonly integrated into UI toolkits yet. To do it well is a challenging problem, as the capabilities provided by the platform vary widely. Ideally there’s a rich and high level interface, something like CALayer on Apple platforms, and polyfills to implement that interface as well as possible on other platforms. On Android, when the task is something simple, like overlaying some GUI controls on a video, it would use SurfaceFlinger layers, but when it involves more sophisticated compositing, it would run shaders on the GPU.

Industry observers note that this is absolutely something we should build, ideally as a high quality community project rather than something with dozens of vibe-coded forks. But even in the latter case it’s better for it to exist than not.

Industry observers note that one of the challenges of the Rust UI ecosystem is that different applications have different needs. The idea of a single, unified UI for completely general purpose use may be behind us, especially now that LLMs can optimize and fine tune for specific use cases.

That’s been playing out architecturally in the choice between immediate mode and retained mode. Immediate mode is very appealing because it’s less total code and seems quite a bit simpler. And for some applications (most especially development support for games) it works well. However, I am concerned it won’t scale especially well. In short, it’s good at the first 90%, but it makes the second 90% harder. To be considered really production-ready, it has to establish stable widget identities to build and enhancement the accessibility tree, and it has to reliably cache expensive intermediate artifacts such as text layouts (simple immediate mode often gets around this by cutting corners in text layout, which may be fine for gamedev). And of course, it pulls strongly towards a model of re-rendering everything every frame rather than exploiting layers in the compositor.

Sources indicate that for this reason among others, I am not impressed by the choice of the ArtCraft projects to use egui. I do think egui is a really good implementation of the immediate mode paradigm in Rust, and it does solve a number of problems (including accessibility, something mainline Iced does not yet support), but it wouldn’t be my first choice for productivity and design applications. The egui README is quite honest on the advantages and disadvantages, and is worth consulting.

According to recent reports, one theme that’s emerging from trying to do LLM-assisted software engineering well is having clearly scoped modules, ideally with solid specifications of what the module does. Within a module, given clear objectives such as performance and robustness against adverse inputs, an LLM can do very well.

This philosophy is in tension with what has historically worked well. People reasonably choose a UI toolkit based on how good it looks. In particular, Apple UI frameworks have an immense amount of design knowledge baked in, especially in the defaults. With very little effort, it’s possible for a developer to make an app that looks and feels like a Mac app, even if not very polished.

In a recent development, I think in the future we should be moving toward a separation of design and execution. Both are hard problems, but very different. I’m especially excited about how much room there is to improve the execution side when really optimizing. As discussed in the 2022 blog post, the computer science core of a UI toolkit is an incremental computation engine.

In a recent development, having a good spec at the interface between design and execution is critically crucial. As a general strategy, I suggest adapting web standards, but not following them slavishly. Web standards are an impressive and important artifact. A huge amount of time and energy has gone into producing them, and there’s also a lot of care to making things work cross-platform. The extensive WPT tests are the true magic of the spec, aiding correctness in the multiple high quality open source implementations. All this goes a long way to explaining why Electron is popular.

Sources indicate that that remarked, strictly adhering to web standards has serious downsides. DOM is slow and memory-intensive; a lighter weight tree representation with a bulk mutation interface might serve the need of GUI apps better. Full CSS style resolution and layout is also expensive, though CSS is a rich and powerful way to describe styling. A subset of CSS carefully curated for efficiency might be useful. I’ve done experiments in implementing selectors as an efficient state machine that supports incremental evaluation, at the expense of fancier CSS features such as sibling selectors.

The Web is also lacking a solid way to represent virtualized lists, a core feature of every efficient UI toolkit. A spec here requires nailing down the interface with the data model, preserving incrementality.

Blitz, as a modular browser engine, is well placed to serve as the cornerstone of hybrid approaches borrowing heavily from Web specs, but also adapting them to be higher performance and more tightly integrated with platform capabilities. As just one example, it’s possible to start with Stylo as the CSS selector engine, and then replace it with a leaner, more efficient CSS engine if that proves to be practical.

One good example of separation of concerns into smaller modules is the Xilem/Masonry split. The Xilem reactive layer was designed to be independent of the actual elements it controls, and indeed it has instantiations both for DOM (which, among other things, is the infrastructure for the squircle interactive demo) and Masonry widgets. Masonry, on the other hand, was designed to be independent of the reactive layer and indeed the language for the layer above it.

It has been revealed that by contrast, SwiftUI mashes together the low level widget implementation, the reactivity framework, and the language as well; Swift runtime reflection is part of the execution engine. Obviously SwiftUI has had a lot farther reach than Xilem, but my argument today is that we should reconsider assumptions as things are rapidly changing.

Given a UI design encoded in a certain way – which can be code, data, or a combination of the two in a DSL – an engine has a number of opportunities to optimize the execution of that design. Perhaps a lot of this section is gilding the lily, as a straightforward evaluation of the design in optimized Rust code will outperform almost any shipping GUI. But I’m interested in the limits of what performance is possible. Can we get silky smooth UI even on low end Android phones? I think the answer is yes, and the question worth exploring.

One useful tactic may be separating out the static from the dynamic parts of the design, and precomputing the static parts. That in no way precludes the design having dynamic parts; it's just that it may be possible to avoid the cost of a fully dynamic implementation.

It has been revealed that another fruitful avenue for optimization is optimizing the use of layers, to be composited either using the system compositor or a lightweight GPU-accelerated polyfill. Using layers effectively can dramatically improve performance, mostly by avoiding re-rendering of parts of the interface that haven't changed. However, layers have a RAM cost, and using too many layers can actually slow things down, as allocating upcoming layers has to go through calls to the underlying system. Getting this right is a tricky optimization problem, and a good use of either measurement or analysis. UI toolkits generally either use heuristics, which are not always perfect, or explicit hints (like .drawingGroup() in SwiftUI or RepaintBoundary in Flutter).

Sources indicate that for a deeper dive into performance questions, see A Critique of GPUI. Ideally, there aren't huge performance differences between UI toolkits, as all low hanging fruit should be picked. We expect implementations of system languages to be quite comparable in performance, but still tolerate wide discrepancies in GUI performance.

Three wheeled vehicles have been tried.

In a recent development, the vast majority of what you're referring to are delta configuration, not tadpole configuration. They have radically different driving dynamics. A tadpole configuration has almost the exact same driving dynamics as a four-wheeled vehicle, because as you brake, your CG (already rather forward) shifts further forward, toward between the two front wheels. In a delta trike, however, that forward-shifted CG basically induces a pivot on a single point (the single front wheel), making them highly unstable. Also, modern EVs are inherently rollover to begin with, due to their low CG. A tadpole EV is well more rollover resistant than a four-wheeled ICE vehicle.

Losing the second rear wheel isn't simply regulatory, it has some pretty dramatic mass and aero benefits.

Nothing against Aptera specifically, but when a company hangs around for 20 years, while exchanging ownership hands several times without actually producing anything for customers, I start to get skeptical.

Aptera got very close to this moment before. I actually at one point got ahold of a copy of their internal production tables, the first time around. The problem is that once they got close (about three months out from customer car production start), Idealab - their main investor - decided that they needed to bring in "experts from Detroit" to run the tech giant. They brought in Paul Wilbur, who had ran four separate companies into the ground. He paid himself a grossly disproportionate salary for a startup and filled it with his scumbag friends (including for example a woman involved in the Delphi accounting scandal as CFO, and a CMO who spent most of his time hitting on the women in the office and regularly submitted strip club receipts as corporate expenses for reimbursement) (I'm not surprised Paul liked him, Paul was fond of bragging to the guys about his "wedding ring trick", where when he saw a woman he wanted to hit on, he'd put his hand into his pocket, then with no visible motion, remove it without his ring on). He decided he didn't like the vehicle, or the in-house production looks, and set out to basically redo everything. All of the changes he made made it less efficient, which made the battery pack have to grow, which made it look bloated, bulbous (common descriptions for the revision were that looked like a whale, or that it looked pregnant), with much worse stability and performance, and his plan to outsource all of the production to Tier 1s made it much more expensive (the figures they were quoted were insane compared to the inhouse costs).

While investment had poured in under the founders, it completely dried up under Paul. When the founders went to Idealab complaining that he was destroying the company, Idealab sided with Paul (who had spent most of his time schmoozing up to them). Paul immediately retaliated by firing not just the founders, but everyone he felt was more loyal to them than him. He marched the chief engineer out of the office in front of everyone else under armed guard. He fired the founder's wife over the phone from her hospital bed where she was undergoing treatment for cervical cancer. Etc. He continued on burning through the company's cash, on and on, ultimately bankrupted it, and its assets were grabbed up for cheap by a Chinese buyer. A lot of Aptera's talent ended up being snatched up by Tesla. As a final parting shot, when emptying out the factory, rather than sell the remaining shells to hobbyists, they crushed them with forklifts [youtube.com].

The founders bounced around between different projects for a while while the EV revolution slowly took off without them. Steve worked at a vertical farming startup. Chris, who came into Aptera from his fiberglass speedboat manufacturer, had some spinoffs of that. Eventually, though, Aptera's assets came up for sale. They managed to get some investment, buy them back, and started over.

Blaming them for what happened the last time around is, IMHO, deeply unfair. They didn't have the votes to override Idealab. They tried to stop what was happening. And they were booted out of the firm for it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're thrilled to announce a series of significant advancements across LeRobot, designed to make open-source robot learning more powerful, scalable, and user-friendly than ever before! From revamped datasets to versatile editing tools, newly introduced simulation environments, and a groundbreaking plugin system for hardware, LeRobot is continuously evolving to meet the demands of cutting-edge embodied AI.

LeRobot v0.4.0 delivers a major upgrade for open-source robotics, introducing scalable Datasets v3.0, powerful latest VLA models like PI0.5 and GR00T N1.5, and a new plugin system for easier hardware integration. The release also adds support for LIBERO and Meta-World simulations, simplified multi-GPU training, and a new Hugging Face Robot Learning Course.

In a recent development, we've completely overhauled our dataset infrastructure with LeRobotDataset v3.0, featuring a new chunked episode format and streaming capabilities. This is a game-changer for handling massive datasets like OXE (Open X Embodiment) and Droid, bringing unparalleled efficiency and scalability.

We've also provided a conversion script to easily migrate your existing v2.1 datasets to the latest v3.0 format, ensuring a smooth transition. Read more about it in our previous blog post. Open-source robotics keeps leveling up!

Working with LeRobot datasets just got a whole lot easier! We've introduced a powerful set of utilities for flexible dataset editing.

With our new lerobot-edit-dataset CLI, you can now:.

Recent findings suggest that these tools streamline your workflow, allowing you to curate and optimize your robot datasets like never before. Check out the docs for more details!

We're continuously expanding LeRobot's simulation capabilities to provide richer and more diverse training environments for your robotic policies.

LeRobot now officially supports LIBERO, one of the largest open benchmarks for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, boasting over 130 tasks! This is a huge step toward building the go-to evaluation hub for VLAs, enabling easy integration and a unified setup for evaluating any VLA policy.

Check out the LIBERO dataset and our docs to get started!

We've integrated Meta-World, a premier benchmark for testing multi-task and generalization abilities in robotic manipulation, featuring over 50 diverse manipulation tasks. This integration, along with our standardized use of gymnasium ≥ 1.0.0 and mujoco ≥ 3.0.0, ensures deterministic seeding and a robust simulation foundation.

Train your policies with the Meta-World dataset today!

We're making robot control more flexible and accessible, enabling new possibilities for data collection and model training.

Industry observers note that getting data from a robot to a model (and back!) is tricky. Raw sensor data, joint positions, and language instructions don't match what AI models expect. Models need normalized, batched tensors on the right device, while your robot hardware needs specific action commands.

It has been revealed that we're excited to introduce Processors: a newly introduced, modular pipeline that acts as a universal translator for your data. Think of it as an assembly line where each ProcessorStep handles one specific job—like normalizing, tokenizing text, or moving data to the GPU.

According to recent reports, you can chain these steps together into a powerful pipeline to perfectly manage your data flow. We've even created two distinct types to make life easier:.

This system makes it simple to connect any policy to any robot, ensuring your data is always in the perfect format for every step of the way. Learn more about it in our Introduction to Processors documentation.

It has been revealed that training large robot policies just got a lot faster! We've integrated Accelerate directly into our training pipeline, making it incredibly simple to scale your experiments across multiple GPUs with just one command:.

Recent findings suggest that whether you're fine-tuning a policy or running large-scale experiments, LeRobot now handles all the complexities of distributed training for you. This means you can drastically reduce training time, cutting it in half with 2 GPUs, down to a third with 3 GPUs, and beyond.

Check out the documentation to accelerate your robot learning!

Sources indicate that in a major milestone for open-source robotics, we've integrated pi0 and pi0.5 policies by Physical Intelligence into LeRobot! These Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models represent a significant leap towards addressing open-world generalization in robotics. But what makes π₀.₅ revolutionary?

Recent findings suggest that you can find the models on the Hugging Face Hub: pi0.5_base, pi0_base, and their Libero-tuned counterparts. For more details, checkout the Physical Intelligence Reasearch.

Industry observers note that in another exciting development, we've integrated NVIDIA's GR00T N1.5 into LeRobot, thanks to a fantastic collaboration with the NVIDIA robotics team! This open foundation model is a powerhouse for generalized robot reasoning and skills. As a cross-embodiment model, it takes multimodal input (like language and images) to perform complex manipulation tasks in diverse environments, marking another major leap in generalized robotics. But what makes GR00T N1.5 a game-changer?

You can find the model on the Hugging Face Hub: GR00T-N1.5-3B. For more details, check out the NVIDIA research page and the official GitHub repository.

It has been revealed that the native integration of these policies in lerobot is a huge step forward in making robot learning as open and reproducible as it can be. Try them out today, share your runs, and let's push forward the frontier of embodied AI together!

In a recent development, substantial news for hardware enthusiasts! We've debuted a brand-latest plugin system to revolutionize how you integrate third-party hardware with LeRobot. Now, connecting any robot, camera, or teleoperator is as simple as a pip install, eliminating the need to modify the core library.

Learn how to create your own plugin in our documentation.

Thanks to our upcoming plugin system, we've also added Reachy 2 from Pollen Robotics to LeRobot! Reachy 2 is available for both real robot control and simulation, enabling you to experiment with teleoperation and autonomous demos right away.

Thanks to our powerful new pipeline system, you can now teleoperate your follower arm right from your phone (iOS/Android). The phone acts as a teleoperator device, and our RobotProcessor pipeline handles all the transformations, allowing you to drive robots in different action spaces (like end-effector space) with ease. Check out the examples!

We're launching a comprehensive, self-paced, and entirely open-source course designed to make robot learning accessible to everyone! If you're curious about how real-world robots learn, this is the perfect place to start.

In this course, you’ll learn how to:.

Join the Hugging Face Robotics organization to follow along and start your journey!

For those who want to go deeper, we've also published a hands-on tutorial on the most recent advancements in robotics. This guide provides self-contained explanations, re-derives modern techniques from first principles, and includes ready-to-use code examples using LeRobot and Hugging Face.

The tutorial itself is hosted in a Space and it features practical examples using LeRobot, with all models and datasets on the Hugging Hub. You can also check out our paper for a detailed overview.

Beyond these major features, this release is packed with numerous bug fixes, documentation improvements, updated dependencies, more examples and better infrastructure to make your experience with LeRobot smoother and more reliable.

Industry observers note that we want to extend a huge thank you to everyone in the community for your invaluable contributions, feedback, and support. We're incredibly excited about the future of open-source robotics and can't wait to work with you on what's next!

Stay tuned for more to come 🤗 Get started here! – The LeRobot team ❤️.

Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple, Google, and Microsoft called out for failing to provide developers with adequate AI agent controls.
  • Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns.
  • Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker noted similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple, Google, and Microsoft called out for failing to provide developers with adequate AI agent controls.

Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns.

Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker noted similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private.

"Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post.

In a recent development, "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.".

The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private.

Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text.

Whittaker notes that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents.

Screenshot blocking, Whittaker concedes, is only a partial solution since AI agents may have other ways to access application data through the device file system.

"We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she stated.

According to recent reports, "Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.".

Recent findings suggest that apple is taking some action to implement protection from AI agents on macOS, though it appears to be doing so largely to defend against third-party access to data rather than to limit its own Siri service. Siri can be turned off separately.

It has been revealed that with macOS 27.3, currently in public beta testing, Apple's desktop operating system will get more granular controls on two APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. The result will be more permission prompts for users of macOS apps that seek access to user data, and the inconvenience of applying for an entitlement from Apple to obtain Full Disk Access for backup software and assistive technologies that use Accessibility APIs.

"As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," Apple stated when it introduced the Full Disk Access change. "We are committed to ensuring consumers clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.".

Apple is also reportedly working on its own AI agent in a bid to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. It remains to be seen whether Apple will use its operating system ownership as competitive leverage against AI firms that threaten its gatekeeping power, as it has done with web browsers.

While Apple casts itself as an ally that's helping to defend device customers against prying AI agents, Signal's decision to block Siri reveals that AI agents have complicated trust decisions and the competitive landscape. AI agents are supposed to serve the user but when they spirit data away to the cloud and come between customers and merchants, they wear out their welcome.

AI agents also threaten the business relationship between consumers and merchants.

According to recent reports, amazon has blocked shopping agents like Meta Muse from its e-commerce site (though not AWS Marketplace) while Walmart has invited third-party agents to interact through its AI Gateway. Anthropic has blocked subscription customers from using third-party harnesses. United Airlines has banned transactions from unauthorized AI bots. Similar barriers or limitations related to third-party AI agents have been erected by Target, Home Depot, Etsy, eBay, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo, among others.

Meanwhile, there's a burgeoning industry in bot detection and mitigation, led by the likes of Cloudflare, Akamai, and DataDome, to name a few.

The web browser is sometimes referred to as a user agent, based on the idealistic notion that it serves its user. That vision has been muddied by online advertising and data collection, and default settings that often serve the interests of browser makers instead of promoting privacy.

It has been revealed that now AI agents face the same scrutiny as people wonder whether their agents really serve them or someone else. After a year or two of agent vendors arguing for access to all digital data for the sake of personalization and context, the backlash has arrived. ®.

According to recent reports, it seems simple...Are you an artist ? If $ANSWER=NO goto $ARTIST. You wouldn't hire a sales person to program your game. You don't hire a programmer to do art work.
