huggingface_hub v1.0: Five Years of Building the Foundation of Open Machine Learning

📅 27 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1925 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: After five years of development, huggingface_hub has reached v1.0 - a milestone that marks the library's maturity as the Python package powering 200,000 dependent libraries and providing core functionality for accessing over 2 million public models, 0.5 million public datasets, and 1 million public Spaces.
  • 🚀 We highly recommend upgrading to v1.0 to benefit from major performance improvements and newly introduced capabilities.
  • Major changes in this release include the migration to httpx as the backend library, a completely redesigned hf CLI (which replaces the deprecated huggingface-cli) featuring a Typer-based interface with a significantly expanded feature set, and full adoption of hf_xet for file transfers, replacing the legacy hf_transfer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: After five years of development, huggingface_hub has reached v1.0 - a milestone that marks the library's maturity as the Python package powering 200,000 dependent libraries and providing core functionality for accessing over 2 million public models, 0.5 million public datasets, and 1 million public Spaces. This release introduces breaking changes designed to support the next decade of open machine learning, driven by a global community of almost 300 contributors and millions of users.

🚀 We highly recommend upgrading to v1.0 to benefit from major performance improvements and newly introduced capabilities.

Major changes in this release include the migration to httpx as the backend library, a completely redesigned hf CLI (which replaces the deprecated huggingface-cli) featuring a Typer-based interface with a significantly expanded feature set, and full adoption of hf_xet for file transfers, replacing the legacy hf_transfer. You can find the full release notes here.

We’ve worked hard to ensure that huggingface_hub v1.0.0 remains backward compatible. In practice, most ML libraries should work seamlessly with both v0.x and v1.x versions. The main exception is transformers, which explicitly requires huggingface_hub v0.x in its v4 releases and v1.x in its upcoming v5 release. For a detailed compatibility overview across libraries, refer to the table in this issue.

Every major library has a story. For huggingface_hub, it began with a simple idea: what if sharing machine learning models could be as easy as sharing code on GitHub?

In a recent development, in the early days of the Hugging Face Hub, researchers and practitioners faced a common frustration. Training a state-of-the-art model required significant compute resources and expertise. Once trained, these models often lived in isolation, stored on local machines and shared via (broken) Google Drive links. The AI community was duplicating work, wasting resources, and missing opportunities for collaboration.

Recent findings suggest that the Hugging Face Hub emerged as the answer to this challenge. Initially, it was primarily used to share checkpoints compatible with the transformers library. All the Python code for interacting with the Hub lived within this library, making it inaccessible for other libraries to reuse.

In a recent development, in late 2020, we shipped huggingface_hub v0.0.1 with a simple mission: extract the internal logic from transformers and create a dedicated library that would unify how to access and share machine learning models and datasets on the Hugging Face Hub. Initially, the library was as straightforward as a Git wrapper for downloading files and managing repositories. Five years and 35+ releases later, huggingface_hub has evolved far beyond its origins.

It has been revealed that the early releases established the basics. Version 0.0.8 introduced our first APIs, wrapping Git commands to interact with repositories. Version 0.0.17 brought token-based authentication, enabling secure access to private repositories and uploads. These were humble beginnings, but they laid the groundwork for everything that followed.

In a recent development, in June 2022, version 0.8.1 marked a pivotal moment: we introduced the HTTP Commit API. Instead of requiring Git and Git LFS installations, users could now upload files directly through HTTP requests. The new create_commit() API simplified workflows dramatically, especially for large model files that are cumbersome to use with Git LFS. In addition, a git-aware cache file layout was introduced. All libraries (not only transformers, but third party ones as well) would now share the same cache, with explicit versioning and file deduplication.

This wasn't just a technical improvement. It was a philosophical shift. We were no longer building a Git wrapper for transformers; we were building purpose-built infrastructure for machine learning artifacts that could power any library in the ML ecosystem.

According to recent reports, as the Hub grew from a model repository into a full platform, huggingface_hub kept pace with an expanding API surface. Core repository primitives matured: listing trees, browsing refs and commits, reading files or syncing folders, managing tags, branches, and release cycles. Repository metadata and webhooks rounded up the offering so teams could react to changes in real time.

It has been revealed that in parallel, Spaces emerged as a simple yet powerful way to host and share interactive ML demos directly on the Hub. Over time, huggingface_hub gained full programmatic control to deploy and manage Spaces (hardware requests, secrets, environment configuration, uploads). To deploy models on production-scale infrastructure, Inference Endpoints were integrated as well. Finally, the Jobs API came later (Q3 2025) to complete our compute offering.

It has been revealed that the social and community layers became first-class citizens too: from APIs for pull requests and comments, to user and organization info, repository likes, following and followers, all the way through Collections to curate and share sets of related resources. Everyday ergonomics improved too: seamless authentication in Colab, resumable downloads, reliable uploads of large-scale folders, and more.

Then came version 0.28.0 and the Inference Providers ecosystem. Instead of a single inference backend, we partnered with multiple serverless providers (Together AI, SambaNova, Replicate, Cerebras, Groq, and more) to serve one API with transparent routing. We adopted a pay-per-request inference architecture that matched how people actually wanted to work.

Version 0.30.0 introduced Xet, a groundbreaking new protocol for storing large objects in Git repositories. Unlike Git LFS, which deduplicates at the file level, Xet operates at the chunk level (64KB chunks). When you update a large file in a dataset or a model, only the changed chunks are uploaded or downloaded, not the entire file.

According to recent reports, the migration was massive, starting with 20 petabytes across over 500,000 repositories. Yet it happened transparently, with full backward compatibility. One year later, all 77PB+ over 6,000,000 repositories have been migrated to the Xet backend, allowing for much faster (and smarter!) uploads and downloads. This happened with no user intervention, and no disruption to existing workflows 🔥.

It has been revealed that measuring the growth and impact of an open-source library is a tricky task. Numbers tell a story of their own:.

According to recent reports, but the real scale becomes clear when you look at the ecosystem. huggingface_hub is a dependency for over 200,000 repositories on GitHub and 3,000 packages on PyPI, powering everything from major third-party frameworks like Keras, LangChain, PaddleOCR, ChatTTS, YOLO, Google Generative AI, Moshi, NVIDIA NeMo, and Open Sora, to countless smaller libraries and tools across the ML landscape. Our own ecosystem (transformers, diffusers, datasets, sentence-transformers, lighteval, gradio, peft, trl, smolagents, timm, lerobot, etc.) benefits from this foundation as well.

Sources indicate that the remarkable part? Most of the third-party integrations happened organically, and we played no role in them. The Hugging Face Hub empowers the ML community in countless ways, yet we're continually humbled by how far it has gone and how widely it's used.

Recent findings suggest that version 1.0 isn't just about reaching a milestone. It's about building the foundation for the next decade of open machine learning. The breaking changes we've made aren't arbitrary; they're strategic decisions that position huggingface_hub to scale with the explosive growth of AI while maintaining the reliability that millions of developers depend on.

Sources indicate that the most significant architectural change in v1.0 is our migration from requests to httpx. This isn't just dependency churn. It's a fundamental upgrade that brings the library into the modern era of HTTP.

According to recent reports, why httpx? The benefits are substantial: native HTTP/2 support for better connection efficiency and true thread safety that enables safe connection reuse across multiple threads. Most importantly, httpx provides a unified API for both synchronous and asynchronous operations, eliminating the subtle behavioral differences that existed between our sync and async inference clients.

The migration was designed to be as transparent as possible. Most users won't need to change anything. For those with custom HTTP backends, we've provided clear migration paths from configure_http_backend() to set_client_factory() and set_async_client_factory().

Additionally, hf_xet is now the default package for uploading and downloading files to and from the Hub, replacing the previously optional hf_transfer, which has now been fully removed.

Recent findings suggest that version 0.32.0 introduced Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration and tiny-agents, fundamentally changing how developers build AI agents. What once required complex framework integration now takes approximately 70 lines of Python.

In a recent development, the MCPClient provides a standardized way for AI agents to interact with tools, while the tiny-agents CLI lets you run agents directly from the Hub. Connect to local or remote MCP servers, use any Gradio Space as a tool, and build conversational agents that feel natural and responsive.

Sources indicate that all of this is built on top of our existing InferenceClient and the dozens of Inference Providers it supports. We do believe Agents are the future, and huggingface_hub is there to provide the building blocks that enable AI builders to play with them.

In a recent development, the CLI has evolved from a simple command-line tool into a comprehensive interface for ML operations. The streamlined hf command replaces the legacy huggingface-cli with a modern resource-action pattern:.

The CLI comes with a sandboxed installer, making it easy to upgrade without breaking existing dev environments:.

With autocompletion support and an installer that works across platforms, the CLI now feels as polished as any modern developer tool.

It has been revealed that version 1.0 removes legacy patterns that were holding us back. The Git-based Repository class is gone. HTTP-based methods like upload_file() and create_commit() are simpler, more reliable, and better suited for modern workflows. The HfFolder token management has been replaced with explicit login(), logout(), and get_token() functions. The old InferenceApi class has been superseded by the more feature-complete InferenceClient. hf_transfer has been fully replaced by hf_xet binary package.

These changes weren't made lightly. Most deprecations were declared months in advance with clear warnings and migration guidance. The result is a cleaner, more maintainable codebase that can focus on forward-looking features rather than supporting deprecated patterns.

We understand that breaking changes are disruptive. That's why we've invested heavily in making the migration as smooth as possible. Our comprehensive migration guide provides step-by-step instructions for every change with explanations of why each change was necessary.

Most importantly, we've maintained backward compatibility wherever possible. HfHubHttpError, for example, inherits from both the old requests and upcoming httpx base HTTPError classes, ensuring that error handling continues to work across versions. With this release, we're fully committing to the future and we will focus exclusively on v1.0 and beyond, ensuring we can deliver the performance, features, and tools the community needs to interact with the Hugging Face Hub. Previous v0.* versions will remain available on PyPI, but they will only receive vulnerability updates.

We’ve worked hard to ensure that huggingface_hub v1.0.0 remains backward compatible. In practice, most ML libraries should work seamlessly with both v0.x and v1.x versions. The main exception is transformers, which explicitly requires huggingface_hub v0.x in its v4 releases and v1.x in its upcoming v5 release. For a detailed compatibility overview across libraries, refer to the table in this matter.

To our 280+ contributors who built this library through code, documentation, translations, and community support, thank you!

We’re also deeply grateful to the entire Hugging Face community for their feedback, bug reports, and suggestions that have shaped this library.

In a recent development, finally, a huge thank you to our users -from individual developers to large enterprises- for trusting huggingface_hub to power your workflows. Your support drives us to keep improving and innovating.

Sources indicate that please star us on GitHub ⭐ to show your support and help us continue building the foundation of open machine learning. It has been five years, but it is still only the beginning!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Agent Anomaly Detection is in Private Preview, including monitoring for agents that run outside Google Cloud. To request access, see the Agent Anomaly Detection overview.

Our launch post introduced Agent Anomaly Detection, which helps you understand and act on agent behavior that drifts outside its intended boundaries. It covered agents on Google Cloud, such as Agent Runtime, Cloud Run, and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Many teams also run agents on other clouds: on AWS Lambda next to an inventory database, as a hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry, or on-premises next to a system that can't move. Those agents carry the same behavioral risks, and until now Agent Anomaly Detection couldn't review them.

According to recent reports, agent Anomaly Detection works from an agent's traces and logs, so it doesn't need access to the agent's runtime. If those traces and logs reach your Google Cloud project, it can detect anomalous behavior wherever the agent runs. In this post, we explain what Agent Anomaly Detection needs from an agent on other cloud, then show what it found for an agent on AWS Lambda and an agent on Microsoft Foundry.

It has been revealed that agent Anomaly Detection reads the logging and observability buckets that you choose when you enable it. Telemetry from anywhere works when:.

Agents built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) for Python, version 2.12.0 or later, can produce this telemetry with ADK's Google Cloud exporters and a few environment variables, which the next section highlights.

Visa, Mastercard theft included info useful for phishing, but not draining bank accounts, say researchers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses.
  • On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information.
  • Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

No financial details, but plenty of other clues.

Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses.

On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information.

Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand.

Researchers at SOCRadar, a threat-intelligence firm that has been tracking n0n since it emerged in September, have parsed all 14 files in the n0n’s published Visa and Mastercard archives, and told us that the files don’t contain any financial details belonging to banking customers.

“We found no card numbers, expiry dates, CVVs, passwords, dates of birth, or home addresses in any file,” Ensar Seker, SOCRadar chief information security officer, told The Register. “Visa's statement that no card numbers were affected matches our scan.”.

Mastercard previously mentioned that stolen data included a “limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information” from a subset of cardholders in a benefits program.

According to SOCRadar’s analysis, the leaked files do contain mobile numbers, Bank Identification Number (BIN) prefixes, and dated airline, hotel, and restaurant bookings. So while the data doesn’t include card or account numbers that crooks could use to drain customers' bank accounts or rack up massive credit card bills, “that detail is what a fraudster needs to pose as a concierge desk or a bank,” in an email or voice-phishing social engineering attack, Seker noted.

Sources indicate that it’s also worth noting that the published files only represent about 0.4 percent of the data n0n claims to have hoovered up in the breach: about 4.3 GB and 1.9 million marketing events. “So a further release is possible,” according to Seker.

Plus, both datasets come from the same upstream provider, we’re told. They use the same 27-column booking layout, placeholder text,  and CRM ID format, Seker remarked, noting that the most recent record in each stops 69 seconds apart on Oct 26.

“This looks like two card programs run on one provider's platform,” he mentioned. “The pattern looks like a batch copy from a marketing and reporting store.”.

The security shop hasn’t analyzed the Chase customer data that n0n also claimed to have published.

All three financial firms attributed the compromises to a third-party provider, and while nothing in the stolen files name the vendor, the timing matches up with a Qubole supply-chain campaign disclosed earlier this month by Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders and AI data security company Sentra.

In that attack, which the threat hunters mentioned began on October 14, cybercrims used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access dozens of downstream-customers’ environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets.

N0n also claimed to have carried out this attack. “The timing fits the Qubole supply-chain campaign,” Seker noted, adding that this is his organization’s assessment, not a confirmed finding. "If it's right, Qubole would be the access path rather than the holder of the data, and the files point to a concierge-services operator behind the brands.”.

Qubole’s parent company Idera did not respond to The Register’s inquiries. The financial institutions declined to answer our questions about which provider(s) was compromised in the breach, and whether Qubole was the access path by which their customers’ data was exposed.®.

#126408. My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75%

📅 2026-11-15 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1532 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tymscar ↗ Open Full Page

My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75%

📅 2026-11-15 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1532 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tymscar

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet.
  • Industry observers note that my ISP is pretty cool.
  • I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite!

Industry observers note that my ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed.

I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.

In a recent development, but as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR. I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦.

Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know.

I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again.

Sources indicate that so it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason.

In a recent development, the adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website, so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault.

Industry observers note that then I tried flow control. I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast….

I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my Sauerbraten game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be.

In a recent development, yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more than that from my external SSD through the monitor’s Thunderbolt port. So the issue is not the monitor again? But it has to be!

Well, I had another idea. How about I connect to my Linux box, which is also on 2.5, and send perfectly smooth UDP traffic at a fixed rate with flow control off? Then I can check the chip’s own counter of dropped frames:.

So basically no drops whatsoever when connected straight to my Mac, but loads of drops after about 168k frames per second (roughly 2 Gbps). Remember that number. That number comes from the adapter’s own counters: however much I sent, the number of frames it managed to hand over to the Mac each second flattened out at about 168,000, and everything above that was dropped.

Why did this not happen on my SSD? What was the only difference I could find? Bursts!

When the Mac reads data from a USB 3 device, the device sends some packets, then has to wait for the Mac to say “lgtm, send more!”. The SSD enclosure sends 16 packets before needing a go-ahead message back. The RTL8156B in my Ethernet adapter sends 4.

Here is a diagram of my best understanding of why this is an glitch. I made this diagram 100 times, and I think I can probably improve it more, but if it helps you understand the issue, I have done my job.

Industry observers note that as you can see, the speed of packets coming into the adapter is 2.5 Gbps. That’s what the router pushes in. The speed going out is around 2 Gbps. The reason is that if you add up the average time it takes to get the go-ahead through my monitor’s hub, which is around 7.6 µs, to the average time it takes to send 4 KB, around 8.2 µs, you can find what the maximum speed is.

Well, if the speed of the drain from my adapter to my Mac is half a gig slower than the speed of the input, then you can imagine the buffer getting filled more and more until it overflows. Those are dropped packets, which result in a hard backoff when the router resends them, so you drop loads in speed. And that’s the reason for all of this.

Sources indicate that I have a cupboard full of USB-C Ethernet adapters. Don’t ask.

The problem is they’re all 1 gig adapters, so any of the tests I made would not tell me anything, because the complications don’t start at 1 gig. They start at around 2… If I run my 2.5 gig adapter at 1 gig speeds, I get 1 gig downloads with the official driver. If I run it at 1.5, I get 1.5. If I run it at 2, well, I get 1….

Industry observers note that so I thought I would do what any human would do, and I spent more money on a latest adapter. Another UGREEN, but this time it’s one that promises 5 Gbps and uses the RTL8157 chip instead: UGREEN 5G USB-C Ethernet adapter. My reasoning was that if this one could get me better speeds, it would help me understand how. And that it did!

With this adapter, I dropped 0 frames:.

Sources indicate that why? Well, looking through what each adapter tells me about itself:.

I can see that instead of sending 4 1 KB packets per burst, it would send 8! And the speed of the link was also 2x faster, so those 8 KB would go 2x faster to the Mac. That means the time spent was 8 times lower to send the same data, and while the wait for the go-ahead was identical, the theoretical speed from the adapter to the Mac, including the wait for the go-ahead, was a maximum of 4.5 Gbps. That’s much bigger than the 2.5 coming into the adapter, so the buffer would never fill up, packets would never drop and everything was great, even if the “go-ahead” response was still much slower than when connected directly to the Mac.

I think the big takeaway from this is that all the things you think are quite easy to understand, such as transfer speeds, have so many cool intricacies that it’s worth diving deep every so often. Who would’ve thought that the speed of the link between the adapter and the Mac was defined not only by the link speed itself in Gbps, but also by the time it took your Mac to reply, by the amount of packets, by the speed of those packets, by the number of packets in a burst, and by the size of those packets?

See you next time, when I will spend just as much time on another trivial thing that we can all learn from!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We boosted load_dataset('dataset', streaming=True), streaming datasets without downloading them with one line of code!

Sources indicate that start training on multi-TB datasets immediately, without complex setups, downloading, no "disk out of space", or 429 “stop requesting!” errors.It's super fast! Outrunning our local SSDs when training on 64xH100 with 256 workers downloading data. We've improved streaming to have 100x fewer requests, → 10× faster data resolution → 2x sample/sec, → 0 worker crashes at 256 concurrent workers.

Loading data, especially at the terabyte scale, is a major pain in any machine learning workflow. We suffered this while training SmolLM3, at one point we had to wait 3 hours before each run to download enough data.

In a recent development, streaming has always been possible in the datasets library, but large scale training with massive datasets remained a challenge. That changes today 🔥. We spent a few months improving the backend, focusing on streaming datasets to make it faster and more efficient.

First things first: our changes are backwards compatible. You can still stream any dataset from the Hub with the same simple streaming=True flag. It's as easy as ever. 🚀.

Thousands of AI developers around the world use datasets daily; they should just get improved performance with zero extra work.

Streaming was a lifesaver to rapidly understand a dataset, but to train models, people were usually downloading the data locally, or using a cloud storage service such as S3. That's what we were doing for training SmolVLM, we had all of our data on S3 and were streaming directly from it.

Sources indicate that we wanted to change that, so we decided to use streaming from the Hub when we were developing nanoVLM. Soon we found a significant issue: our test run generated over 100,000 requests in under a minute, which got our IP blocked by the Hub! 😅 This happened because every DataLoader worker was initializing the dataset independently. As we dug deeper, we found that this creates a storm of redundant requests, many of which are unnecessary. Our changes ultimately reduced startup requests by a factor of 100. In total, our improvements delivered:.

So, what changed? We focused on two phases: startup and streaming.

In a recent development, 1. Startup⚡️ The initial resolution of data files was creating a ton of requests. We made two major changes:.

2. Streaming 🏎️ To improve throughput during streaming itself, we've introduced two new features:.

This is how we can increase the minimum request size when streaming from 32MiB (default) to 128MiB and configure prefetching:.

Together, these improvements can double your data throughput, allowing you to train faster and more efficiently.

In a recent development, hugging Face uses Xet: a dedupe-based storage which enables fast deduped uploads and downloads. Unlike traditional remote storage, data transfers are faster on Xet because duplicated data is only transferred once. For example: uploading a large scale dataset to Hugging Face leverages Xet which accelerates uploads. Once the dataset is uploaded, it can be streamed right away.

Deduplication for Parquet is enabled through Parquet Content Defined Chunking (CDC). Thanks to Parquet CDC and Xet deduplication, uploading datasets on Hugging Face is faster than on any traditional remote storage.

Recent findings suggest that this is supported by our pyspark_huggingface package, a Spark Data Source to read/write HF datasets. It includes Parquet CDC and Xet support, accelerating data transfers on HF dramatically.

Industry observers note that some data file formats are not supported in datasets, and sometimes there is a need for more control, so we made it easy to build custom streaming pipelines. This has been battle-tested in the LeRobot library to sample video frames, and in the WebDataset library to stream TAR archives.

We improved the HfFileSystem in the huggingface_hub library to efficiently read files from remote Hugging Face dataset repositories and stream data:.

Passing a HfFileSystem to a torch DataLoader reuses the cached results from .ls() and .glob() which eliminates the need for additional requests when listing data files.

We're now using these streaming enhancements in nanoVLM to train the next generation of SmolVLMs. With these tweaks, we achieve better performance from streaming than from training on our cluster's hierarchical hard disk setup. In fact, streaming is now as fast as reading the data from local SSDs! Previously, transferring data to local SSDs was the process that used to delay our trainings by three-hours. For more details, check out our GitHub.

In a recent development, these powerful latest features landed in the datasets and huggingface_hub libraries. To take advantage of them, simply update your libraries and check out the documentation:.

In a recent development, to celebrate this, we preconcatenated and shuffled all the data sources in FineVision into FineVisionMax. You can use this single combined dataset to train your VLM – no need to handle multiple datasets manually!

And you can see how we do it at scale in nanoVLM!

#126406. What If Netscape Did SSL the HTTP Way?

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3538 w)

What If Netscape Did SSL the HTTP Way?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Billpg

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When you visit a secure website today, your browser connects to port 443 and immediately starts speaking TLS.
  • According to recent reports, this is why so many good ideas from HTTP had to be reinvented, years later, inside TLS.
  • In a recent development, it didn’t have to be this way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you visit a secure website today, your browser connects to port 443 and immediately starts speaking TLS. Only once the encryption is up and running does it get around to speaking HTTP. That’s two protocols stacked on top of each other, and the one at the bottom doesn’t know or care about anything the one on top has learned over the decades.

According to recent reports, this is why so many good ideas from HTTP had to be reinvented, years later, inside TLS. The most notorious is SNI, which is a Host header with extra steps.

In a recent development, it didn’t have to be this way. Let’s take a trip into a parallel universe where Netscape didn’t take the easy way out.

Sources indicate that when Netscape released SSL in 1995, it came with a upcoming URL scheme (https://) and a new port number (443). Plenty of people grumbled. The web already had a protocol and a port, so why invent new ones? Why not secure the conversation you’re already having?

Industry observers note that to be fair to Netscape, in 1995 there wasn’t really a “proper” way to do that. HTTP/1.0 had no mechanism for handing a connection over to another protocol. The Upgrade header didn’t arrive until HTTP/1.1 in 1997, and the Host header, which made it possible to run many websites on one IP address, came with it. Netscape couldn’t have used either of them because neither existed yet.

But this is my parallel universe, so let’s say HTTP grew those headers a couple of years early and Netscape decided to wait for them.

It has been revealed that in our universe, a TLS connection begins with a ClientHello and the server replies with its certificate. In the parallel universe, that first exchange is just plain HTTP in the clear.

The browser wants to buy something from shop.example.com. It connects to port 80, the same as always, and asks for the server’s certificate.

(Yes, /.well-known/ is from 2010. It’s a parallel universe. Let me have this one.).

Industry observers note that the server responds with its certificate, and the certificates of any intermediate CAs, as an ordinary HTTP response. The browser checks the chain against its list of root CAs, exactly as it would in our universe. Is it signed by someone we trust? Is it for shop.example.com? Has it expired?

Recent findings suggest that if you’re worried about sending the certificate in the clear, don’t be. Every version of SSL and TLS up to 1.2 sent the certificate unencrypted too. A certificate is public by design. An attacker can swap it for a different one, but they can’t make one that’s valid for shop.example.com without a CA’s help, and if they can get one of those, you have bigger problems.

Sources indicate that once the browser is happy, it knows the server’s public key. It invents a random secret, encrypts it with that key and asks to upgrade.

It has been revealed that only the real server, holding the private key, can decrypt that secret. It replies with a random value of its own and switches protocols.

Both sides now derive their encryption keys from the browser’s secret, the server’s random value and a hash of everything that was said in the clear up to this point. Mixing in that hash means that if anyone tampered with the plaintext part, the two sides end up with different keys and the connection fails. From this point on everything on the connection is encrypted, starting with the response to GET /checkout.

I’m describing the 1995 approach, where the browser encrypted a secret with the server’s RSA key. When Diffie-Hellman key exchange came along, it would have been just a different pair of headers: the browser sends its half of the exchange, and the server replies with its half, signed by the key in its certificate. Changing how keys are exchanged becomes header negotiation, which HTTP is already very good at.

It has been revealed that browser: Hello, shop.example.com. Who are you?Server: Here’s my certificate.Browser: That checks out. Here’s a secret only you can read. Shall we go somewhere private?Server: 101.Eavesdropper: Aw.

The first thing we get for free is the one that took our universe the longest to sort out.

According to recent reports, that very first request for the certificate has a Host header. A server hosting a thousand websites on one IP address knows exactly which certificate to send back, because the browser told it, using a header the server already understands. There’s nothing to retrofit.

In our universe, the server had to pick a certificate before it knew which website you wanted. For years, every secure website needed its own IP address, which was one of the reasons HTTPS stayed expensive and rare for so long. The fix was SNI, standardized in 2003: an extension that lets the browser mention the website’s name at the very start of the TLS handshake. In other words, a Host header, reinvented inside TLS. The parallel universe never needs it.

And it’s all on one port. Firewalls, proxies and load balancers deal with port 80 and nothing else. A URL is a URL.

So if SNI was standardized in 2003, why couldn’t a website rely on it until the mid-2010s? This is the part I find most interesting.

In a recent development, in our universe, TLS is a black box. Your application hands a socket to a TLS library, and the library takes care of everything: negotiating versions, swapping certificates, exchanging keys and the encryption itself. The box comes with a large “do not touch” sign, which is good advice. People who write their own cryptography tend to get it wrong.

Sources indicate that the trouble is that a black box that does everything can only be improved by whoever owns it. Browsers couldn’t use SNI until their TLS library supported it, and on many platforms that library was part of the operating system. Internet Explorer on Windows XP never got SNI at all. A website couldn’t rely on SNI until XP was finally gone.

It has been revealed that in the parallel universe, the black box is much smaller. Finding the certificate, checking it and exchanging keys all happen in HTTP, in code that browsers and web servers already patch all the time. What’s left inside the box is the genuinely hard part: given these keys, encrypt and authenticate everything that follows. That still deserves a “do not touch” sign, but it’s a box that rarely needs touching. The bits people keep wanting to change live outside it.

The parallel universe’s first request can do another job, too: it makes life much easier for new certificate authorities.

In a recent development, in our universe, a server sends one certificate chain to everyone, before it knows anything about who’s asking. In practice, that means a server operator can only use a CA that every browser on Earth already trusts. Nobody will pick a CA with less than 100% support, however good it is, so a new CA can’t get started. Even Let’s Encrypt, which had about the most compelling offer imaginable (free certificates, issued automatically), had to launch with a cross-signature from IdenTrust, an established CA, so that older browsers would accept its certificates. When that old IdenTrust root expired in 2021, devices that had never learned to trust Let’s Encrypt directly started failing.

In the parallel universe, the browser simply says which CAs it trusts, in the request:.

The server can hold certificates from several CAs and pick one the browser will accept. That’s content negotiation, which HTTP has done since the beginning. A upcoming CA can start out with only the newest browsers, and sites can use it alongside their old CA until everyone catches up.

It’s worth noting that a list of trusted CAs, sent in the clear, is one more thing a website could use to fingerprint its visitors. I’d be surprised if it told them much, though. For most people, the list would be whatever came with their browser and operating system, which the User-Agent header already gives away. The exception would be anyone whose employer has added its own root CA to their machine, whose list would announce exactly where they work.

It has been revealed that early implementations in the parallel universe might simply have sent the entire list. As trust stores grew, browsers would probably have evolved more efficient ways to express the same information: compact identifiers, Bloom-filter-style summaries, or a two-stage negotiation where the browser sends a reduced list and the server replies, “I don’t have certificates for any of those authorities, but I do have these.” HTTP has had a status code for exactly that answer since the 1990s: 300 Multiple Choices. At that point the browser can make a second request with a CA it knows is acceptable to both sides.

According to recent reports, our universe is, once again, getting there slowly. TLS 1.3 has an extension that lets a browser list the CAs it trusts, but no browser sends it, partly because a full list is so large. There’s now a proposal called Trust Anchor Identifiers that would let browsers say the same thing in a compact form, so that servers can pick the right certificate. It’s still a draft. And just like SNI, it will only be usable once the TLS library in every browser, operating system and server has caught up.

There’s another secure protocol that was born in 1995: SSH. Look at how it works and it’s already halfway into the parallel universe. An SSH connection opens with both sides exchanging version strings and lists of supported algorithms in the clear, then exchanging keys, and only then switching over to encrypted packets.

Industry observers note that so in the parallel universe, someone at the standards meeting would notice that the TLS people and the SSH people are building the same thing. Both have a handshake that ends with “here are our keys”. Both then need the same thing after that: chop the data into records, number them, encrypt them, authenticate them, and notice if anything is replayed, reordered or dropped. Why have two committees writing two versions of the hardest part?

Industry observers note that I think the two groups would merge and settle on a common core. TLS would keep its handshake, with certificates and CAs and an HTTP Upgrade. SSH would keep its own, with host keys you’re asked to trust the first time you connect. Each would finish by handing a set of keys to the same small, heavily-reviewed piece of code. Every improvement to that core, whether a faster cipher or a fix for a subtle attack, would land in both protocols at once.

Remember the small black box from earlier? This is where it ends up. HTTP owns the TLS handshake. SSH owns its own. That doesn’t make the handshake easy. Checking a certificate chain is still code where one wrong line can undo everything, as Apple found in 2014 when a single duplicated line skipped the signature check in its TLS handshake. But the handshake lives alongside the rest of the protocol, where it can be reviewed and updated by the same people, on the same schedule. Something like SNI ships with the next browser enhancement, not the next operating system.

The real “do not touch” sign hangs on the shared core that both protocols hand their keys to. It would still be free software, in the GNU sense: anyone can read it, study it, fork it and change it. But the official version would be maintained by cryptographers, and getting a change accepted into it would mean convincing them. Instead of every secure protocol carrying its own big black box, there’s one small one, with the strictest gatekeepers, and everyone uses it.

According to recent reports, this isn’t as far-fetched as it sounds. QUIC, the protocol underneath HTTP/3, already works this way. It borrows the TLS 1.3 handshake and nothing else: once the handshake produces keys, they are handed to QUIC’s own packet encryption, and TLS’s record layer is never used. The handshake and the core have already come apart. Our universe just took until 2021 to do it.

There’s a warning in our universe too. In 2023, an attack called Terrapin demonstrated that an attacker could quietly delete messages from the start of the encrypted part of an SSH connection. It worked by slipping extra messages into the plaintext handshake, which threw off the message numbering the encryption relied on, without either side noticing. The handover from “talking in the clear” to “talking securely” is exactly where the parallel universe would need to be most careful. It’s also exactly the sort of thing you’d want one shared core and one set of eyes on, rather than two.

Once the two protocols share a core, the wall between them starts to look a bit thin. In a universe where every secure connection already starts with an HTTP Upgrade, it’s a short step to one more. Sooner or later, someone would modify OpenSSH to accept a shell over HTTP.

That request is sent after the connection has already been upgraded to TLS, so it’s encrypted, and the server knows exactly who’s asking, because the browser (or the SSH client) presented a certificate during the handshake. The server replies 101 Switching Protocols, and what follows is SSH, with its channels, port forwarding and all. TLS has already done the encryption and checked both sides’ identities, so SSH can skip its own key exchange and get straight to the shell. In our universe, WebSocket had to be invented to tunnel things through HTTP. The parallel universe just asks.

In a recent development, port 22 would still have its fans. Plain SSH doesn’t depend on a CA, so nobody else’s mistake can let an attacker pretend to be your server, and nothing breaks because a certificate expired over the weekend. I expect it would live on in the corner of the server room, run by people who know exactly why they want it.

I’d be a poor advocate if I didn’t look at the downsides, and there’s one big one: stripping.

Credit where it’s due: having https:// as a separate URL scheme does give our real universe something genuinely useful. It’s an explicit sign that security is expected, and that the browser shouldn’t proceed without it. When you click on an https:// link, the author of that page is telling your browser “this must be encrypted, and if it isn’t, stop”.

Recent findings suggest that the parallel universe gives that up. Its security is opportunistic: the browser asks whether the server can do encryption and uses it if so. That’s great, right up until someone hides the opportunity before the handshake completes. The negotiation happens in the clear, so an attacker sitting in the middle doesn’t need to break the encryption. They just stop it from ever starting. Anyone who has set up STARTTLS for email will recognize this one.

Recent findings suggest that so what’s a browser to do? You connect to your bank’s website, ask for /.well-known/tls-cert, and get back “404 Not Found”. Maybe the bank really has forgotten to set up its certificate. Maybe someone in the coffee shop is lying to you. The browser can’t tell the difference. Does it keep going without security?

Sources indicate that in fairness, our universe has the same problem. When you type bank.example into your browser, it has traditionally tried plain HTTP on port 80 first. The bank’s server replies with a redirect to https://, and an attacker can simply hide that redirect and keep you on the insecure version. A tool called sslstrip demonstrated exactly that in 2009. Our universe’s answer, for many years, was to train consumers to look for the padlock.

The parallel universe would end up in much the same place. The padlock would survive as the sign that security was correctly established, and customers would be trained to look for it just as ours were. (Our universe has since turned the padlock inside out. Chrome retired it in 2023, but plain HTTP pages have carried a massive “Not Secure” warning since 2018. These days the sign that a connection is secure is that the warning isn’t there.).

Sooner or later, something like HSTS would be introduced, a header the server sends to say “from now on, never talk to me without encryption”. In our universe, HSTS arrived in 2012. In the parallel universe, with no s in the URL to fall back on, I suspect it would have been needed much sooner.

Here’s a twist. The parallel universe might end up inventing https:// anyway, but with a different meaning. It wouldn’t mean “use a different protocol on a different port”. It would mean “do HTTP on port 80 as normal, but this time, stop if security can’t be negotiated”. A link author could once again promise that a page must be encrypted, and the bank’s 404 becomes an error page instead of a shrug.

Recent findings suggest that our universe has even written the mirror image of this down. RFC 8164 (2017) describes “opportunistic security” for plain http:// URLs, where a browser can quietly use TLS if the server offers it, while https:// keeps its meaning of “secure or nothing”. Both universes end up with https:// making the same promise. They just got there from opposite ends.

There’s an old argument that the parallel universe would replay, from the other side.

Before Let’s Encrypt arrived in 2015 and made certificates free, a few people ran their servers with self-signed certificates, vouched for by nobody but themselves. Browsers greeted those servers with big scary here-be-dragons warnings. The people running them hated this, and they had a point: a website with no security at all got no warning at all. The browser was treating “encrypted, but I can’t tell who by” as worse than “not encrypted”.

In the parallel universe, the same struggle would happen in a different way. Connect to a site for the first time, with no https:// in the link and no HSTS history, and the opportunistic security kicks in. If the certificate checks out, you get the padlock. If it doesn’t, there’s no padlock, but there’s no need for a warning either. An unknown certificate is much the same as no security at all, and the browser treats it that way.

Recent findings suggest that going to the effort of TLS without verifying the certificate sounds a bit pointless, but it isn’t entirely. It won’t stop an attacker who can sit in the middle and hand you a certificate of their own. It does stop anyone who can only listen, which is the cheaper and far more common kind of snooping. The IETF came round to this view in 2014, declaring that pervasive monitoring is an attack (RFC 7258) and describing opportunistic encryption as “some protection most of the time” (RFC 7435).

Industry observers note that and if you know the magic spell to get into the experts-only configuration, you’ve got the basis for SSH-style security. Tell your browser to remember that certificate, and complain loudly if it ever changes. The first connection is a leap of faith, and every connection after that is checked against it. Our universe’s browsers half-did this already: Firefox had a “Permanently store this exception” checkbox, buried behind enough scary warnings that only the determined ever found it.

Is that a good thing? Depends how you feel about SSH.

Recent findings suggest that here’s the funny thing. Our universe keeps quietly doing it the HTTP way anyway.

Sources indicate that not every lesson points my way, though. Email went the parallel-universe route with STARTTLS, upgrading a plain connection on the normal port. In 2018, RFC 8314 recommended that email clients use a dedicated port with TLS from the very first byte instead, because of the stripping problem.

So was Netscape lazy, or right?

Industry observers note that I think the honest answer is “right for the wrong reasons”, and the parallel universe highlights which part was right. The thing that protects you from an attacker quietly downgrading your connection isn’t the separate port. It’s the s in the URL: a promise, made in advance, that this connection must be secure. Netscape almost certainly didn’t choose a newly introduced scheme for that reason. A new scheme and a new port were simply the easiest way to bolt encryption onto software that already existed. But the scheme is the part that earned its keep.

The port, I’m less sure about. I can’t help noticing how much of the past thirty years of TLS work has been spent rebuilding, inside a black box, things HTTP already had. I’d have liked to visit the universe where the s in https:// means “this must be secure” and everything else is just HTTP.

Industry News: PHP 8.6: Things are gonna get a lot more strict around here

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (752 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Like a parent disciplining a misbehaving child, PHP’s annual upgrade clamps down on loose default behaviors to curb malicious hacker horseplay.
  • On Thursday,  PHP version 8.6 was released on its usual yearly schedule, popping up as if the web scripting language hadn’t been under intense scrutiny this past month.
  • Sources indicate that for those who missed it: a swarm of unearthed vulnerabilities has plagued PHP since October, allowing unauthenticated attackers to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code on the server.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Like a parent disciplining a misbehaving child, PHP’s annual upgrade clamps down on loose default behaviors to curb malicious hacker horseplay.

On Thursday,  PHP version 8.6 was released on its usual yearly schedule, popping up as if the web scripting language hadn’t been under intense scrutiny this past month.

Sources indicate that for those who missed it: a swarm of unearthed vulnerabilities has plagued PHP since October, allowing unauthenticated attackers to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code on the server. Customers of every PHP-based application, including WordPress, Laravel, and Symfony, had to scramble to update their PHP instances.

The PHP core development community, along with the PHP Foundation, responded with a coordinated release of patched versions of PHP (8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and the new 8.6) that closed seven critical remote code execution (RCE) flaws in one sweep.

In addition to patching specific exploitable holes in the PHP engine, the fresh version of PHP also tamps down some of PHP’s historically liberal configuration settings.

Lucky for PHP, and for the rest of us, core developer Jörg Sowa called out these lax settings in June, when he posted a proposal to set more security-friendly defaults.

Sowa saw that three configuration settings of PHP’s session extension – Strict Mode, HttpOnly, and SameSite – were designed to boost security but shipped “with defaults that leave applications unnecessarily exposed.”.

In a retrospective posted last month, the PHP Foundation admitted that consensus-driven gridlock had stalled complex fixes for months and vowed to get patches out the door sooner, should the vulnerabilities leak ahead of the agreed-upon deadline.

Sources indicate that code-wise, Sowa’s proposal to harden PHP settings was accepted for PHP 8.6. These changes won’t stop the flood of AI-generated CVEs, but at least these holes will be more difficult to exploit.

Recent findings suggest that for Strict Mode, PHP will no longer accept uninitialized session IDs that it didn’t create itself. Before, an attacker could just plant a made-up session ID on the victim to gain entry. “The built-in files handler checks whether a session file for that ID exists on disk; because an attacker-planted ID has no corresponding file, a fresh random ID is generated instead,” Sowa wrote.

Collectively, these changes should thwart session hijacking and cross-site request forgeries. They won’t stop remote code execution hacks, though they will make it a lot more difficult for attackers to gain entry.

The newly introduced release brings some other security-minded changes as well.

Recent findings suggest that the PHP engine will be a lot stricter when it encounters strings with null values (“\0”). In many cases, it will now throw an error rather than silently letting it pass. Null values are a favored trick for triggering RCEs. A C function will treat the null value as the end of the string, processing everything before the null byte and ignoring everything after, much to an attacker’s delight.

Continuing in this spirit of “if you see something, say something,” a number of other PHP functions will also no longer remain silent when things go awry. Operations for closing a file or copying data, for instance, will explicitly return a false value when terminating prematurely or failing, an alert developers could use to minimize data integrity bugs.

Beyond security, PHP 8.6 also comes with a number of upcoming goodies.

PHPers are abuzz over Partial Function Application (PFA), which will let them pre-fill some of a function’s arguments to generate a reusable closure on the fly — leapfrogging JavaScript in this ability.

The new edition also gets a native polling API, which will be handy for event-driven networking; a stopwatch-like Duration class that can track elapsed time across more than 250 years; and a clamp() function to ensure a given value stays within an acceptable range.

For administrators, this PHP revision round may be a bit of a shambles.

As backend software engineer Rajekevin Dourepoulle notes in a blog post, these changes will take effect post-installation only if the configurations aren’t specified elsewhere, such as in an application, framework, or even another php.ini file – all of which can override the PHP settings themselves.

“In practice: if your deployment reuses the old php.ini (an Ansible template, a COPY php.ini in a Dockerfile, a file copied from server to server), you move to 8.6 and gain nothing, because the explicit session.use_strict_mode = 0 line overrides the newly introduced default,” he wrote.

Recent findings suggest that despite all these heroic efforts, PHP remains the champion of inscrutability. ®.

Voice Cloning with Consent

📅 28 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1442 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in this blog post, we introduce the idea of a 'voice consent gate' to support voice cloning with consent.
  • Industry observers note that realistic voice generation technology has gotten uncannily good in the past few years.
  • Sources indicate that voice generation, and in particular the subtask of voice cloning, has notable risks and benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in this blog post, we introduce the idea of a 'voice consent gate' to support voice cloning with consent. We provide an example Space and accompanying code to start the ball rolling on the idea.

Industry observers note that realistic voice generation technology has gotten uncannily good in the past few years. In some situations, it’s possible to generate a synthetic voice that sounds almost exactly like the voice of a real person. And today, what once felt like science fiction is reality: Voice cloning. With just a few seconds of recorded speech, anyone’s voice can be made to say almost anything.

Sources indicate that voice generation, and in particular the subtask of voice cloning, has notable risks and benefits. The risks of “deepfakes”, such as the cloned voice of former President Biden used in robocalls, can mislead people into thinking that people have said things that they haven’t said. On the other hand, voice cloning can be a powerful beneficial tool, helping people who’ve lost the ability to speak communicate in their own voice again, or assisting people in learning latest languages and dialects.

So how do we create meaningful use without malicious use? We’re exploring one possible answer: a voice consent gate. That’s a system where a voice can be cloned only when the speaker explicitly says they consent. In other words, the model won’t speak in your voice unless you say it’s okay.

We provide a basic demo of this idea below:.

Sources indicate that the voice consent gate is a piece of infrastructure we're exploring that provides methods for ethical principles like consent to be embedded directly into AI system workflows. In our demo, this means the model only starts once the speaker’s consent phrase has been both spoken and recognized, effectively making consent a prerequisite for action. This turns an abstract principle into a concrete system condition, creating a traceable, auditable interaction: an AI model can only run after an unambiguous act of consent.

It has been revealed that such design choices matter beyond voice cloning. They illustrate how AI systems can be built to respect autonomy by default, and how transparency and consent can be made functional, not just declarative.

To create a basic voice cloning system with a voice consent gate, you need three parts:.

Our observation: Since some voice-cloning systems can now generate speech similar to a speaker’s voice using just one sentence, a sentence used for consent can also be used for voice cloning.

In a recent development, the consent bit: To create a voice consent gate in an English voice cloning system, generate a short, natural-sounding English utterance (~20 words) for a person to read aloud that clearly states their informed consent in the current context. We recommend explicitly including a consent phrase and the model name, such as “I give my consent to use the < MODEL > voice cloning model with my voice”. We also recommend using an audio recording that cannot be uploaded, but that instead comes directly from a microphone, to make sure that the sentence isn’t part of an earlier recording that’s been manipulated. Pairing this with a novel (previously unsaid) sentence further helps to directly index the current consent context - supporting explicit, active, context-specific, informed consent. While this design reduces risks of reusing prior recordings, it’s not foolproof; a person could still generate a matching phrase using another TTS system. Future iterations could explore lightweight audio provenance checks, speaker-embedding similarity, or metadata from real-time capture to help verify that the consent audio originates from the intended speaker.

The suitable-for-voice-cloning bit: Previous work on voice cloning has shown that the phrases provided by the speaker must have phonetic variety, covering diverse vowels and consonants; have a “neutral” or polite tone, without background noise and with the speaker in a comfortable position; and have a clear start and end (i.e., don’t trim the clip mid-word).

According to recent reports, to enact both of these aspects within the demo, we prompt a language model to create pairs of sentences: one expressing explicit consent, and another neutral sentence that adds phonetic diversity (covering different vowels, consonants, and tones). Each prompt utilizes a randomly-chosen everyday topic (like the weather, food, or music) to keep the sentences varied and comfortable to say, aiding in creating recordings that are clear, natural, and phonetically rich, while also containing an unambiguous statement of consent. This generation step is automated rather than pre-written so that each user receives a unique sentence pair, preventing reuse of the same text and ensuring that consent recordings are specific to the current session. In other words, the language model generates two fresh sentences per consent instance: one for explicit consent and one for phonetic variety. For example, the language model might generate: “I give my consent to use my voice for generating audio with the model EchoVoice. The weather is bright and calm this morning.” This approach ensures that every sample used for cloning contains verifiable, explicit consent, while remaining suitable as technical input for high-quality voice synthesis. (Note: It's not required that the language model be a "large" language model, which brings its own consent complications.).

Once the speaker’s input matches the generated text, the voice cloning system can start, using the speaker’s consent audio as the input.

Industry observers note that there are a few options for doing this, and we’d love to hear further ideas. For now, there’s:.

You can copy the code to suit your own use.

The code is modular so it can be sliced and diced in different ways to incorporate into your own projects. We’ll be working on making this more robust and secure over time, and we’re curious to hear your ideas on how to improve.

In a recent development, handled responsibly, this technology doesn’t have to haunt us. It can instead become a respectful collaboration between humans and machines — no ghosts in the machine, just good practice. 🎃.

Not a substantial fan of trying to legislate every problem away but if malicious deep fakes are already illegal in most jurisdictions it seems that malicious voice cloning ought to be too.

I think the problem with enforcement will be offshore usage (i.e. if a person from country X is illegally using a voice clone of a person from country Y, how will enforcement work?), as has already been shown with widespread global IP misuse. The second issue is going to be detection. Who is going to check that every single AI voice was or was not cloned with consent? Anything that would truly prevent misuse with robust checks would probably stifle the ability to iterate and develop promptly and anything that didn't stifle the ability to iterate and develop quickly probably wouldn't truly prevent misuse. The classic regulatory Catch-22.

It's problems like these that kind of necessitate a global response and whilst I'm usually not one to advocate for supranational law-making, it would be nice to see the so-called international community create a joint response or at least initiative on this topic because it's going to be a brutal wake-up call one day.

Industry observers note that at this point even just outreach and education on this topic would be helpful. In my time working with random developers and others in the OSS community, I've come across several suspicious requests from people I hardly know asking me for seemingly random recordings of my voice. Someone who doesn't understand the potential for misuse might provide such a recording and inadvertently have their voice used in scam campaigns.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that anthropic declared on November 20, 2026 that it had closed a 1.127 billion-share Class A initial public offering at $83 per share, including underwriters’ full exercise of an option to buy 147 million additional shares. The IPO produced approximately $93.5 billion in aggregate gross proceeds before underwriting discounts, commissions and other offering expenses.

In a recent development, the final offering comprised 1,103,351,354 shares sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 sold by certain selling stockholders. Approximately $91.6 billion of the gross proceeds went to Anthropic, which received no proceeds from the stockholders’ sales.

In a recent development, anthropic’s November 18, 2026 pricing announcement had covered 980 million shares, including 956,351,354 from the manufacturer, and granted underwriters a 30-day option for the additional shares. The selling-stockholder allocation remained unchanged when the option was exercised, so the full exercise expanded only Anthropic’s portion of the offering.

Sources indicate that the final prospectus put the original offering’s aggregate price at $81.34 billion and stated that underwriters would receive no discount or commission on shares sold through the option. The higher final gross figure therefore reflects the additional shares rather than a change in the offering price.

Alongside the IPO, Anthropic closed the sale of 313,253,007 Class N shares at the same $83 per-share price to Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, NVIDIA and TSMC Partners. The private placement had an aggregate purchase price of approximately $26.0 billion. Together, the IPO—including the selling-stockholder shares—and the placement generated approximately $119.5 billion in aggregate gross proceeds before underwriting discounts, commissions and other offering expenses.

Industry observers note that the prospectus describes Class N holders as primarily strategic business partners. Each Class A share carries one vote, while Class N shares have no voting rights except where required by law. Class N shares generally convert into Class A when sold or transferred to an unaffiliated third party; Class A shares are not convertible.

According to recent reports, the Class N sale was an unregistered private placement, and underwriters received no discounts or commissions on those shares. The placement shares were not subject to underwriter lock-up agreements, but they were restricted securities that could be resold only under an effective registration statement or an available exemption.

In a recent development, anthropic’s Class A shares began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on November 19, 2026. Official Nasdaq market data recorded a November 20 regular-session close of $88.91, down $8.26, or 8.50%, from the prior session’s $97.17 close. The session low was $83.05, just above the $83 offering price, leaving the stock above its IPO terms despite the day’s decline.

Sources indicate that the completed transactions give Anthropic substantial new capital and place nonvoting Class N shares with seven technology investors. Public Class A holders have a different position: their shares carry voting rights, but their value now moves with the market rather than the fixed IPO terms, as the second-session decline demonstrated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that today we are excited to share Granite 4.0 Nano, our smallest models yet, released as part of IBM's Granite 4.0 model family. Designed for the edge and on-device applications, these models demonstrate excellent performance for their size and represent IBM's continued commitment to develop powerful, useful, models that don't require hundreds of billions of parameters to get the job done.

Recent findings suggest that like all Granite 4.0 models, the Nano models are released under an Apache 2.0 license with native architecture support on popular runtimes like vLLM, llama.cpp, and MLX. The models were trained with the same improved training methodologies, pipelines, and over 15T tokens of training data developed for the original Granite 4.0 models. This release includes variants benefiting from the Granite 4.0’s latest, efficient hybrid architecture, and like all Granite language models, the Granite 4.0 Nano models also carry with them IBM's ISO 42001 certification for responsible model development, giving users added confidence that models are built and governed to global standards.

Specifically, Granite 4.0 Nano comprises of 4 instruct models and their base model counterparts:.

Building sub-billion to ~1 billion parameter models is an active and competitive space, with advancements in performance and architectures recently made by a number of model developers such as Alibaba (Qwen), LiquidAI (LFM), Google (Gemma) and others. When compared to these other models, Granite 4.0 Nano models demonstrate a significant increase in capabilities that can be achieved with a minimal parameter footprint, as measured by a series of general benchmarks across General Knowledge, Math, Code, and Safety domains.

Chart 1. Average accuracy of 0.2B–2B parameter models across Knowledge, Math, Code, and Safety benchmarks. See Appendix I for full details.

In addition to more general benchmarks, Granite Nano models outperformed several similarly sized models on tasks critical for agentic workflows, including instruction following and tool calling, as measured by IFEval and Berkley's Function Calling Leaderboard v3 (BFCLv3) benchmarks.

Chart 2. Accuracy on IFEval and BFCLv3 benchmarks.

Full details of the Granite 4.0 Nano can be found on the Hugging Face model cards. Moving forward, expect to see more releases from IBM as we continue to grow the Granite 4.0 family and work to make AI a more efficient and effective tool for developers.

In a recent development, appendix I. Breakdown of General Performance Benchmarks.

We just tested local granite-4-h-tiny model for contract analysis in Word: https://youtu.be/acX1CqF8TDA.

Sources indicate that it's impressive. We plan to give nano a try soon.

The whole Granite series is underrated. I've been training the Granite 3 and 4 small models and they learn very promptly. They're my go-to models for specialized tasks.

A hands-on guide to collecting data, training policies, and deploying autonomous medical robotics workflows on real hardware.

It has been revealed that simulation has been a cornerstone in medical imaging to address the data gap. However, in healthcare robotics until now, it's often been too slow, siloed, or difficult to translate into real-world systems.

NVIDIA Isaac for Healthcare, a developer framework for AI healthcare robotics, enables healthcare robotics developers in solving these challenges via offering integrated data collection, training, and evaluation pipelines that work across both simulation and hardware. Specifically, the Isaac for Healthcare v0.4 release provides healthcare developers with an end-to-end SO - ARM based starter workflow and the bring your own operating room tutorial. The SO-ARM starter workflow lowers the barrier for MedTech developers to experience the full workflow from simulation to train to deployment and start building and validating autonomous on real hardware right away.

In this post, we'll walk through the starter workflow and its technical implementation details to help you build a surgical assistant robot in less time than ever imaginable before.

The SO-ARM starter workflow introduces a new way to explore surgical assistance tasks, and providing developers with a complete end-to-end pipeline for autonomous surgical assistance:.

This workflow gives developers a safe, repeatable environment to train and refine assistive skills before moving into the Operating Room.

The workflow implements a three-stage pipeline that integrates simulation and real hardware:.

Notably, over 93% of the data used for policy training was generated synthetically in simulation, underscoring the strength of simulation in bridging the robotic data gap.

The workflow combines simulation and real-world data to address the fundamental challenge that training robots in the real world is expensive and limited, while pure simulation often fails to capture real-world complexities. The approach uses approximately 70 simulation episodes for diverse scenarios and environmental variations, combined with 10-20 real-world episodes for authenticity and grounding. This mixed training creates policies that generalize beyond either domain alone.

Notably, developers could run all the simulation, training and deployment (3 computers needed for physical AI) on one DGX Spark.
