  • It has been revealed that this comparison focuses on monday work management, rather than its separately packaged CRM, dev, or service products.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unite.AI may receive compensation when you use links to products we review. This does not influence our editorial evaluations. Read our affiliate disclosure.

A project manager needs to see the launch as a whole. A designer needs the next assignment, its brief, and the conversation around it. monday.com and ClickUp serve both audiences, but their emphasis differs. monday.com is our pick for teams that want clear boards and repeatable departmental workflows. ClickUp is our recommendation when tasks, documents, chat, and delivery detail need to live together.

It has been revealed that this comparison focuses on monday work management, rather than its separately packaged CRM, dev, or service products. Both platforms appear in our AI collaboration tools guide.

Industry observers note that monday.com is appealing when different teams need to follow the same process without working in the same way. A board can capture incoming requests, owners, dates, and status; views and dashboards turn those records into a picture that managers can use. The board provides a common reference even when each department has its own responsibilities.

The useful part is how directly a team can shape those records. Columns can capture the details an approval, campaign, or operational request requires. Automations then handle selected handoffs, while integrations move information between the board and other systems. This makes monday.com a strong option for recurring work that follows a recognizable path.

Official monday.com tutorial on AI blocks for columns and automations.

In a recent development, we recommend it for operations teams, marketing coordination, and organizations that need a visible process across several departments. It still needs thoughtful design. Too many similar boards and inconsistent statuses can fragment reporting, so the best implementation starts with a shared definition of the process and the few measures that matter.

In a recent development, clickUp works well when an assignment needs more than a row on a board. Tasks and subtasks sit within a hierarchy, and the team can connect them to supporting Docs, conversations, time records, and scheduling views. Contributors and managers can work at different levels while referring to the same underlying assignments.

Sources indicate that that breadth is particularly useful for a launch, a client delivery process, or an internal program with many interdependent pieces. A brief can live in a Doc, the discussion can stay close to the task, and the schedule can show the order in which the work needs to happen. Its connected Docs also support collaborative writing alongside execution.

Official ClickUp walkthrough of project management with ClickUp Brain.

ClickUp is our preferred option for teams trying to consolidate several parts of their delivery routine. The cost is setup complexity. A clear hierarchy, consistent fields, and a manageable set of statuses matter more than enabling every possible feature. Teams willing to establish those conventions get the strongest benefit from its range.

Industry observers note that consider a ten-person marketing team receiving campaign requests from sales, product, and regional managers. It needs to understand each request, route it for approval, produce the work, and keep the requester informed. Here is how we would organize the same process in each platform.

It has been revealed that our choice: monday.com for a visible cross-team queue. Give each request a board item with the requester, owner, due date, priority, and approval status. Use a small set of consistent labels so different departments can follow the same process without interpreting different task conventions.

ClickUp can also collect requests and organize them into tasks. We would favor it at this stage when the request naturally belongs inside a project that the delivery team already manages there.

Recent findings suggest that our choice: ClickUp when the request becomes a detailed project. Break the campaign into copy, design, landing-page, and launch tasks. Keep the brief in a connected Doc, assign owners, and make the order of the handoffs explicit. The advantage is having the assignment, its supporting material, and its progress in the same delivery workspace.

Recent findings suggest that in monday.com, we would keep the approved request on its board and use the relevant project structure for production. Boards suit repeatable operational processes; its more structured Projects feature is available on Pro and Enterprise, with portfolio connection reserved for Enterprise. A familiar board does not automatically include every portfolio-management feature.

Sources indicate that we prefer monday.com when the recurring management question is where requests stand across departments. We prefer ClickUp when the difficult question is which delivery task, dependency, or approval is holding up the campaign. A clear process matters in either tool: one owner should keep the working record current instead of writing the same upgrade in several places.

Consider a marketing request that moves from intake to approval, production, and launch. monday.com’s board structure makes each stage and owner easy to represent. We favor it when the main management question is where a request stands and which department needs to act next.

ClickUp has the stronger case when that request expands into a detailed project: several creative versions, dependent tasks, supporting documentation, and ongoing team discussion. We would choose it when contributors need the project system to carry more of their daily working context.

Recent findings suggest that monday.com’s AI feature catalog describes actions such as extracting information, labeling items, suggesting priorities, and generating documents. Those actions are useful in an intake workflow: incoming text can become structured fields that the team can sort and route. Sidekick adds contextual assistance across the workspace.

According to recent reports, clickUp’s AI tools can create and edit tasks and Docs. Its Brain² assistant works with delivery context, which makes it more compelling for gathering project information and turning it into work inside the same platform. We prefer monday.com for AI-assisted handling of structured board records and ClickUp when the desired output belongs in an active project and its documents.

Sources indicate that the billing models also differ. monday.com uses a shared AI credit pool across supported capabilities, while some built-in assistance does not consume credits. ClickUp Business includes standard model use and a pooled allowance for premium usage. A credit in one platform is not equivalent to a credit in the other.

It has been revealed that for an incoming campaign request, we would use a defined AI action to classify the text, extract useful details, or draft a short summary into board columns. A custom prompt can reference the relevant fields and preview its result before the configuration is saved. That makes the output usable in the same queue the operations team reviews.

Sources indicate that A useful instruction would be: “Summarize the requested campaign using these fields. Keep the supplied deadline and audience, and identify missing approval information.” The team should keep the available labels distinct and review ambiguous requests before routing them automatically.

Recent findings suggest that for ClickUp, we would start with the campaign brief or meeting notes and ask Brain to extract actions, keeping the stated owner and deadline.   • Nov 22, 2026 2 min read.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News PostgreSQL 19 Released with Online Table Repacking and Query Planning Controls.

Nov 22, 2026 2 min read.

The PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19, introducing changes to database maintenance, query planning, replication, and application development. The release focuses on reducing administrative overhead and improving performance, with newly introduced tools for reorganizing tables without downtime and controlling query looks.

One of the main additions is REPACK, which reclaims unused table space and can reorder data to match an index. Its CONCURRENTLY option allows the operation to run without blocking reads or writes, making it a potential replacement for common uses of VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER. PostgreSQL 19 also introduces pg_plan_advice and pg_stash_advice, extensions that let administrators influence query plan selection and apply stored advice to queries by identifier, without changing application code.

In a recent development, other maintenance improvements include parallel index vacuuming, changes to autovacuum prioritization, and additional monitoring views. EXPLAIN ANALYZE and related logging now report asynchronous I/O activity and WAL generated for full-page images. PostgreSQL also reports that changes to foreign key checks made bulk inserts nearly twice as fast in testing. Query planner improvements include more efficient anti-joins for eligible NOT IN clauses and eager aggregation before joins.

Recent findings suggest that the release adds several features for replication and application development. Logical replication now supports sequence values, and PostgreSQL automatically raises the effective WAL level to logical when the first logical replication slot is created. The fresh WAIT FOR LSN command lets applications wait until a standby has replayed a specified WAL position before querying data, providing read-your-writes consistency. Developers also get INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT for get-or-create operations, JSON output from COPY, additional SQL/JSON string methods, and IGNORE NULLS support for window functions.

Security and compatibility changes include server-side TLS Server Name Indication (SNI), which allows a server to present different certificates based on the hostname used by the client. PostgreSQL 19 also warns after successful MD5 password authentication. MD5 was deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 and is planned for removal in a future release, with SCRAM recommended instead. JIT compilation is now disabled by default because its cost estimates proved unreliable, while LZ4 becomes the default TOAST compression method when supported by the build.

The release has also prompted discussion on Hacker News about whether production people should wait for PostgreSQL 19.1.

Another user recommended waiting for the first minor release on critical production systems:.

Personally, I would say, for critical production systems, it's still good to wait for the .1 release.

PostgreSQL 19 is available now. The complete list of changes is available in the official release notes.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • While everyone (and their grandma 👵) is spinning up new ASR models, picking the right one for your use case can feel more overwhelming than choosing your next Netflix show.
  • Most benchmarks focus on short-form English transcription (<30s), and overlook other important tasks, such as (1) multilingual performance and (2) model throughput, which can a be deciding factor for long-form audio like meetings and podcasts.
  • In a recent development, over the past two years, the Open ASR Leaderboard has become a standard for comparing open and closed-source models on both accuracy and efficiency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While everyone (and their grandma 👵) is spinning up new ASR models, picking the right one for your use case can feel more overwhelming than choosing your next Netflix show. As of 21 Nov 2025, there are 150 Audio-Text-to-Text and 27K ASR models on the Hub 🤯.

Most benchmarks focus on short-form English transcription (<30s), and overlook other important tasks, such as (1) multilingual performance and (2) model throughput, which can a be deciding factor for long-form audio like meetings and podcasts.

In a recent development, over the past two years, the Open ASR Leaderboard has become a standard for comparing open and closed-source models on both accuracy and efficiency. Recently, multilingual and long-form transcription tracks have been added to the leaderboard 🎉.

As of 21 Nov 2025, the Open ASR Leaderboard compares 60+ open and closed-source models from 18 organizations, across 11 datasets.

In a recent preprint, we dive into the technical setup and highlight some key trends in modern ASR. Here are the big takeaways 👇.

Industry observers note that models combining Conformer encoders with large language model (LLM) decoders currently lead in English transcription accuracy. For example, NVIDIA’s Canary-Qwen-2.5B, IBM’s Granite-Speech-3.3-8B, and Microsoft’s Phi-4-Multimodal-Instruct achieve the lowest word error rates (WER), showing that integrating LLM reasoning can significantly boost ASR accuracy.

💡 Pro-tip: NVIDIA introduced Fast Conformer, a 2x faster variant of the Conformer, that is used in their Canary and Parakeet suite of models.

Recent findings suggest that while highly accurate, these LLM decoders tend to be slower than simpler approaches. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, efficiency is measured using inverse real-time factor (RTFx), where higher is better.

For even faster inference, CTC and TDT decoders deliver 10–100× faster throughput, albeit with slightly higher error rates. This makes them ideal for real-time, offline, or batch transcription tasks (such as meetings, lectures, or podcasts).

OpenAI’s Whisper Large v3 remains a strong multilingual baseline, supporting 99 languages. However, fine-tuned or distilled variants like Distil-Whisper and CrisperWhisper often outperform the original on English-only tasks, showing how targeted fine-tuning can improve specialization (how to fine-tune? Check out guides for Whisper, Parakeet, and Voxtral).

According to recent reports, that stated, focusing on English tends to reduce multilingual coverage 👉 a classic case of the tradeoff between specialization and generalization. Similarly, while self-supervised systems like Meta’s Massively Multilingual Speech (MMS) and Omnilingual ASR can support 1K+ languages, they trail behind language-specific encoders in accuracy.

⭐ While just five languages are currently benchmarked, we’re planning to expand to more languages and are excited for upcoming dataset and models contributions to multilingual ASR through GitHub pull requests.

🎯 Alongside multilingual benchmarks, several community-driven leaderboards focus on individual languages. For example, the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard compares models across Modern Standard Arabic and regional dialects, highlighting how speech variation and diglossia challenge current systems. Similarly. the Russian ASR Leaderboard provides a growing hub for evaluating encoder-decoder and CTC models on Russian-specific phonology and morphology. These localized efforts mirror the broader multilingual leaderboard’s mission to encourage dataset sharing, fine-tuned checkpoints, and transparent model comparisons, especially in languages with fewer established ASR resources.

In a recent development, for long-form audio (e.g., podcasts, lectures, meetings), closed-source systems still edge out open ones. It could be due to domain tuning, custom chunking, or production-grade optimization.

Among open models, OpenAI’s Whisper Large v3 performs the best. But for throughput, CTC-based Conformers shine 👉 for example, NVIDIA’s Parakeet CTC 1.1B achieves an RTFx of 2793.75, compared to 68.56 for Whisper Large v3, with only a moderate WER degradation (6.68 and 6.43 respectively).

Industry observers note that the tradeoff? Parakeet is English-only, again reminding us of that multilingual and specialization tradeoff 🫠.

Recent findings suggest that ⭐ While closed systems still lead, there’s huge potential for open-source innovation here. Long-form ASR remains one of the most exciting frontiers for the community to tackle next!

Given how fast ASR is evolving, we’re excited to see what latest architectures push performance and efficiency, and how the Open ASR Leaderboard continues to serve as a transparent, community-driven benchmark for the field, and as a reference for other leaderboards (Russian, Arabic, and Speech DeepFake Detection).

We’ll keep expanding the Open ASR LeaderBoard with more models, more languages, and more datasets so stay tuned 👀.

👉 Want to contribute? Head on over to the GitHub repo to open a pull request 🚀.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: GitHub Actions accepts several invalid YAML productions, making it difficult (read: impossible) to parse some real-world action and workflow definitions with a properly conforming YAML parser.

This is related to zizmor#1116, which has been bugging me for a year and a half.

Last April, a user reported that zizmor was rejecting a workflow containing a step that looks like this:.

Apart from the use of a multi-line flow-style string for the json: key, nothing particularly stands out about this step.

In a recent development, except: it isn't valid YAML! YAML claims this about flow-style nodes that are nested inside of a block-style parent collection (read: map or array):.

Flow nodes must be indented by at least one more space than the parent block collection. Note that flow nodes may begin on a following line.

That means the correct syntax is instead:.

The difference is barely visible:.

YAML is a massive and complicated spec, so it didn't even occur to me that this was invalid. Instead, I opened tree-sitter-yaml#36 to "fix" it. I've now opened tree-sitter-yaml#51 to revert that misbegotten fix.

On GitHub's side, I'm not sure if they have a clean path towards spec conformance here. Much of the code behind Actions is proprietary, but it seems likely that the underlying parser on their end is YamlDotNet.

In a recent development, actions appears to use YamlDotNet 5.3.0, which was released in 2018. However, even upgrading to the newest version (18.1.0 as of writing) wouldn't fix this particular bug, since it's still present on that version (note the !isSingleQuoted guard).

My best guess is that a 2020 patch (YamlDotNet#467) only fixed the double-quoted form because YAML's official test suite only tests rule 8.2.3 with a double-quoted string, despite it applying to both forms.

Recent findings suggest that elon Musk said in an X reply on November 22, 2026, that Tesla’s AI5 computer is intended for Optimus, cars will continue using AI4, and AI4 is sufficient for superhuman driving. He was responding to an owner who asked when AI5 would reach new cars and whether to wait before upgrading from AI3.

In a recent development, the reply followed an earlier technical post in the same discussion, where Musk explained how Tesla’s Reality View visualization fits within AI4. Two linked in-car workloads sit underneath that explanation: a model producing driving actions and a separate generative model producing the interface visualization. Together, the posts give the chip choice a concrete infrastructure context: Tesla is dividing limited compute among connected driving and visualization functions.

Musk described Tesla’s approximately pixel-perfect world model as critical for synthetic data generation. Its much smaller in-car version is a conditional mean-flow model based on a recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder, or UVE, features. Those same features feed a 3B encoder model that produces driving actions.

In a recent development, musk mentioned Reality View branches from those features into a separate, roughly 1B-parameter diffusion model. The process starts with a noisy version of the preceding output and reconstructs the current visualization, creating an eight-image video chunk at 36 frames per second and the interface screen’s resolution. This work is performed every UVE frame at 18 hertz and spread across four cycles.

In a follow-up post, Musk said Tesla had moved its small decoder into SRAM, leaving only half of one TRIP out of three on SoC B for Reality View. TRIP basically handles only 8-bit integers, and softmax must run in emulation mode over 28 steps.

Those details apply specifically to the visualizer, not to a stated limit on driving actions. They show that Reality View’s practical budget depends on engine allocation and numerical execution as well as model size.

Musk attributed the current, somewhat high Reality View latency to compute constraints and proposed interleaving newer UVE features through the diffusion transformer layers to cut roughly 35% of it.

Sources indicate that musk described AI5 as a substantial improvement with roughly 12 times more compute. The post gives no baseline for that multiple, so it does not establish a 12-fold gain in visualization frame rate, latency or driving performance.

Musk’s account separates confidence in driving capability from the practical limits of rendering Reality View. AI4 is presented as sufficient for superhuman driving, yet the visualization branch running on it still has a narrow compute allocation and only a proposed route to lower latency. The immediate rendering improvement he described depends on reorganizing vision-feature inputs within that environment, making software efficiency central to the in-car workload he detailed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face TRL now officially integrates with RapidFire AI to accelerate your fine-tuning and post-training experiments. TRL users can now discover, install, and run RapidFire AI as the fastest way to compare multiple fine-tuning/post-training configurations to customize LLMs without major code changes and without bloating GPU requirements.

When fine-tuning or post-training LLMs, teams often do not have the time and/or budget to compare multiple configs even though that can significantly boost eval metrics. RapidFire AI lets you launch multiple TRL configs concurrently--even on a single GPU--and compare them in near real time via a new adaptive, chunk-based scheduling and execution scheme. In internal benchmarks referenced in the TRL page, this delivers ~16–24× higher experimentation throughput than sequentially comparing configs one after another, enabling you to reach much better metrics much faster.

RapidFire AI establishes live three-way communication between your IDE, a metrics dashboard, and a multi-GPU execution backend.

Drop-in TRL wrappers — Use RFSFTConfig, RFDPOConfig, and RFGRPOConfig as near-zero-code replacements for TRL's SFT/DPO/GRPO configs.

Adaptive chunk-based concurrent training — RapidFire AI shards the dataset into a given number of chunks and cycles configs at chunk boundaries to enable earlier apples-to-apples comparisons and also maximize GPU utilization.

Interactive Control Ops (IC Ops) — From the dashboard itself, you can Stop, Resume, Delete, and Clone-Modify, possibly with Warm-Start, any runs in flight to avoid wasting resources on underperforming configs and double-down on better performing configs--no job restarts, no juggling separate GPUs or clusters, no resource bloat.

Clone promising configurations with modified hyperparameters, optionally warm-starting from the parent's weights, all from the live dashboard.

Sources indicate that multi-GPU orchestration — The RapidFire AI scheduler automatically places and orchestrates configs across available GPUs on chunks of data via effcient shared-memory mechanisms. You focus on your models and eval metrics, not plumbing.

In a recent development, MLflow-based dashboard — Real-time metrics, logs, and IC Ops in one place as soon as you start your experiment. Support for more dashboards such as Trackio, W&B, and TensorBoard coming soon.

RapidFire AI splits your dataset randomly into "chunks" and cycles LLM configurations through the GPUs at chunk boundaries. You get incremental signal on eval metrics across all configs much more swiftly. The automatic checkpointing via an efficient shared-memory-based adapter/model spilling/loading mechanism keeps training smooth, stable, and consistent. Use IC Ops to adapt mid-flight to stop low-performers earlier and clone promising ones with tweaked config knobs, optionally warm-starting from the parent's weights.

Recent findings suggest that sarvam AI released Sarvam-105B-1711 on November 22, 2026, a new open-weight checkpoint aimed at customer support, voice agents and other high-volume enterprise work. The release includes BF16 weights for further training and a compact 4-bit NVFP4 version designed to run on one workstation GPU.

In a recent development, the model card identifies the same 105-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts base used by Sarvam-105B, with 10.3 billion active parameters. The new checkpoint adds post-training for tool calling, instruction following, agentic tasks and Indian languages. This is therefore an patch to an existing model, with the changes concentrated in how the base handles enterprise work rather than a newly introduced foundation model.

Sarvam reports that instruction following on IFBench rose from 32.5 for the February checkpoint to 82.5, customer-service tool use on Tau2 from 46.2 to 85.5, and Indian-language performance on its Indic suite from 30.1 to 79.1. On Tau2’s pass^4 measure, which counts tasks completed correctly in all four independent attempts, the new model scored 69.5%, compared with 63.9% for Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and 62.1% for Gemma 4 31B.

Sarvam reports an average of 73.9 across eight conversational-agent benchmarks for the NVFP4 build, up from 42.6 in February. Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite scored 74.0 at a blended $0.85 per million tokens, while Gemma 4 31B scored 73.0 at $0.54. Sarvam-105B-1711’s blended price is $0.15, down from $0.44 for its predecessor.

All scores come from Sarvam’s own runs, with open-weight models served through vLLM and API models accessed through OpenRouter. The evaluation defaults use temperature 1.0 in thinking mode, up to 65,536 output tokens and a mean over four samples; out-of-budget, context-overflow and malformed responses score zero. The Indic suite is Sarvam’s internal Indian-language benchmark and uses Gemini 3.1 Pro as a rubric judge, an important qualification for the reported language gain.

It has been revealed that sarvam claims its 8-bit MXFP8 training recipe raised pretraining throughput from 5,500 to 10,900 tokens per second per GPU on 64 NVIDIA B200 GPUs at 8K context. For reinforcement learning, 8-bit precision and DSpark speculative decoding, which uses a draft model to propose tokens for verification, reduced a step from 758 seconds to roughly 420–440 seconds, while mean reward remained essentially unchanged in the company’s test.

Continued pretraining on 330 billion tokens, using 512 B200 GPUs for a little over seven days, extended the model to a 160K-token context. That training work addresses a different constraint from the post-training gains: how much material an agent can retain while working through long documents or extended tasks.

Recent findings suggest that at 64 concurrent requests, Sarvam measured 6,067 decode tokens per second per B200 for the NVFP4 checkpoint with DSpark, about 2.1 times its BF16 configuration. The resulting serving efficiency is the basis for the lower blended token price, connecting the infrastructure work directly to the model’s high-volume enterprise pitch.

According to recent reports, sarvam reports that the 65 GB NVFP4 checkpoint fits on one 96 GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU and delivers 99 tokens per second of per-user decode speed for a single request with a 10K-token prompt. That footprint allows an Indus Cowork agent to run on-premises without sending documents to a third-party API.

The NVFP4 checkpoint is the exact model served through Sarvam Token Factory, while the BF16 release is intended for fine-tuning and further post-training. The repository carries an Apache-2.0 license tag, and the model card documents hosting with vLLM 0.33.0, optional DSpark support, thinking enabled by default, and recommended temperatures of 1.0 with thinking and 0.6 without it.

For enterprises, the release pairs API access with a private-deployment path that can keep sensitive document work inside their own networks. The open question is whether the vendor-reported agent gains recur in production workflows, where the single-GPU footprint and lower token price could be most relevant to adoption.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki on November 22, 2026 released internal perplexity measurements and proposed shared limits on frontier AI development, warning that alignment and monitoring research may not keep pace if pretraining advances accelerate as soon as 2027.
  • The disclosure concerns log-perplexity, the logarithm of perplexity, also called cross-entropy loss.
  • Pachocki reports that GPT-3.5 measured about 0.99 and supported fluent conversation, forming the basis for the original ChatGPT, while GPT-4 measured about 0.91 and could productively use chain-of-thought reasoning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki on November 22, 2026 released internal perplexity measurements and proposed shared limits on frontier AI development, warning that alignment and monitoring research may not keep pace if pretraining advances accelerate as soon as 2027.

The disclosure concerns log-perplexity, the logarithm of perplexity, also called cross-entropy loss. Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower values indicate better predictions. OpenAI’s figures use a fixed snapshot of held-out data from its internal codebase, the main evaluation dataset it has tracked since GPT-3.5.

Pachocki reports that GPT-3.5 measured about 0.99 and supported fluent conversation, forming the basis for the original ChatGPT, while GPT-4 measured about 0.91 and could productively use chain-of-thought reasoning. Newly introduced cybersecurity and mathematics capabilities emerged at losses below 0.8. At about 0.76, a model began producing notable results on open mathematics problems after OpenAI had spent more than a year posing such problems to its models.

Pachocki expects further significant capabilities around the 0.68–0.70 log-perplexity window, extrapolating from recent progress, while acknowledging that he does not know what they will be and that current evaluations may not test for them. The proposal asks frontier developers not to cross limits based on perplexity and other measurements until researchers’ ability to understand and monitor AI behavior reaches a concrete milestone. One example is a successor to chain-of-thought monitors, which inspect a model’s written reasoning for signs of misalignment.

Industry observers note that developers would also jointly establish evaluation norms, red-team safety cases before such models are first used, and shared transparency standards. The initial limit is intended to lead toward a common framework for successive limits. Pachocki says OpenAI disclosed the figures despite giving competitors a clearer picture of its position because he considers shared safety measures urgent.

The acceleration scenario is conditional: Pachocki says a rapid series of fundamental pretraining advances could conceivably occur if AI begins contributing substantially to algorithmic research, while alignment and monitoring progress is unlikely to keep pace with the full potential acceleration.

OpenAI attributes the steep acceleration in its 2026 loss curve mostly to long-term research and compute investments, with automation playing a smaller role. Its most recent models have nevertheless included meaningful AI design contributions.

In a recent development, openAI’s November 18, 2026 research report gives those contributions concrete form. Pretraining researchers attributed the named ideas for GPT-6 Astra to people; for GPT-6.2 Astra, they described developing ideas with Codex, including one case where Codex identified key insights and another where its suggested change made an idea work well. Estimated zero-intervention success rates also varied sharply: 79% for monitoring training runs, 35% for launching them and 25% for writing inference and serving code. That variation supports the report’s conclusion that research uplift remains uneven and humans remain central to the loop.

Industry observers note that A November 10, 2026 OpenAI monitorability study examines two imperfect proxies for monitorability: no-chain-of-thought capability, meaning reasoning in a forward pass without chain-of-thought or tool-call tokens, and chain-of-thought controllability, meaning the ability to add, remove or otherwise manipulate those reasoning tokens when prompted. The study reports a strong correlation between lower base-model perplexity and no-chain-of-thought capability, and a weaker correlation with greater controllability.

The study also found that reinforcement learning increased controllability even without process supervision beyond length constraints and final-answer grading, and that supervised fine-tuning on outputs from a more controllable teacher model could transmit controllability to a student model.

In a recent development, openAI cautions that controllability is noisy and does not always correspond to monitor evasion, while expecting further pretraining progress to require new approaches to monitorability. That is the technical gap behind Pachocki’s example of a successor to chain-of-thought monitors as a possible development milestone.

Perplexity itself cannot carry the entire standard. Cross-lab comparisons are difficult because developers use different evaluation datasets and training mixtures, and the metric does not directly measure an actionable task. It also misses capability gains outside pretraining: chain-of-thought reasoning can sharply increase capabilities without reducing the base model’s perplexity.

Sources indicate that the measurement also has an unknown floor. Pachocki cautions that loss is not expected to reach zero; as it approaches the data’s inherent entropy, apparent progress will slow, while smaller perplexity gains could correspond to larger intelligence gains. A fixed numerical increment would therefore not necessarily carry a fixed practical meaning.

The proposal turns a technical measurement into a governance test: whether developers can make results comparable across labs and agree on a concrete oversight milestone before crossing thresholds that Pachocki associates with capabilities current evaluations may not yet detect.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 22, 2026 4 min read.
  • At QCon San Francisco 2026, Manju Rajashekhar, founder and CEO of Mad Labs, opened the conference with the keynote "The Harness Is the New Operating System.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: The Harness Is the New Operating System.

Nov 22, 2026 4 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Manju Rajashekhar, founder and CEO of Mad Labs, opened the conference with the keynote "The Harness Is the New Operating System.".

In a recent development, rajashekhar argued that the harness around an AI model, rather than the model itself, decides what an agent can do and how safely it does it. Each part of a harness, the keynote proposed, maps onto a job that operating systems already perform.

According to recent reports, rajashekhar began with a split that shaped computing history. Applications encoded behavior, while operating systems abstracted the hardware beneath them, and that separation made portable, composable software possible.

AI agents break that arrangement because they generate behavior at runtime. Software therefore needs a new layer that makes that behavior useful, reliable and repeatable, and Rajashekhar called that layer the harness.

In Rajashekhar's framing, model plus harness equals agent, and the harness is "everything in an agent that isn't the model." It supplies the tasks, context, tools, state, permissions, feedback loops and a definition of done.

The simplest agent is a model running in a loop that the harness controls. But "a loop isn't enough. Every iteration has to count," and Rajashekhar described four parts of the loop that make each iteration count.

Context works like virtual memory. The harness assembles what the model needs for its next decision inside the hard limit of the context window, and the advice was to "give the model a pointer, not the whole thing.".

The interface works like system calls and "puts a ceiling on the agent's effective capability." Rajashekhar pointed to the SWE-agent paper, in which GPT-4 Turbo resolved 11.0% of SWE-bench Lite problems through a plain shell and 18.0% through an interface designed for agents.

Execution works like processes and permissions. The harness enforces boundaries through isolation and scoped credentials, such as a test database with no production access, because "instructions guide. Boundaries enforce.".

In a recent development, feedback works like return codes. The harness keeps "tests failed," "could not run" and "outcome unknown" apart, so the model does not have to guess what happened.

That matters because errors compound. On a 20-step task with a 95% chance of each step going right, the whole job succeeds 36% of the time, and catching 80% of errors lifts that to 82%.

Recent findings suggest that when an agent goes in circles, Rajashekhar said, most engineers swap the model. A better first step is to keep the model and change the harness.

According to recent reports, deepSeek's model card for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reports the same model scoring from 65.5% to 74.2% on DeepSWE across eight harnesses. The minimal harnesses scored highest, which Rajashekhar read as a sign that more harness is not automatically better.

In a second study, Qwen3.8-27B passed 66.8% of 100 hard LiveCodeBench problems with a single call. Inside a manager-worker scaffold with a shared ledger, it passed 92.4%.

Industry observers note that rajashekhar made a related point on LinkedIn earlier this year. Frontier models are forgiving, the post said, while "open-weight models are less forgiving. They make you think deeply about the harness and how it aligns to the model.".

The harness also determines what an agent is allowed to affect. Rajashekhar contrasted an agent that fixes failing tests with one that deletes the tests so they pass, observing that "the difference isn't ability. It's authority.".

Recent findings suggest that the example offered was the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI evaluation agents on a capture-the-flag benchmark reached the internet through an open code sandbox. They held admin access on Hugging Face's internal clusters for about two and a half days.

Human approval alone is a weak gate, Rajashekhar argued, citing Anthropic's work on Claude Code auto mode, which InfoQ covered in May. People approve the large majority of permission prompts, and "a tired gatekeeper is a rubber stamp.".

According to recent reports, the keynote extended a talk Rajashekhar gave at QCon AI Boston 2026. That talk argued that production agents "are just distributed systems in disguise" and proposed the actor model as their runtime.

Sources indicate that in the Boston design, each agent task owns its state, receives events through a mailbox, writes each state change to a durable store and runs under a supervisor. The talk closed with a variation on Greenspun's tenth rule, suggesting that any sufficiently complicated agent loop contains half of an actor system.

Recent findings suggest that the San Francisco keynote widened the lens from the runtime to everything the model sees, calls and runs inside. Rajashekhar brings a systems background to that question, having led caching systems on Twitter's early engineering team, which open-sourced twemproxy.

The talk arrives as "harness" has become the common term for everything around the model. Thoughtworks Distinguished Engineer Birgitta Böckeler described it in a February memo as covering "the tooling and practices we can use to keep AI agents in check.".

In a recent development, rajashekhar closed on why a harness design is never finished. Every component "encodes an assumption about what the model can't do," and those assumptions expire as models improve.

Sources indicate that anthropic's harness for long-running apps needed context resets because Claude Sonnet 4.5 demonstrated "context anxiety" near its context limit. That behavior largely disappeared with Opus 4.5, as InfoQ reported in April.

Recent findings suggest that the reverse also holds. LangChain moved checks the model kept skipping into the harness and lifted GPT-5.2-Codex from 52.8% to 66.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 without changing the model.

Rajashekhar asked attendees to open an agent they already use and read its system prompt and tool list. Then, on a task where it struggles, change one part of the loop and rerun what already worked.

Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the keynote and can view the keynote abstract and resources here.

Latest Update: Building Deep Research: How we Achieved State of the Art

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that research agents are rapidly becoming one of the most vital applications of AI.
  • The task of building an agent harness is to create a software layer that enhances a model’s runtime execution through context management, tool invocations, loop control, orchestration, and error handling.
  • This requires forecasting how models will evolve, staying optimistic about their progress, limiting assumptions, and avoiding hand-crafted optimizations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that research agents are rapidly becoming one of the most vital applications of AI. Research is a foundational knowledge-work task: collecting, reading, and synthesizing information underpins everything from writing and decision-making to coding itself. Yet human-driven research is constrained by memory, reading speed, and time. AI research agents, by contrast, can process vast amounts of information, synthesize insights instantly, and scale effortlessly. Because of this, research agents are emerging as a top use case for AI today and will soon become a core subcomponent of broader agentic workflows across content generation, coding, sales, and more. In this post, we share the technical and philosophical lessons we’ve learned building a state-of-the-art research agent, and where we believe the field is headed.

The task of building an agent harness is to create a software layer that enhances a model’s runtime execution through context management, tool invocations, loop control, orchestration, and error handling. Building applications on top of rapidly improving models is, however, a modern engineering challenge. How can we design software today that absorbs the performance gains from future model releases?

This requires forecasting how models will evolve, staying optimistic about their progress, limiting assumptions, and avoiding hand-crafted optimizations.

Industry observers note that we learned this the hard way seven months ago, when we had to abandon our first attempt at deep research and rebuild the entire system from scratch. The first architecture was complicated and sophisticated (we thought this was a good thing), but its assumptions became bottlenecks when the next generation of models arrived.

Over the last seven months, model capabilities have quietly but meaningfully evolved (especially in their tool-calling abilities). This single optimization focus has pushed us from workflows to agents. We believe future models will be trained to solve the current pain points of agent developers. Every model is ultimately consumed by a harness, so models should evolve in service of that harness. We hope to see models improve in high-recall summarization (for context compression), tool-calling reliability, and concision in writing.

Similarly, tools should evolve to support LLMs and widely adopted agent harnesses. The best tools should perform some context engineering on the tool side, abstracted away from the agent. They should return only the most relevant data instead of dumping large volumes of tokens into the context window. As a tool provider, we’ve invested heavily in our advanced search feature, which has context engineering baked in. This in turn lowers hallucinations and latency for the downstream agent processes.

To build agents that improve over time, we followed a few guiding principles:.

Industry observers note that long-horizon research tasks expose a fundamental challenge in current agent design: the task of maintaining a clean, optimized context window over time. If curating context is not a task the engineer pays close attention to, the agent is almost destined for failure. The following outlines our thinking around this concept within the deep research domain.

Sources indicate that using Tavily’s Advanced Search is the natural first step to take in overcoming this challenge, in that it abstracts away the processing of raw web content and returns only the most relevant content chunks from each source. In leveraging this functionality, we let Tavily Search do the heavy lifting and allow Tavily Research to reap the benefit, gathering the most valuable content in a latency-efficient manner.

Sources indicate that ensuring that the agent does not overfit to a single research thread is the next step towards an effective context-gathering pipeline. It is in this regard that global state persistence and source deduplication is paramount, and in our case, it helps threefold:.

At Tavily, interacting with the web is our bread and butter. Architecting a refined web-retrieval system engineered for deep research was a foundational building block for our deep research agent design as a whole.

Industry observers note that humans research in an inherently unstructured, iterative way. We start by defining the task: what we’re trying to accomplish and what information we need. We next gather data from our sources, extracting the key insights and holding them in short-term memory, letting these distilled thoughts guide our subsequent actions.

This cycle repeats: collect information, distill it, decide what to do next. Only once we’ve gathered enough understanding to produce the final deliverable do we return to the original sources, using them as references to assemble the finished product.

We believe that deep research agents should be designed in a similar manner, in that tool outputs should be distilled into reflections, and only the set of past reflections should be used as context for your tool caller. Similar to humans, it is only at the point when your agent begins to prepare the final deliverable that you must provide the raw information as context, so as to ensure there is no information loss.

This approach differs from traditional context structuring in a ReAct agent-based architecture. Typically, tool calls and outputs are propagated through the tool calling loop, with previously retrieved/generated tokens being persisted in the context window on each subsequent iteration. This pattern can be seen in LangChain’s Open Deep Research agent implementation, and from a token consumption perspective, it can be modeled by the following quadratic series, where n n n is the amount of tokens the tool calling model is invoked with on each tool calling iteration, and m m m is the number of tool calling iterations.

n+2n+3n+⋯+mn  =  n⋅m(m+1)2n + 2n + 3n + \cdots + mn \;=\; n \cdot \frac{m(m+1)}{2}n+2n+3n+⋯+mn=n⋅2m(m+1)​.

Contrarily, our proposed method of context engineering removes this token propagation (as the knowledge distillations, even when aggregated, are negligible when compared to the quantity of tokens gathered from web) and can be modeled by the following linear series.

n+n+n+⋯+n  =  nmn + n + n + \cdots + n \;=\; nmn+n+n+⋯+n=nm.

When comparing the two approaches, tokens are saved on a per-agent basis by a factor of m+12 \frac{m+1}{2} 2m+1​, and when extrapolating this over a multi-agent system and with consumption at scale, the absolute value of tokens saved becomes even more significant.

Through this methodology, we were able to reduce token consumption by 66% (when compared to Open Deep Research) while achieving SOTA on DeepResearch Bench – the intersection of quality and efficiency in full effect.

It has been revealed that building production-grade agents is a balancing act. We leaned into autonomy to maximize performance and quality, while still meeting strict requirements for latency, cost, and reliability.

LLMs are inherently non-deterministic, and we found that giving them guard-railed freedom to reason and iterate produces the strongest results. Autonomy, when gone wrong, can cause agent behavior to go off track. Tools can be called incorrectly, LLMs can overfit to a subtopic, and expected reasoning patterns may break. No single safeguard will catch all of these issues.

Industry observers note that A shift in engineering mindset is required: treat failure modes as core design considerations, not afterthoughts. Simple guardrails like tool-call retries or model cascades help, but proactively anticipating anomalies, reinforcing proper patterns in prompting and edge-case testing is what enables production-grade, long-running agents.

In a recent development, from our experience, it’s better to expose a small, essential toolset to the agent rather than a large, complex one. We were tempted to over-engineer by adding many tools that seemed useful in theory, but in practice this created new failure modes and made it harder for LLMs to consistently choose the right tool and iterate effectively.

It has been revealed that we used evals to steer our development process but also recognize their shortcomings. LLM-as-a-judge evals are difficult to trust: current models are non‑deterministic, uninterpretable in their reasoning, and can turn into bottlenecks, especially for long‑running agents where a single experiment can take days to complete.

According to recent reports, rather than optimizing for benchmark scores, we optimized for directional feedback. The core question was always: did this change make the agent more reliable and more useful in practice? Evals became a tool for validating that direction, not the optimization target. Intuition and careful agent‑trace monitoring consistently provided higher‑signal feedback than any single eval score. Overall, the best outcome is rarely the highest numerical score. For production systems, improvements like reduced token usage, reliability, lower latency, and fewer failures are more valuable than a one‑point bump on an eval.

What is r in your solution ? Is it a scratch pad that is updated in the LLM context between each round of research ?

r in the solution is the research insight from previous tool call.

A great insight on getting more by doing less.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Moon is now a few days past its First Quarter phase, and we're well into the Waxing Gibbous stage, which means each night, a little more of its surface is illuminated. This pattern will continue until we reach the Full Moon.

As of Friday, Nov. 20, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Gibbous phase, with 77% of its surface visible.

If you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Serenitatis and Tranquillitatis, as well as the Kepler Crater. With binoculars, you'll also see the Posidonius Crater, the Clavius Crater, and the Mare Nectaris. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 11, 14, and 17 landing spots.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

It has been revealed that according to NASA, the Moon goes through a complete cycle of phases roughly every 29.5 days. As it orbits Earth, the portion of its sunlit surface visible to us changes, giving rise to the different lunar phases. The cycle begins with a New Moon, progresses to a Full Moon, and then gradually returns to a New Moon before starting all over again.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere).

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

Continuous batching from first principles

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: in this blog post, starting from attention mechanisms and KV caching, we derive continuous batching by optimizing for throughput.
  • If you've ever used Qwen, Claude, or any other AI chatbot, you've probably noticed something: it takes a while for the first word of the response to appear, and then words appear one-by-one on your screen with (hopefully) a regular and fast-paced frequency.
  • This generation process is computationally expensive: it requires passing the input through billions of parameters for each token generated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: in this blog post, starting from attention mechanisms and KV caching, we derive continuous batching by optimizing for throughput.

If you've ever used Qwen, Claude, or any other AI chatbot, you've probably noticed something: it takes a while for the first word of the response to appear, and then words appear one-by-one on your screen with (hopefully) a regular and fast-paced frequency. That's because at the heart of it, all LLMs are just fancy next token predictors. An LLM first processes your entire prompt to produce one fresh token. Then it keeps adding tokens one by one, each time reading everything that came before, until it decides generation is over.

This generation process is computationally expensive: it requires passing the input through billions of parameters for each token generated. To make these models practical for real-world applications, particularly when serving many users simultaneously, researchers and engineers have developed a range of efficient inference techniques.One of the most impactful optimizations is continuous batching, which attempts to maximize performance by processing multiple conversations in parallel and swapping them out when they are done.

To understand how continuous batching works and why it's so effective in high-load serving scenarios, we'll build up from the fundamentals of how LLMs process tokens.

The attention mechanism is the central piece of how LLMs work. A language model processes text by breaking it down into pieces that we call tokens. We can conceptually think of "tokens" as "words", but sometimes a word might be composed of several tokens. For each token sequence, the network computes a prediction of what the next token should be.

Many operations in the network are token-wise: each token is processed independently, and the output for a given token depends only on that token's content, not on any other tokens in the sequence. Operations like this include layer normalization or matrix multiplication. However, to create connections between words in a sentence, we need operations where tokens can influence each other.

It has been revealed that this is where attention comes in. Attention layers are the only place where different tokens interact with each other. Understanding how a network connects tokens together means understanding attention.

Let's see how this works in practice, in the case where there is only one input prompt.

Recent findings suggest that consider the initial prompt I am sure this project, tokenized as 7 tokens: [, I, am, sure, this, pro, ject]. The , or "Beginning of Sequence", is a special token we add at the start of the prompt to tell the language model that a fresh conversation starts here.

Sources indicate that each token is represented inside the network with a vector of length d (the hidden dimension). Therefore, the seven incoming tokens form a tensor xxx with shape [1,7,d]\left[1, 7, d \right][1,7,d]. 1 is the number of sequences, or batch size, which is just one in our case. 7 is the sequence length, and d is the hidden dimension, or the size of each token representation. Going forward, we'll use nnn instead of 7 as the sequence length.

Industry observers note that input tensor x x x is then projected by three matrices: the query projection Wq W_q Wq​, the key projection Wk W_k Wk​ and the value projection Wv W_v Wv​. This produces three tensors Q Q Q, K K K and V V V, all of shape [1,n,A] \left[1, n , A \right] [1,n,A], where A A A is the dimension of the attention head. We call them the query, key and value states, respectively. This is represented on the left in the figure below.

According to recent reports, next, tensors Q Q Q and K K K are multiplied together to measure similarity between tokens, producing a tensor of shape [1,n,n] \left[ 1, n , n \right] [1,n,n]. This is why we say that attention has quadratic complexity in sequence length. Computing QKT QK^T QKT requires O(n2d) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 d \right) O(n2d) operations, so the cost is a square of n n n the sequence length. It is represented on the right in the figure above.

In a recent development, we then apply a boolean attention mask to QKT QK^T QKT to control which tokens can interact, as represented in the figure below. In this figure, the attention mask is a causal mask, meaning each token only interacts with tokens that came before it. This follows the intuition that a cause must come before its consequence, hence the name causal mask. The attention mask is crucial because it dictates all token interactions in the network. Set all attention mask values to False and no token will ever interact with another in the whole network. We'll examine attention masks more closely in a few paragraphs.

It has been revealed that finally, after applying the attention mask, we take a token-wise softmax (which is the same as saying a row-wise softmax) and multiply the result by the value projection V V V to get the output of one attention head, of shape [1,n,A] \left[ 1, n , A \right] [1,n,A]. We offer a visual summary of the whole process in the following figure.

We are going to use a lot of attention visualization in this post, so to simplify things, we are going to condense the figure above just a bit.

Why this matters: In continuous batching, Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V can have different numbers of tokens because, as we'll see, we'll be processing different stages (prefill and decode) at the same time. To make it more general, let's say Q Q Q has shape [1,nQ,A] \left[1, n_Q , A \right] [1,nQ​,A], K K K has shape [1,nK,A] \left[ 1, n_K , A \right] [1,nK​,A], and V V V has shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A].

The attention scores QKT QK^T QKT then have shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​], and the attention mask has the same shape since it's applied point-wise to the scores.

Recent findings suggest that after applying the attention mask and row-wise softmax, we multiply by V V V. Since we're multiplying a matrix of shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​] by one of shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A], the inner dimensions must match: nK=nV n_K = n_V nK​=nV​. This means V V V and K K K always have the same length, so we can simplify our visualizations by only showing K K K.Don't worry if this seems abstract: the figures will make it concrete.

Furthermore, since we know that the attention mask is applied to QKT QK^T QKT, we know they have the same shape. Instead of representing the attention scores, we will represent the attention mask in its place. Finally, since Q Q Q, K K K and V V V are direct projections of x x x, no need to represent x x x. This gives the simplified figure where we only represent Q Q Q, K K K and the attention mask:.

This representation also underlines how we can read an attention mask.

We read the mask row-by-row, which is the same as reading token-by-token: each row corresponds to one token's attention computation. A green square at position (row i, column j) means True: token j can influence token i. A white square means False: no interaction allowed.

For example, look at the third row for token "am". The "I" column is green, so "I" influences the computation of "am". The "pro" column is white, so "pro" doesn't influence "am" . This is causal masking at work: future tokens can't affect past ones.

The last layer of the model outputs a token prediction for each input token. In our context, generating the continuation of a single prompt, we only care about the next token prediction from the last token. The last token is "ject" in the figure above, and the associated prediction is "will".

It has been revealed that the process we just described, where we take an entire input sequence, pass it through multiple attention layers and compute a score for the next token, is called prefill. This is because, as we'll see in a moment, much of the computation we performed can be cached and reused – hence, we are prefilling the cache. Thanks to the use of this cache, sequence generation can proceed using much less compute in a phase called decoding. In the decoding phase, generating one latest token will be much faster than the initial full-sequence computation. Let's see why.

To continue generation, we begin a fresh forward pass, which would naively look like this:.

According to recent reports, to compute the attention scores of the new token, we still need the key and value projections of the previous tokens. So we need to repeat the matrix multiplication of the old tokens (in grey in the figure above) with Wk W_k Wk​ and Wv W_v Wv​ to retrieve a result that was already computed once before. In other terms, we are wasting compute. Let's see how we can avoid that.

Right off the bat, we notice that the last token does not impact the attention calculation of the other tokens:.

This follows the idea of the causal mask: since "will" comes after all previous tokens, it does not change their attention calculation. For text generation, causal attention is by far the most common, so we will focus on that case from now on. Keep in mind that non-causal attention schemes can also be used, especially when dealing with images. Considering we only need the next-token prediction for the "will" token, we can simplify the attention mechanism by only computing the output for this token.

Sources indicate that moreover, we already computed the K K K and V V V states for the tokens "", … , "ject" during the previous forward pass: if they have been stored, we do not need to recompute them again. This is the KV cache: the list of key and value states created during generation. It essentially allows one to reduce the compute cost of generating token n+1 n+1 n+1 from O(n2) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 \right) O(n2) to O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n) by avoiding recomputation of key and value projections, while paying a memory cost of O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n).

In the figure above, only the tokens in white are computed: instead of computing the keys and values for 8 tokens, we compute them for 1. You can see that through KV caching, a lot of compute is saved.You can check this post for more visualizations of KV caching, or this one for a practical implementation example.

Let's be a bit more specific about the cache size, because it's a good opportunity to examine the shapes present in our model. For a model with L \mathcal L L attention layers and H H H attention heads with head dimension A A A, the total cache size needed to store one token will be 2∗L∗AH 2 *\mathcal L * AH 2∗L∗AH with a factor of 2 2 2 to account for both K K K and V V V.For instance, Llama-2-7B with L=32 \mathcal{L}=32 L=32 layers, H=32 H=32 H=32 heads, and A=128 A=128 A=128 requires 2×32×128=8,192 2 \times 32 \times 128 = 8,192 2×32×128=8,192 values per token per layer. With float16 precision, this takes 2AH×2 2AH \times 2 2AH×2 bytes =16 = 16 =16 KB in memory.

KV caching is useful when we want to generate the next token, which is a stage we call decoding. But it can also be useful in the prefill stage, when we process the initial prompt and have many input tokens. Especially when there are large initial prompts that don't fit in GPU memory all at once.

According to recent reports, up till now, we have looked at an example of prefill where we have n=7 n=7 n=7 tokens, but in practice initial prompts can be much longer. For instance, when using Cursor, you can add your repository to the prompt, where it acts as context: this significantly increases the prompt size. In such cases, the memory needed to store the activations for n n n tokens can be larger than the available memory on the GPU. Thus we cannot perform prefill in a single forward pass: we have to split the prefill in chunks. This is called chunked prefill, and it's going to be one of the components needed to enable efficient inference.

In a recent development, let's pretend that the available memory is very constrained, and that we can only pass m=4 m=4 m=4 tokens per forward pass. If we have an initial prompt with n=7 n = 7 n=7 tokens, we need to split it in ⌈n/m⌉=2 \lceil n /m \rceil = 2 ⌈n/m⌉=2 chunks (rounding up 7/4 = 1.75 to 2). We illustrate the example below using the same n n n and m m m notations:.

According to recent reports, we can do that thanks to the KV cache. We store the KV states during the first prefill split, and during the second prefill split, we prepend the stored KV states to the new KV states. We also adapt the attention mask accordingly. Visually, it looks like we split the non-chunked prefill in the middle.

The key insight: cached KV states let us process the prompt incrementally without losing information.

Although we showed here an example where we split the prefill into 2 chunks, chunked prefill can be used to split the prefill in any way we want, adapting flexibly to memory constraints.

We are now finally equipped with all the tools we need to understand Continuous Batching.

In our previous examples we have only considered the case of batch size one, i.e. we only generate tokens for one prompt at a time. In the context of evaluation or model serving, we want to generate tokens for a large number of prompts. To increase the throughput, which is the number of tokens generated per second, the best course of action is to generate tokens in parallel for a batch of several prompts.

To batch prompts together, the naive way is to add an axis to both input tensors: token sequence and attention mask. However, this comes with a constraint on the shape of the inputs: we need all prompts to have the same length, because tensors must be rectangular. To achieve this, we usually add padding on the left so the new token prediction always comes from the rightmost token. We also modify the attention mask of each prompt accordingly, as shown below:.

Recent findings suggest that where the padding tokens are coloured in orange. Then we can perform the forward pass as we used to, with the added dimension of the batch size. This is called batched generation: efficient for same-length prompts, but wasteful when lengths vary.It is illustrated below, through 4 steps of generation: one prefilling step (at the top) and 3 decoding steps (below each "Forward pass" lines).

where means "End Of Sequence", this is a special token to indicate the model has reached the end of generation for the corresponding sequence.

The drawback of batched generation is that if one prompt finishes generation before the other one by generating an token, all further generated tokens are useless. And this goes on until the longest request of the batch finishes. Of course, we can remove the prompts that have reached an token from the batch and save some compute and memory, but saving resources is not the goal here: throughput is.

It has been revealed that instead of just removing the finished prompt from the batch, we can replace it with a prompt that's waiting for generation. We will call this dynamic scheduling, or dynamic batching. Dynamic scheduling is great to maintain throughput while ensuring any token generated by a forward pass is relevant. But because of the way we batched prompts together, it has a major drawback: we need a lot of padding when swapping prompts. That's because the newly-inserted prompt needs to go through prefill while the other prompts are decoding one token at a time. So there is almost as much padding as there are tokens in the newly-inserted prompt.

The problem becomes even worse when batch size increases and initial prompts are long. The padding cost grows quadratically with both batch size and prompt length. If we have a batch of B B B prompts that are in decoding phase and one finishes, dynamically introducing a prompt of n n n initial tokens in the batch requires (n−1)(B−1) (n-1)(B-1) (n−1)(B−1) padding tokens. For instance, with B=8 B=8 B=8 and n=100 n=100 n=100, we'd need 99×7=693 99 \times 7 = 693 99×7=693 padding tokens!

Furthermore, practical optimizations like CUDA graphs or torch.compile require static tensor shapes. This forces us to pad all prompts to a fixed maximum length, dramatically increasing the padding waste.

At this point, our main problem is padding, which is a consequence of the axis we added to batch sentences together. Thus, the ideal would be to get rid of this axis entirely, a radical rethinking of batching. If we do so, the only way to batch prompts together is to concatenate them:.

But we don't want tokens from prompt 0 to interact with the tokens of prompt 1! Luckily for us, we have a way to control how tokens interact with one another: the attention mask. How we do this is displayed below:.

Although we use different tints of green to illustrate the different parts of the attention mask, this is still a boolean mask with only greens for True and white for False. This way of batching prompts together is called ragged batching (because sequence lengths are 'ragged' or uneven), and it offers the benefit of added throughput without introducing the need for padding tokens.

According to recent reports, in the figure above, we use ragged batching to combine two full prompts together, but we can batch as many as memory allows. The only limit is m m m, the number of tokens we can fit in a batch, with m m m depending on the available memory on the GPU.

Ragged batching is one of the key components of continuous batching. To maximize throughput, we can combine prefill and decoding sequences following an algorithm like this:.

Dynamic scheduling is the final piece that contributes to the continuous batching technique: we remove finished prompts from the batch as soon as they are done, and replace them with new chunked prompts that correspond to incoming requests.

This combination of ragged batching and dynamic scheduling is called continuous batching, and it's the technique that powers modern LLM serving systems.

Continuous batching combines three key techniques to maximize throughput in LLM serving:.

According to recent reports, by removing the batch dimension and using attention masks to control token interactions, continuous batching allows mixing prefill and decode phases in the same batch, dramatically improving efficiency for serving multiple requests. This is why services like ChatGPT can handle thousands of concurrent users efficiently.

In the next article in this series, we make continuous batching much more efficient by introducing asynchronous batching. Read it here!If you'd like to see a deep dive on other continuous batching topics, please let us know in the comments!

Recent findings suggest that thanks for the article! I'd like to add one note: the primary reason we need chunked prefill isn't the memory constraint (otherwise we could simply solve it with Flash Attention). The more practical reason is that a long prefill blocks all decode requests in the batch. Chunking it lets decode requests make progress between chunks. Moreover, since prefill chunks make the forward pass compute-bound, decode tokens can piggyback on the same batch at nearly zero marginal cost - they're just extra rows in an already large matmul. This turns memory-bound decode-only batches into better-utilized compute-saturating ones. See the SARATHI paper for details.

Today's NYT Strands hints will be easy if you have a good eye.

Strands, the New York Times' elevated word-search game, requires the player to perform a twist on the classic word search. Words can be made from linked letters — up, down, left, right, or diagonal, but words can also change direction, resulting in quirky shapes and patterns. Every single letter in the grid will be part of an answer. There's always a theme linking every solution, along with the "spangram," a special, word or phrase that sums up that day's theme, and spans the entire grid horizontally or vertically.

By providing an opaque hint and not providing the word list, Strands creates a brain-teasing game that takes a little longer to play than its other games, like Wordle and Connections.

Brennan described parallel scrutiny from multiple congressional committees and federal prosecutors over Nvidia’s role in sending advanced AI chips to China. It has been revealed that brennan also raised the risk of circular financing, describing Nvidia’s use of cash to finance data centers and support demand for its own chips.
